x: World War I (1914–1918) # Causes: rival alliances (Germany and Austria-Hungary vs France, Russia and Britain), an arms race, nationalism and imperial competition. The spark was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 . On the Western Front , trench warfare with machine guns, artillery and poison gas killed millions for a few kilometres of ground (Verdun, the Somme). About 20 million people died. The war destroyed four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, Ottoman) and produced the Russian Revolution (1917) and the League of Nations . India’s role: about 1.3 million Indian soldiers served in France, Mesopotamia, Gallipoli, Egypt and East Africa; around 74,000 died. Indian Victoria Cross recipients included Khudadad Khan . India Gate in Delhi commemorates them. Promises of self-government were broken, fuelling the 1919 protests. Between the wars # The Great Depression (from 1929), resentment of the Versailles Treaty and fear of communism helped fascists take power in Italy (Mussolini, 1922) and Nazis in Germany (Hitler, 1933). Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) and China (1937). World War II (1939–1945) # Main phases - **1939–41:** Germany conquers Poland, France and much of Europe; the Battle of Britain. - **1941:** Germany invades the Soviet Union; Japan attacks **Pearl Harbor**, bringing the USA into the war. - **1942–43:** turning points at **Midway**, **El Alamein** and **Stalingrad**. - **1944:** D-Day landings in Normandy; Soviet advance in the east; **Kohima and Imphal** stop Japan's invasion of India. - **1945:** Germany surrenders (8 May); atomic bombs on **Hiroshima** (6 Aug) and **Nagasaki** (9 Aug); Japan surrenders (15 Aug, signed 2 Sept). About 70–85 million people died, most of them civilians, including about 27 million Soviet citizens and perhaps 15–20 million Chinese. In the Holocaust the Nazis systematically murdered six million Jews , along with Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners and others. India’s role: the British Indian Army grew to 2.5 million , the largest volunteer army in history, fighting in North Africa, Italy and Burma. The Bengal famine of 1943 killed 2–3 million people. Subhas Chandra Bose’s Indian National Army fought alongside Japan. Deadliest conflicts (estimated deaths, millions) World War II World War II 75 m Mongol conquests Mongol conquests 35 m Taiping Rebellion Taiping Rebellion 25 m World War I World War I 20 m Thirty Years' War Thirty Years' War 8 m Partition violence (1947) Partition violence (1947) 1 m Source: Mid-range estimates; Partition estimates range 0.2–2 million After the wars # The United Nations (1945), the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), the Cold War , and a rapid wave of decolonisation , starting with India’s independence in 1947. Sources: Wikipedia: World War I · Wikipedia: World War II · CWGC: India and the World Wars

d: How empires ended after 1945, the Cold War and Non-Alignment, the Green Revolution, the digital age, and the challenges of the 21st century.
x: In 1945 European empires still ruled much of Africa and Asia. Within 30 years almost all colonies were independent, with India and Pakistan (1947) leading the way, followed by Burma and Sri Lanka (1948), Indonesia (1949), Ghana (1957), most of Africa around 1960 , Algeria after a brutal war (1962), and the Portuguese colonies in 1974–75 (India took Goa in 1961 ). The Cold War (1947–1991) # The USA and USSR competed for influence through alliances (NATO, Warsaw Pact), proxy wars (Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan), a nuclear arms race and the space race (Sputnik 1957, Apollo 11 in 1969). India’s Jawaharlal Nehru , Egypt’s Nasser, Yugoslavia’s Tito, Indonesia’s Sukarno and Ghana’s Nkrumah founded the Non-Aligned Movement (Belgrade, 1961). The Cold War ended with the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the dissolution of the USSR (1991) . A transformed world # Population grew from 2.5 billion (1950) to over 8 billion today. Food: the Green Revolution averted famine in Asia. Health: life expectancy worldwide rose from about 46 years (1950) to about 73. Technology: computers, the internet (1969/1989), mobile phones and now AI. India: from the 1951 elections to 1991 liberalisation, the IT boom, Chandrayaan-3 (2023) and becoming the world’s most populous country (2023). World population through history (millions, approx.) 0 2,000 4,000 6,000 8,000 10,000 10000 BCE 3000 BCE 1 CE 1000 1500 1800 1900 1950 2000 2025 10000 BCE: 4 3000 BCE: 45 1 CE: 230 1000: 300 1500: 460 1800: 990 1900: 1,650 1950: 2,500 2000: 6,150 2025: 8,200 Source: HYDE / Our World in Data / UN (rounded) Challenges of the 21st century # Climate change, inequality, pandemics (COVID-19), nuclear proliferation, misinformation and the governance of artificial intelligence. Sources: Wikipedia: Decolonization · Our World in Data: Life expectancy

d: What a day was like for an ordinary person in the Ice Age, a Neolithic village, Harappa, Rome, a medieval village, Mughal Agra and an industrial city: homes, work, clothes, children, health and fun.
x: History often tells of kings and battles. This page is about everybody else. Each era page in the Eras catalog also describes “How people lived”. Era Home Work Clothes Life expectancy at birth Ice Age hunter-gatherer (~20,000 years ago) Caves, hide tents, mammoth-bone huts Hunting, gathering, toolmaking Sewn furs and hides ~30 (many children died; adults could reach 60+) Neolithic farmer (~7000 BCE) Mud-brick or wattle houses Farming, herding, pottery, weaving Wool, flax ~25–30 Harappan city dweller (~2300 BCE) Brick house with a bathroom Farming, crafts, trade Cotton ~30 Roman citizen (~100 CE) Rented flat (insula) or villa Trades, farming, army Wool tunic, toga ~25–30 Medieval European peasant (~1300) One-room cottage shared with animals Field work for the lord Wool, linen ~30 Mughal Agra (~1600) Mud or brick house; havelis for the rich Crafts, trade, farming, court service Cotton, silk for elites ~25–30 Industrial Manchester (~1840) Back-to-back slum housing 12–16 hour factory shifts Cheap cotton ~25–30 in slums Today (2025) Apartments, houses Services, industry, farming Synthetics, cotton ~73 (world), ~72 (India) Low life expectancy mostly reflects very high child mortality : in most pre-modern societies about a quarter of babies died in their first year and nearly half of children before age 15 (Our World in Data). Childhood # Children worked from an early age: herding, carrying water, spinning. Toys appear in every era: Harappan clay carts and whistles, Egyptian dolls, Roman marbles. Schooling was rare: Indian gurukuls and pathshalas , Buddhist monasteries and maktabs / madrasas taught some boys; girls’ education was rarer until the 19th–20th centuries (Savitribai Phule opened a girls’ school in Pune in 1848). Fun and festivals # People played board games (the Royal Game of Ur; India’s chaturanga , ancestor of chess; pachisi , which became Ludo; snakes and ladders, from moksha patam ), told stories, sang and danced, wrestled and raced. Festivals marked harvests and seasons. Health # Without germ theory, infections were the big killers: diarrhoeal diseases, malaria, tuberculosis, smallpox and plague. Yet ancient medicine had real successes: Sushruta’s surgery, Egyptian bone-setting, Chinese and Indian variolation against smallpox. Related: Food through history · Peoples and tribes Sources: Our World in Data: Child and infant mortality · Wikipedia: Life expectancy

d: What people ate from the Ice Age to today: hunter-gatherer diets, the first bread and beer, Roman garum, Indian spices, the Columbian Exchange, famine, and the modern food system.
x: Hunter-gatherers # Ice Age people ate a wide range of foods: mammoth, reindeer, horse, fish, shellfish, birds, eggs, nuts, roots, berries and wild grains. Starch grains on 30,000-year-old grinding stones show they made a kind of flour. Cooking with fire, possibly for a million years, made food easier to digest. The first farmers’ food # Early farmers ate porridge and flatbread made from wheat, barley, millet or rice; pulses ; and dairy once animals were milked (traces of milk fats appear in pots ~9,000 years old). Beer appears in the Near East by ~5,000 years ago and possibly much earlier; wine in Georgia by ~6000 BCE. Ancient cuisines # From Egypt to the Indus to Rome - **Egypt:** bread and beer were wages; onions, garlic, lentils, figs, dates, fish; feasts of goose and beef for the rich. - **Indus:** wheat and barley breads, millets, lentils, peas, sesame oil, dairy, beef and mutton; scientists have found turmeric and ginger residues in Harappan pots at Farmana. - **Vedic India:** barley cakes, milk, curd, ghee, honey; later rice dishes such as *payasa* (kheer). - **China:** millet and rice, soybeans, pork; soy sauce and tofu later; tea from the Han era onward. - **Rome:** wheat porridge, bread, olive oil, wine, *garum* fish sauce; pepper from Kerala. - **Maya and Aztec:** maize tortillas and tamales (with nixtamalisation, soaking maize in lime), beans, squash, chillies, turkey and **chocolate drinks**. - **Inca:** potatoes (freeze-dried as *chuño*), quinoa, maize, llama meat, guinea pig. India’s food story # Indian cuisine grew in layers: native millets, rice, pulses, dairy and spices ( black pepper, cardamom, turmeric, ginger, long pepper ); Persian and Central Asian influences under the Sultanate and Mughals ( biryani, pulao, kebabs, naan, kormas, sherbets ); Portuguese-brought American crops ( chilli, potato, tomato, maize, cashew, papaya, pineapple , groundnut); and British-era tea drinking, which became mass culture only in the 20th century. Traditional texts such as the Manasollasa (12th century, Chalukya king Someshvara III) describe recipes for dosa-like dishes, rice preparations and sweets. Famine and plenty # For most of history, harvest failure meant famine : the Great Famine of Europe (1315–17), Bengal 1770, Ireland 1845–52, India 1876–78, China 1959–61. Today the world produces enough calories for everyone; about 700 million people still go hungry because of poverty and conflict, while more than a billion are obese. Sources: Wikipedia: History of Indian cuisine · Wikipedia: Columbian exchange

d: Ongoing research streams in archaeology and history, with the latest status and sources.
x: Status date: 15 November 2026 . # Stream Status Next milestone 1 Herculaneum scrolls PHerc. 1667 read end to end without being opened (25 June 2026) ~600 scrolls remain unopened 2 Keeladi (Tamil Nadu) 11th phase since 18 Mar 2026: continuous brick structures, drains, 1,300+ artefacts, iron furnace Ancient-DNA papers expected by Dec 2026 3 Indus script Still undeciphered Computational analyses 4 Ancient DNA of South Asia Rakhigarhi (2019); Keeladi, Adichanallur and Sivagalai markers (2026) More genomes 1 · Herculaneum scrolls **Status:** On **25 June 2026** in Naples, the **Vesuvius Challenge** announced that scroll **PHerc. 1667** had been virtually unwrapped and read **from beginning to end**, the first Herculaneum papyrus read in full without being opened. Another scroll was identified as Philodemus, *On Gods*, Book 8. The work used X-ray scans (including ESRF's BM18 beamline) and machine learning, building on Brent Seales's virtual-unwrapping research at the University of Kentucky. The challenge has awarded about **$1.8 million** in prizes since 2023. **Next:** More than **600** Herculaneum scrolls remain unopened. Sources: [Vesuvius Challenge: "We read an entire scroll"](https://scrollprize.org/firstscroll) · [ESRF](https://www.esrf.fr/home/news/general/content-news/general/the-day-the-herculaneum-scrolls-began-speaking-again.html) · [Reuters via Express Tribune](https://tribune.com.pk/story/2615079/researchers-use-ai-to-unlock-the-complete-text-of-burnt-herculaneum-scroll-for-the-first-time) · [Pompeii and Vesuvius](/wiki/events/eruption-of-vesuvius.html) 2 · Keeladi (Tamil Nadu) **Status:** The Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology began the **11th excavation phase** on **18 March 2026**. Excavators exposed continuous brick structures in all nine quadrants, a terracotta pipeline and closed drain, and more than **1,300 artefacts**, including beads, spindle whorls, iron knives and swords, ivory dice and gold ornaments. An **iron-working furnace** was reported in July 2026. Madurai Kamaraj University's ancient-DNA lab has extracted about **75,000 genetic markers** from the Konthagai burial site; results so far show affinity with present-day South Indians and Sri Lankan Tamils, with papers expected by December 2026. Sources: [South First](https://thesouthfirst.com/tamilnadu/keeladi-excavation-unearths-rare-furnace-reinforcing-evidence-of-early-tamil-iron-production/) · [Deccan Herald](https://www.deccanherald.com/amp/story/india/tamil-nadu/75000-markers-decoded-genetic-roots-of-ancient-tamils-unveiled-4099243) · [Sangam-era Tamilakam](/wiki/civilizations/sangam-era-tamilakam.html) 3 · Indus script **Status:** About 400 signs on 4,000+ objects; no bilingual text has been found and inscriptions average only about five signs, so the script remains undeciphered. Sources: [Indus script](/wiki/beliefs/indus-script.html) · [Indus Valley Civilisation](/wiki/ancient/indus-valley-civilisation.html) 4 · Ancient DNA of South Asia **Status:** The Rakhigarhi genome (Shinde et al. 2019) and the 2019 South and Central Asia study (Narasimhan et al.) reshaped understanding of Indian ancestry; Tamil Nadu labs are now analysing Sangam-era burials. Sources: [Research papers](/wiki/papers/index.html)

d: Known from a crushed skull nicknamed Toumaï ('hope of life'), found in 2001 in the Djurab desert of Chad, Sahelanthropus tchadensis lived about 7 million years ago, near the time humans and chimpanzees split. Its brain was chimp-sized (about 360 cm³), but its small canine teeth and a forward-placed foramen magnum (the hole where the spine meets the skull) suggest it may have walked upright. A thigh bone found nearby has fuelled debate. Its location, 2,500 km west of the Rift Valley, showed early hominins were widespread in Africa.

d: Orrorin tugenensis ('original man' in the Tugen language) is known from about 20 fossils found in Kenya's Tugen Hills in 2000, dated to about 6 million years ago. Its thigh bones have a long neck and features suggesting it walked on two legs, while its curved finger bones show it still climbed trees. Its teeth have thick enamel, more human-like than chimp-like. It lived in a mix of forest and open woodland.

d: Found in Ethiopia's Middle Awash and dated to 5.8–5.2 million years ago, Ardipithecus kadabba is known from teeth, jaws, hand and foot bones. A toe bone suggests upright walking. Its canine teeth were somewhat ape-like, rubbing against lower teeth to sharpen themselves. It may be the ancestor of Ardipithecus ramidus.

d: Ardi, a partial female skeleton from Aramis in Ethiopia, about 4.4 million years old, was described in 2009 after 15 years of painstaking work. She stood about 1.2 m and weighed about 50 kg, with a pelvis adapted for upright walking but a grasping, opposable big toe for climbing. Fossil plants and animals around her show she lived in woodland, overturning the idea that bipedalism began on open savanna. Males had small canines, perhaps suggesting less aggressive competition.

d: Living about 4.2–3.8 million years ago in Kenya and Ethiopia, A. anamensis is the earliest known Australopithecus. A nearly complete 3.8-million-year-old skull from Woranso-Mille, Ethiopia (2019) revealed its face. Its leg bones show clear bipedalism. It is probably the ancestor of A. afarensis, though the two may have overlapped.

d: Lucy, discovered in 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia, by Donald Johanson and Tom Gray, is a 40% complete skeleton about 3.2 million years old, named after the Beatles song played in camp. Her species lived from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago, stood 1–1.5 m, and had a brain of about 400–500 cm³. The Laetoli footprints and the 'First Family' fossils show they walked upright and lived in groups; long arms and curved fingers show they still climbed. Cut-marked bones at Dikika suggest they may have used stone to butcher meat.

d: Kenyanthropus platyops ('flat-faced man of Kenya') is known from a 3.5-million-year-old skull found in 2001 at Lomekwi, west of Lake Turkana. Its flat face and small molars distinguish it from Lucy's species, showing early hominin diversity. Some researchers think it made the 3.3-million-year-old Lomekwi stone tools found nearby.

d: The first australopithecine identified, by Raymond Dart in 1925 from the Taung Child skull in South Africa, which revealed that humanity's roots lay in Africa. Living about 3.3–2.1 million years ago, it is also known from Sterkfontein's 'Mrs Ples' and 'Little Foot', a nearly complete skeleton about 3.67 million years old. Brains were about 450 cm³. Damage to the Taung skull's eye sockets shows an eagle killed the child.

d: Discovered in 2008 by nine-year-old Matthew Berger at Malapa, South Africa, A. sediba lived about 2 million years ago. Its skeletons show a mosaic: a small brain (420 cm³) and climbing arms, but a human-like hand with a long thumb and a modern-like pelvis. Some researchers suggested it could be close to the ancestor of Homo.

d: Known from the 'Black Skull' (KNM-WT 17000) found near Lake Turkana in 1985, about 2.5 million years old, P. aethiopicus had a huge sagittal crest for chewing muscles and a projecting face. It is the earliest robust australopithecine and probably the ancestor of P. boisei.

d: Discovered by Mary Leakey at Olduvai Gorge in 1959, 'Nutcracker Man' lived about 2.3–1.2 million years ago in East Africa. Its huge molars and massive jaw muscles were long thought to crack nuts, but chemical studies of its teeth show it ate mostly grasses and sedges. It coexisted with early Homo for about a million years before dying out.

d: 'Handy man', named by Louis Leakey and colleagues in 1964 from Olduvai Gorge fossils, lived about 2.4–1.4 million years ago. Its brain (about 550–700 cm³) was larger than australopithecines', and it is associated with Oldowan stone tools. Its long arms suggest it still climbed. Some scientists think its fossils include more than one species.

d: The 'Turkana Boy', found at Nariokotome, Kenya, in 1984, is the most complete early human skeleton, about 1.5 million years old. He was a youth about 8–12 years old and 1.6 m tall, with long legs and modern body proportions suited to walking and running long distances in heat. Some scientists treat H. ergaster as African Homo erectus. They made Acheulean hand-axes.

Their small brains (546–775 cm³) and great variation suggest early Homo left Africa before big brains and hand-axes. One toothless individual survived years after losing teeth, perhaps with help from others.

d: Homo erectus ('upright man') appeared about 1.9 million years ago in Africa and spread to Georgia, Java ('Java Man', found by Eugène Dubois in 1891), China ('Peking Man' at Zhoukoudian) and India. It had human-like body proportions, a brain of about 600–1,100 cm³, made Acheulean hand-axes and likely controlled fire. It survived in Java until about 110,000 years ago — over 1.5 million years, the longest of any human species.

d: Named from a jaw found near Heidelberg in 1907, H. heidelbergensis lived about 700,000–200,000 years ago in Africa and Europe. With a brain of about 1,100–1,400 cm³, it made hand-axes and wooden spears (Schöningen). It is often considered the ancestor of Neanderthals in Europe and Homo sapiens in Africa. The Narmada skull from India may be related.

Its feet and hands were human-like, but shoulders were adapted to climbing. Researchers controversially argue it buried its dead and engraved cave walls.

d: Homo neanderthalensis lived across Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. Stocky and cold-adapted, they had brains as large as ours (about 1,500 cm³), made Mousterian tools, controlled fire, buried their dead, made jewellery from eagle talons and may have painted in Spanish caves. They interbred with Homo sapiens; most non-Africans carry 1–2% Neanderthal DNA. Svante Pääbo sequenced their genome (Nobel 2022).

A jaw from Tibet (Xiahe) and a molar from Laos confirm their range. Melanesians and Aboriginal Australians carry up to 4–6% Denisovan DNA, and Tibetans inherited a Denisovan gene (EPAS1) that helps at high altitude.

d: Some Homo sapiens reached Arabia and the Levant earlier, but the main dispersal from Africa happened about 70,000–50,000 years ago. Within 20,000 years they reached South Asia, Southeast Asia and Australia; by 45,000 years ago Europe; and by about 20,000–15,000 years ago the Americas. They interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans, and became the only surviving human species.

t: Pangaea and the age of dinosaurs
d: From about 335 to 175 million years ago most land formed one supercontinent, Pangaea, surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean. The Mesozoic Era (252–66 million years ago) — Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous — began after the Great Dying, the worst mass extinction, and saw dinosaurs dominate land, pterosaurs the air and marine reptiles the seas. Mammals appeared about 200 million years ago but stayed small and mostly nocturnal; birds evolved from feathered dinosaurs, and flowering plants spread in the Cretaceous. India drifted north as an island, and the Deccan Traps erupted near the end.
x: Overview # From about 335 to 175 million years ago most land formed one supercontinent, Pangaea, surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean. The Mesozoic Era (252–66 million years ago) — Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous — began after the Great Dying, the worst mass extinction, and saw dinosaurs dominate land, pterosaurs the air and marine reptiles the seas. Mammals appeared about 200 million years ago but stayed small and mostly nocturnal; birds evolved from feathered dinosaurs, and flowering plants spread in the Cretaceous. India drifted north as an island, and the Deccan Traps erupted near the end. How people lived # No humans existed; the ancestors of mammals were shrew-sized creatures living in the shadows of dinosaurs, feeding on insects and seeds at night. What people ate # — Species of the time # Dinosaurs, early mammals, cycads, conifers

d: After the Chicxulub impact 66 million years ago, mammals diversified into the niches left by dinosaurs: early whales evolved in the Tethys Sea near India and Pakistan (Pakicetus), horses, elephants and primates appeared, and grasslands spread as the climate cooled. India collided with Asia, raising the Himalaya and creating the monsoon. Apes evolved in Africa and Eurasia around 25–20 million years ago, and the human line split from chimpanzees about 7 million years ago.

What people ate # — Species of the time # Early whales, horses, primates, grasslands

d: Between about 4.2 and 2 million years ago, Australopithecus species such as anamensis, afarensis (Lucy) and africanus lived in eastern and southern Africa. They walked upright with an arched foot but still had long arms for climbing and ape-sized brains of 400–500 cm³. The Laetoli footprints and Lucy's skeleton (found 1974 at Hadar) are their most famous evidence; some may have used sharp stones to butcher meat. Robust Paranthropus with huge chewing teeth lived alongside early Homo.

What people ate # Fruit, seeds, roots, termites Species of the time # Australopithecus afarensis (‘Lucy’), Paranthropus, giant hyenas

d: The Lower Paleolithic, from the first stone tools 3.3 million years ago to about 300,000 years ago, is the longest chapter of human history. Oldowan choppers gave way to Acheulean hand-axes around 1.76 million years ago, made by Homo erectus, who spread out of Africa to Georgia, Java, China and India (Attirampakkam, about 1.5 million years ago). Control of fire appears by about 1 million years ago (Wonderwerk Cave), and wooden spears at Schöningen show big-game hunting by 300,000 years ago.

d: From about 300,000 to 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals in Europe and western Asia and early Homo sapiens in Africa made tools with the Levallois technique, striking prepared cores to get flakes of a planned shape. Homo sapiens appeared by 315,000 years ago (Jebel Irhoud); Denisovans lived in Asia. People buried their dead, used ochre and shell beads, made glue from birch tar, and spread Out of Africa around 70,000–50,000 years ago, interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans.

How people lived # Groups lived in caves and open camps, hunting deer, bison and horses with hafted spears, gathering plants and shellfish, and caring for injured or elderly members, as Neanderthal skeletons with healed injuries show. What people ate # Hunted large game, shellfish, plants Species of the time # Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo floresiensis, cave bears, woolly rhino

d: Between about 50,000 and 12,000 years ago, Homo sapiens spread across the globe, reaching Australia, Siberia and the Americas. Blade tools, bone needles, spear-throwers, bows and harpoons appeared, along with explosive creativity: cave art at Sulawesi, Chauvet and Lascaux, the Venus figurines, bone flutes and personal ornaments. Neanderthals disappeared around 40,000 years ago, and dogs were domesticated. In India, Bhimbetka's rock shelters contain some of the oldest art.

How people lived # Hunter-gatherers lived in larger, networked bands, sewing fitted clothing, building mammoth-bone huts in Ukraine, trading shells and stone over hundreds of kilometres, and holding feasts and rituals. What people ate # Mammoth, reindeer, horse, fish, wild plants Species of the time # Woolly mammoth, cave lion, Irish elk, giant ground sloth, Megalania

d: Around 26,000–19,000 years ago ice sheets reached their maximum. Sea level was about 120 m lower, opening land bridges like Beringia; much of northern Europe was polar desert and people retreated to southern refugia. Deserts expanded, and in India the Thar was larger and drier. Mammoths, woolly rhinos and reindeer roamed the steppe-tundra.

What people ate # Hunted reindeer, mammoth Species of the time # Mammoths, woolly rhinos, cave bears

d: The Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age), from about 12,000 to the arrival of farming (varying by region), followed the Ice Age. Forests spread over Europe, and people adapted with microliths — tiny flint blades set into arrows and harpoons — fishing and canoes. In India, sites like Bagor, Langhnaj and Sarai Nahar Rai show microlithic hunters and early burials, and Bhimbetka's paintings depict hunting and dancing.

How people lived # Communities gathered seasonally by rivers, lakes and coasts, eating fish, shellfish, deer, nuts and wild grains; some became semi-settled, like the Natufians of the Levant. What people ate # Fish, deer, nuts, wild grain Species of the time # Aurochs, red deer, wild boar

d: Beginning about 10,000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent and independently in China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica, the Andes, Africa and India, people domesticated plants and animals. Wheat, barley, lentils, sheep and goats came first in West Asia; rice and millet in China; maize in Mexico. In South Asia, Mehrgarh (from about 7000 BCE) grew barley and wheat and kept cattle. Farming fed more people, leading to villages, pottery, property and later inequality, though early farmers were often shorter and less healthy than foragers.

What people ate # Wheat, barley, rice, millet, maize, lentils; goats, sheep, cattle, pigs Species of the time # Domestic animals; aurochs (wild cattle) still roam

d: From about 5000 to 3000 BCE (later in some regions), people used copper alongside stone. Copper smelting appeared in Serbia, Iran and Anatolia; Ötzi the Iceman (about 3300 BCE) carried a copper axe. In India, Chalcolithic cultures such as Ahar-Banas, Malwa and Jorwe flourished, and early Harappan villages grew. The wheel, plough and wool sheep spread, and the first towns appeared in Mesopotamia.

What people ate # Grains, dairy, wine Species of the time # Domestic horses (Botai, ~3500 BCE)

d: Bronze — copper alloyed with tin — became widespread from about 3300 BCE in the Near East, Indus Valley and Aegean, and later in China and Europe. Cities, writing, kings, temples, armies and long-distance trade developed: Sumer, Egypt's pyramids, the Indus cities, Shang China and Minoan Crete. Tin had to be traded over long distances, linking civilisations. Horses and chariots spread around 2000 BCE.

Farmers paid taxes in grain, and many worked on state building projects. What people ate # Bread, beer, dates, fish Species of the time # Domestic horses, camels, chickens spread

d: Around 2200 BCE a mega-drought lasting about two centuries affected regions from Egypt to India and China, coinciding with the end of the Akkadian Empire and Egypt's Old Kingdom and stress on the Indus cities. The International Commission on Stratigraphy uses it to mark the start of the Meghalayan Age, named after Mawmluh cave in Meghalaya, whose stalagmites record it.

What people ate # Shortages of grain Species of the time # —

d: Around 1200–1150 BCE, the interconnected world of the eastern Mediterranean fell apart: the Hittite Empire collapsed, Mycenaean palaces burned, Ugarit was destroyed, and Egypt was weakened by the Sea Peoples. Drought, earthquakes, famine, migrations, rebellions and the breakdown of trade networks probably combined in a 'systems collapse'. Writing disappeared in Greece for centuries.

What people ate # Famine Species of the time # —

d: Iron working, harder to master than bronze but using common ore, spread after about 1200 BCE across the Near East and Europe, and independently or earlier in India (iron at sites in the Ganga valley and south India by 1800–1500 BCE) and in Africa (Nok, Meroë). Cheap iron tools and weapons let farmers clear forests and armies equip more soldiers. In India the Iron Age saw the later Vedic period and the rise of the mahajanapadas; in Europe, Celts and the Greek city-states.

What people ate # Grains, olives, wine Species of the time # —

d: The Vedic period (about 1500–500 BCE) is named after the Vedas, composed in Sanskrit by Indo-Aryan-speaking people in the northwest and later the Ganga plain. Early clans herded cattle and fought over pastures; later kingdoms (janapadas) formed, the varna system developed, and the Upanishads explored philosophy. Iron, rice farming and cities emerged by its end.

What people ate # Barley, milk, ghee, later rice Species of the time # Cattle central to wealth

d: Between about 800 and 200 BCE, new philosophies and religions emerged almost simultaneously: the Upanishads, Buddha and Mahavira in India; Confucius and Laozi in China; Zoroaster in Persia; Hebrew prophets; and Greek philosophers from Thales to Aristotle. Karl Jaspers named it the Axial Age. These traditions questioned ritual and emphasised ethics, personal transformation and reason.

What people ate # — Species of the time # —

d: Classical antiquity in the Mediterranean ran from about the 8th century BCE to the 5th century CE — Greece's city-states and philosophers, Alexander's Hellenistic world, and the Roman Republic and Empire. It produced democracy, theatre, history, geometry, Roman law, roads and concrete, and the spread of Christianity. It ended with the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

What people ate # Bread, olive oil, wine, garum fish sauce Species of the time # Lions and elephants captured for arenas

d: From 322 BCE the Mauryas united most of India; after 185 BCE the Shungas, Satavahanas, Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushans ruled different regions. Trade with Rome boomed, Gandhara and Mathura art flourished, Buddhism spread, and the Sangam poets wrote in Tamil.

How people lived # Cities like Pataliputra, Taxila and Ujjain hosted guilds of merchants and artisans; farmers grew rice, wheat and cotton; and monasteries became centres of learning. What people ate # Rice, wheat, pulses, spices Species of the time # War elephants

d: From about 200 BCE to 200 CE, the Han dynasty in China and the Roman Empire were the world's two great empires, each with about 60 million people. The Silk Road linked them through Parthia and the Kushans. Both built roads, standardised coins and administered vast territories, and both fell into crisis in the 3rd century.

How people lived # Peasants paid taxes in grain and labour; soldiers guarded frontiers; and silk, spices and glass moved across Eurasia. What people ate # Millet, rice, wheat Species of the time # —

d: From about 320 to 550 CE, the Gupta Empire under Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and Chandragupta II ruled north India from Pataliputra and Ujjain. It was a classical age of Sanskrit literature (Kalidasa's Shakuntala and Meghaduta), mathematics and astronomy (Aryabhata's place-value system and rotating Earth), the codification of Puranas and law books, early stone temples such as Deogarh, and the paintings of Ajanta under the allied Vakatakas. Nalanda was founded around 427. Huna invasions and the rise of feudatories ended Gupta power by the mid-6th century.

Guilds of merchants and artisans were powerful, gold coins circulated, and kings increasingly granted land to Brahmins and temples. What people ate # Rice, wheat, sugar Species of the time # —

d: Three major volcanic eruptions in 536, 540 and 547 CE cooled the Northern Hemisphere by up to 2 °C for over a century (until about 660), according to tree rings. Crop failures, the Plague of Justinian from 541 and migrations of steppe peoples like the Avars coincided. The Byzantine and Sasanian empires were weakened just before the Arab conquests, and the Chinese Sui and Tang dynasties rose from the turmoil.

d: From about 500 to 1000 CE, the Western Roman Empire gave way to Germanic kingdoms — Franks, Visigoths, Anglo-Saxons — while the Byzantine Empire continued in the east. Islam rose and spread from Spain to Sindh; Tang China flourished; in India, the Chalukyas, Pallavas, Rashtrakutas, Palas and Pratiharas competed, and temple architecture blossomed. The Vikings raided Europe from 793, and Charlemagne briefly revived a western empire.

What people ate # Bread, porridge, ale Species of the time # —

d: From roughly the 8th to the 13th century, scholars in Baghdad's House of Wisdom, Cairo, Córdoba, Bukhara and Samarkand translated and expanded Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge. Al-Khwarizmi founded algebra and spread Indian numerals; Ibn al-Haytham pioneered optics and experimental method; Ibn Sina wrote the Canon of Medicine; al-Biruni studied India; astronomers built observatories. Paper, learned from China, made books cheap. The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 is often seen as its end.

What people ate # Rice, citrus, sugar, coffee (later) Species of the time # —

d: From about 950 to 1250, the North Atlantic and parts of the world were warmer. Vikings settled Iceland and Greenland and reached North America; Europe's population roughly doubled; vineyards grew in England. Elsewhere it brought droughts, contributing to the decline of the Ancestral Puebloans and possibly Angkor's water stress later.

d: From the 9th to the 13th centuries, the Cholas ruled south India and Sri Lanka and raided Southeast Asia, building the Brihadeeswarar temple. The Palas in Bengal patronised Buddhist universities, Rajputs ruled the north, and temple building reached its peak at Khajuraho, Konark and Bhubaneswar. Mahmud of Ghazni's raids and the Ghurid conquest led to the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.

d: In the 13th and 14th centuries the Mongol Empire, founded by Genghis Khan, became the largest contiguous land empire, stretching from Korea to Hungary. Conquests killed millions, but the Pax Mongolica revived the Silk Road, allowing Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta to travel, and spreading gunpowder, printing and paper money west. The Delhi Sultanate repelled Mongol invasions. It split into the Yuan, Ilkhanate, Chagatai and Golden Horde.

What people ate # Meat, dairy, kumis Species of the time # Mongol horses

d: The Black Death, caused by Yersinia pestis, reached Crimea in 1346 and swept through the Middle East, North Africa and Europe by 1353, killing about a third to half of Europe's people and many elsewhere. Labour shortages raised wages and weakened serfdom; peasants rebelled (England 1381); Jews were persecuted; art became preoccupied with death. Plague recurred for centuries.

d: From about 1300 to 1850, global temperatures fell slightly, with colder periods in the 1600s linked to low solar activity and volcanic eruptions. Glaciers advanced in the Alps, the Thames froze for 'frost fairs', and crop failures contributed to famines and revolts in the 17th-century 'General Crisis' — including the fall of the Ming and the Thirty Years' War. India and China suffered droughts and famines.

d: From 1206 to 1526, the Delhi Sultanate's Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties ruled north India, repelling the Mongols. In the south, Vijayanagara (1336–1646) and the Bahmani Sultanate competed. Indo-Islamic architecture, the Persian wheel, Urdu–Hindavi, and the Bhakti and Sufi movements developed.

d: Beginning in 14th-century Florence and spreading across Europe by the 16th, the Renaissance revived classical Greek and Roman learning. Greek scholars fleeing Constantinople, the printing press and wealthy patrons like the Medici fuelled art (Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael), literature (Petrarch, Shakespeare), and science (Copernicus, Vesalius). Humanism focused on human potential.

d: From the 15th to 17th centuries, Portuguese and Spanish sailors, followed by the Dutch, English and French, used caravels, the compass and astrolabe to reach Africa, India, the Americas and the Pacific. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (1498), Columbus the Caribbean (1492), and Magellan's crew circled the globe (1519–22). It began colonial empires, the Columbian Exchange and the Atlantic slave trade.

d: From Babur's victory at Panipat in 1526 to the deposition of Bahadur Shah Zafar in 1857, the Mughals ruled much of South Asia, reaching their height under Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb. They built the Taj Mahal, Red Fort and Fatehpur Sikri, developed the mansabdari system and produced 25% of world manufacturing output. After 1707 the empire fragmented into successor states.

d: From the 16th to the mid-20th century, European powers colonised the Americas, much of Asia and nearly all of Africa. Colonial rule extracted resources and labour, imposed borders, spread European languages and Christianity, and caused famines and genocides, while also introducing railways and modern education. Independence movements ended most empires after 1945.

d: From Copernicus (1543) to Newton's Principia (1687), observation and mathematics transformed science; the Enlightenment of the 18th century applied reason to politics and society. Thinkers like Locke, Voltaire, Rousseau and Kant argued for rights, tolerance and limits on power, inspiring the American and French Revolutions.

d: Beginning in Britain around 1760, machines, coal and steam power transformed textiles, iron and transport, spreading to Europe, the US and Japan. Railways, factories and cities grew rapidly. Cheap British textiles undercut Indian handloom weavers, contributing to deindustrialisation. It brought great wealth but also child labour, pollution and slums.

d: From 1858, after the 1857 rebellion, to 1947, India was ruled by the British Crown through a Viceroy. Railways, telegraphs, canals and universities were built, but famines killed tens of millions and wealth drained to Britain. The national movement grew from the Congress (1885) to Gandhi's mass campaigns and independence with Partition.

d: From 1914 to 1945, two world wars killed about 100 million people. Empires collapsed, the Russian Revolution created the Soviet Union, fascism rose in Italy and Germany, the Great Depression struck, and the Holocaust murdered six million Jews. The atomic bomb ended the second war.

d: From 1947 to 1991 the US and the Soviet Union competed without direct war, through an arms race, the space race and proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan. Decolonisation created new nations; India led the Non-Aligned Movement. It ended with the collapse of the USSR.

India became a major IT services centre, and digital payments reached hundreds of millions. Artificial intelligence is the latest phase.

d: Scientists proposed the Anthropocene as a new epoch defined by human impact on Earth: climate change from greenhouse gases, plastic and radioactive markers in sediments, species extinctions and altered landscapes. In 2024 geologists voted not to formally adopt it as an epoch, but the term is widely used.

d: The first civilisation with cities and writing.
x: Overview # The first civilisation with cities and writing. Government and society # Each Sumerian city-state (Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish, Nippur, Eridu) was independent. Early power lay with the temple, whose priests managed land, herds and storehouses; by about 2800 BCE war leaders (lugal, ‘big man’) became hereditary kings who built palaces beside the temples. Assemblies of elders and citizens may have advised rulers in early times. Society ranged from the royal family and priests through scribes, merchants and craftsmen to farmers, labourers on temple estates and enslaved war captives. Reforms by Urukagina of Lagash (~2350 BCE) tried to curb officials’ abuses, one of the first recorded attempts at social justice. How people lived # Most Sumerians were farmers who worked irrigated barley fields owned by temples, palaces or families, paid in rations of barley, oil and wool; city life was crowded in mud-brick houses around a central courtyard. Scribes trained for years in schools called edubba (‘tablet houses’), where boys copied texts and were beaten for mistakes. Women could own property, run businesses and serve as priestesses, and children helped in fields and workshops. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Each city belonged to a god — Enlil at Nippur, Inanna at Uruk, Nanna at Ur — whose ziggurat temple dominated the skyline. Sumerians believed humans were created to serve the gods and that the dead went to a gloomy underworld. They invented cuneiform, the sexagesimal number system (behind our 60-minute hour), and wrote proverbs, lullabies, the Gilgamesh poems and the Lament for Ur. Food # Barley was the staple: baked as flat bread and, above all, brewed into thick beer drunk through straws, with temple workers paid daily rations of bread and beer. Dates, onions, garlic, lentils, chickpeas, fish from canals and marshes, and mutton for the wealthy filled out the diet; the Yale culinary tablets (~1750 BCE, Babylonian) preserve the oldest written recipes, mostly stews. Construction and architecture # Sumerians built almost entirely in mud brick, since stone and timber were scarce. Temples stood on raised platforms that grew into stepped ziggurats, such as the Ziggurat of Ur (~2100 BCE), with a shrine on top where the city god lived. Cities had thick walls (Uruk’s were about 9 km long), narrow lanes, courtyard houses, canals, harbours and palaces. They used the arch, the vault and the dome long before the Romans, and decorated walls with cone mosaics. Technology and knowledge # Sumer produced many of civilisation’s foundational inventions: cuneiform writing (from ~3200 BCE, first for accounts), the potter’s wheel and the wheeled cart, the seed plough, large-scale irrigation canals and dykes, bronze casting, a sexagesimal (base-60) number system that survives in our 60-minute hour and 360° circle, standard weights and measures, and early astronomy tracking lunar months. d: Collapsed around the 4.2-kiloyear drought.
x: Overview # Collapsed around the 4.2-kiloyear drought. Government and society # Sargon created the first territorial empire, ruling diverse city-states through loyal Akkadian governors and a standing army of perhaps 5,400 men who ‘ate bread daily before him’. His grandson Naram-Sin went further, declaring himself a living god and ‘king of the four quarters’ of the world. Akkadian, a Semitic language, became the language of government beside Sumerian. How people lived # Life continued much as in Sumer, with farmers growing barley along canals, but now under Akkadian governors and a standing army; for the first time an empire collected tribute from across Mesopotamia. Akkadian, a Semitic language, became the language of government and later of diplomacy across the Near East. Long-distance trade reached Magan (Oman) and Meluhha (the Indus). Culture, beliefs and heritage # Akkadian kings blended Sumerian and Semitic religion; Naram-Sin even declared himself a god, shown with a horned crown on his victory stele. Enheduanna’s hymns to Inanna united the two traditions. Royal art became more naturalistic, as in the bronze head thought to be Sargon. Food # Like Sumer, Akkad lived on irrigated barley and emmer, turned into bread and beer, with dates, sesame oil, onions and fish. State workshops issued standard rations, and sheep and goats supplied wool, milk and meat for feasts. Construction and architecture # Akkadian kings built palaces and temples in their capital Akkad, which archaeologists have never found. Their art is known from victory monuments such as the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin, showing the king climbing a mountain above his defeated enemies, and from a bronze head possibly of Sargon. Technology and knowledge # The empire standardised weights and measures and the calendar across Mesopotamia, built roads and a courier system, and developed a bureaucracy that recorded taxes and trade on clay tablets. Akkadian cuneiform became the script used across the Near East for 2,000 years. How it rose # Sargon, according to legend a foundling raised by a gardener who became cupbearer to the king of Kish, seized power around 2334 BCE, defeated Lugalzagesi of Uruk and conquered all of Sumer, then campaigned from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean and Anatolia. He controlled trade routes for metals, timber and stone. How it declined or fell # Revolts broke out under almost every ruler. Around 2200–2150 BCE a severe drought, the 4.2-kiloyear event, ruined harvests in northern Mesopotamia; settlements like Tell Leilan were abandoned. Gutian highlanders from the Zagros overran the weakened state, and Akkad collapsed into a period of chaos remembered in the poem ‘The Curse of Akkad’. Legacy # The Akkadian Empire became the model of universal kingship for later Mesopotamian, Persian and even Roman rulers. Akkadian remained the international diplomatic language of the Bronze Age, used in letters between Egypt, the Hitti

d: Babylonian astronomers tracked planets and eclipses for centuries.
x: Overview # Babylonian astronomers tracked planets and eclipses for centuries. Government and society # Babylon’s kings ruled with governors, judges and scribes. Hammurabi (r. ~1792–1750 BCE) united Mesopotamia and published 282 laws on a stele, covering trade, property, family, wages and crime, with punishments that depended on social class (nobles, commoners and slaves). The Neo-Babylonian kings (626–539 BCE), notably Nebuchadnezzar II, ruled a large empire through provincial governors and deportations. How people lived # Babylonians lived in mud-brick houses around courtyards; merchants, scribes and craftsmen formed a middle class, and slavery existed for debt and war captives. Hammurabi’s Code regulated wages, doctors’ fees, rents, marriage and divorce, showing a complex urban economy. Women could own property, and contracts were recorded on clay. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Marduk, patron god of Babylon, became king of the gods in the creation epic Enuma Elish, recited at the New Year (Akitu) festival. Babylonian astronomers kept records of the planets for centuries, predicting eclipses, and developed the zodiac. Their mathematics solved quadratic equations and approximated √2. Food # Babylonians ate barley bread, beer, dates, lentils, onions, leeks and garlic, cooked with sesame oil; the Yale tablets record some 25 stews of lamb, pigeon and vegetables seasoned with mint and coriander. Fish and dates were cheap staples, and the Code of Hammurabi even regulated beer sellers. Construction and architecture # Babylon became one of the largest cities in the world, with double walls, the blue glazed-brick Ishtar Gate decorated with dragons and bulls, the Processional Way, the great ziggurat Etemenanki (probably the origin of the Tower of Babel story) and Esagila, temple of Marduk. The Hanging Gardens, one of the Seven Wonders, may have been in Babylon or, as some historians argue, in Nineveh. Technology and knowledge # Babylonian scholars developed advanced mathematics, including place-value notation in base 60, solutions to quadratic equations and approximations of √2 accurate to six decimal places (tablet YBC 7289). Astronomers kept nightly diaries for over 600 years and could predict lunar eclipses and planetary positions, knowledge later used by Greek and Indian astronomers. They also produced the zodiac. How it rose # Babylon was a minor town until the Amorite king Hammurabi conquered rival cities such as Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari in the 18th century BCE. Its central position on the Euphrates and control of trade made it the cultural capital of Mesopotamia for over a thousand years. How it declined or fell # The first Babylonian dynasty ended when the Hittite king Mursili I sacked the city in 1595 BCE; Kassites then ruled for four centuries. After Assyrian domination, the Neo-Babylonian Empire rose under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar, but in 539 BCE Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon, reportedly without a battle, af

d: Ashurbanipal's library preserved thousands of clay tablets.
x: Overview # Ashurbanipal’s library preserved thousands of clay tablets. Government and society # Assyrian kings were the god Ashur’s earthly representatives and led annual military campaigns. The empire was divided into provinces governed by royal appointees, with vassal kings paying tribute. Assyrians used mass deportation, moving perhaps 4.5 million people over three centuries, to break local resistance and supply labour. A network of royal roads and relay posts carried messages, letting kings track distant provinces. How people lived # Assyrians were farmers and herders in the rain-fed north, but the state was built for war: men served in campaigns, and conquered peoples were deported in huge numbers — perhaps 4.5 million over three centuries — to work on royal projects. Merchants of Ashur ran trading colonies in Anatolia as early as 1900 BCE, recorded in thousands of tablets at Kanesh. Palaces were filled with scribes, soldiers and craftsmen. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ashur, the national god, was worshipped as the source of royal power. Kings decorated palaces at Nimrud and Nineveh with stone reliefs of lion hunts and sieges, and winged human-headed bulls (lamassu) guarded gateways. Ashurbanipal assembled the first great library, with tens of thousands of tablets including the Epic of Gilgamesh. Food # Assyrians farmed barley and wheat in rain-watered northern Mesopotamia and kept sheep and cattle. Ashurnasirpal II’s banquet stele boasts of feeding 69,574 guests with oxen, sheep, deer, fowl, fish, bread, beer and 10,000 skins of wine. Construction and architecture # Kings built grand capitals: Assur, Nimrud (Kalhu), Dur-Sharrukin (Khorsabad) and Nineveh. Palaces were guarded by colossal winged human-headed bulls (lamassu) and lined with carved stone reliefs of battles, sieges, hunts and tribute. Sennacherib built an aqueduct at Jerwan and gardens at Nineveh watered by canals. Technology and knowledge # Assyria was the first empire to equip mass armies with iron weapons. Its engineers built siege towers, battering rams and ramps, and organised cavalry and logistics on a new scale. Ashurbanipal’s library at Nineveh collected about 30,000 clay tablets on medicine, omens, literature and science, preserving the Epic of Gilgamesh. How it rose # Assur was a trading city whose merchants ran a famous network into Anatolia (the Kültepe tablets, ~1900 BCE). After centuries of ups and downs, the Neo-Assyrian Empire expanded from 911 BCE under kings such as Ashurnasirpal II, Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II and Sennacherib, eventually ruling from Egypt to western Iran. How it declined or fell # After Ashurbanipal’s death (~631 BCE), civil war between his sons weakened the empire. Babylonians under Nabopolassar and the Medes under Cyaxares rebelled and sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE; the last Assyrian army was defeated at Harran (609) and Carchemish (605). A drought may also have contributed. Legacy # Assyria created the model

d: Lasted three millennia, ending with Cleopatra and Rome.
x: Overview # Lasted three millennia, ending with Cleopatra and Rome. Government and society # The pharaoh was a living god, son of Ra, responsible for maat, the cosmic order. Beneath him the vizier ran the government, with officials for treasury, granaries and public works, and nomarchs governing the 42 provinces (nomes). Priests controlled enormous temple estates. Scribes, trained for years, kept records of taxes, harvests and labour. Women could own property, run businesses and sue in court, more rights than in most ancient societies. How people lived # About 80% of Egyptians were farmers whose lives followed the Nile’s three seasons: inundation, growing and harvest; during the flood many worked on royal building projects for wages in bread and beer. Families lived in mud-brick houses, and women could own property, divorce and run businesses. Scribes, priests, craftsmen and soldiers formed specialised classes; workers at Deir el-Medina even went on strike over late rations around 1157 BCE. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Egyptians worshipped hundreds of gods such as Ra, Osiris, Isis and Horus, with the pharaoh as a living god. They believed in an afterlife judged by the weighing of the heart, which led to mummification, tombs and the Book of the Dead. Hieroglyphs, monumental art with strict conventions, music, board games like senet, and festivals like Opet filled their culture. Food # Bread and beer made from emmer and barley were so basic that wages were paid in them; onions, garlic, lentils, chickpeas, lettuce and Nile fish were everyday foods. The rich ate beef, roast fowl, figs, pomegranates, honey cakes and wine; tomb paintings show bakeries and breweries in detail. Construction and architecture # Egyptians built in stone for eternity: the Step Pyramid of Djoser (~2670 BCE, designed by Imhotep), the Great Pyramid of Giza (~2560 BCE, 146 m tall), the Sphinx, the temples of Karnak and Luxor with their forests of columns, Hatshepsut’s terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari, the rock-cut tombs of the Valley of the Kings and Ramesses II’s Abu Simbel. Ordinary homes were mud brick. Technology and knowledge # Egypt developed hieroglyphic writing and papyrus paper, the 365-day calendar based on the Nile and the star Sirius, advanced surveying and geometry for re-marking fields after floods, medicine described in the Edwin Smith and Ebers papyri (including surgery and hundreds of remedies), mummification, glass and faience, sails and large ships, the shaduf for lifting water, and remarkable stone-cutting and transport techniques. How it rose # Farmers and herders settled the Nile valley as the Sahara dried after about 5000 BCE. Chiefdoms in Upper and Lower Egypt competed until King Narmer (or Menes) united them around 3100 BCE. The Nile’s predictable flood gave reliable harvests; the desert protected Egypt from invasion; and the river was a highway for trade and administration. How it declined or fell # Egypt’s 3,000-year h

d: Fell in the Bronze Age collapse.
x: Overview # Fell in the Bronze Age collapse. Government and society # The Hittite great king ruled from Hattusa with a council of nobles (the panku), managed vassal kings by written treaties sworn before gods, and had a law code with fines rather than mutilation for many crimes. How people lived # Hittite society included farmers working land for the king or temples, chariot warriors, scribes and many deportees from conquered lands. Their laws, unusually, often prescribed compensation rather than death or mutilation. Women, especially queens such as Puduhepa, had significant power, including in diplomacy. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Hittites called themselves the land of ‘a thousand gods’, absorbing deities of conquered peoples; the storm god Tarhunt and the sun goddess of Arinna were the chief deities. Their archives at Hattusa contain treaties, prayers and rituals in many languages, and the rock sanctuary of Yazılıkaya shows a procession of gods. Food # Hittites ate barley and emmer bread in dozens of named shapes, porridge, lentils, figs, grapes, honey and cheese. Beer and wine were offered to gods, and royal storage pits at Hattusa could hold grain for thousands of people for a year. Construction and architecture # Hattusa had 6 km of walls with the Lion Gate, the Yazılıkaya rock sanctuary with carved gods, and huge granaries. Technology and knowledge # Early iron working, light three-man chariots, and archives of thousands of cuneiform tablets in several languages. How it rose # Hattusili I unified central Anatolia around 1650 BCE; Mursili I sacked Babylon in 1595 BCE; Suppiluliuma I made the Hittites a superpower rivalling Egypt. How it declined or fell # Around 1180 BCE drought, famine, attacks by the Kaska and Sea Peoples and internal strife led to the abandonment of Hattusa during the Bronze Age collapse. Legacy # The Treaty of Kadesh (~1259 BCE) with Ramesses II is the oldest known peace treaty; Hittite is the oldest written Indo-European language.

d: Their alphabet is the ancestor of Greek, Latin and Arabic scripts.
x: Overview # Their alphabet is the ancestor of Greek, Latin and Arabic scripts. Government and society # Independent city-states such as Tyre, Sidon and Byblos were ruled by kings with powerful merchant councils. How people lived # Phoenicians lived in crowded island and coastal cities, working as sailors, merchants, shipbuilders, glassmakers, dyers and carpenters; the cedars of Lebanon were felled for ships and temples. Families sent sons to trading posts across the Mediterranean, from Cyprus to Spain. Purple dye-making was a smelly, labour-intensive industry, and slaves were traded. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Phoenicians worshipped Baal, Astarte and Melqart, the god of Tyre. Their greatest cultural gift was the alphabet of 22 consonants, adapted by Greeks, Aramaeans and others. Greek and Roman sources accused them of child sacrifice (tophet sites at Carthage), which archaeologists still debate. Food # Phoenicians ate barley and wheat bread, olives and olive oil, fish, figs and dates, and traded wine across the Mediterranean in amphorae. Their colonists spread vine and olive cultivation to North Africa and Spain. Construction and architecture # Harbour cities with breakwaters and dry docks; Carthage’s circular military harbour (cothon). Technology and knowledge # The 22-letter consonantal alphabet (~1050 BCE), Tyrian purple dye made from murex snails, glass production, and navigation by the Pole Star that took them past Gibraltar and possibly around Africa (Herodotus). How it rose # After the Bronze Age collapse weakened Egypt and the Hittites, the Phoenician cities filled the trade vacuum from about 1200 BCE and founded colonies across the Mediterranean. How it declined or fell # They fell under Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian domination; Alexander destroyed Tyre in 332 BCE after a seven-month siege. Legacy # Their alphabet is the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Arabic and possibly Brahmi scripts.

d: Its scriptures shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
x: Overview # Its scriptures shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Government and society # Early Israelites were tribes led by judges; according to the Bible, Saul, David and Solomon ruled a united monarchy (~1050–930 BCE), which split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Prophets criticised kings for injustice. How people lived # Most Israelites farmed small hillside plots of wheat, barley, olives and grapes and herded sheep and goats, living in four-room houses in villages. The family and clan were central, and the Sabbath gave a weekly day of rest. Kings in Jerusalem and Samaria taxed and conscripted, and prophets like Amos criticised the rich for oppressing the poor. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Israelite religion developed toward monotheism — worship of one God, Yahweh — centred later on the Temple in Jerusalem. The Hebrew Bible’s laws, psalms, prophets and histories took shape during and after the Babylonian exile. Festivals like Passover, Sukkot and Shavuot marked the agricultural year and memory of the Exodus. Food # The Seven Species of the Bible — wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates (honey) — were the basis of the diet. Most people ate bread, lentil stews, cheese and yoghurt from goats and sheep; meat was for festivals and sacrifices, and dietary laws (kashrut) defined permitted animals. Construction and architecture # Jerusalem’s First Temple (traditionally Solomon’s), Hezekiah’s water tunnel (~700 BCE) and fortified cities like Megiddo and Lachish. Technology and knowledge # Terrace farming of hill country, water cisterns, and early Hebrew alphabetic writing. How it rose # Hill-country villages emerged around 1200 BCE; the kingdoms formed around the 10th–9th centuries BCE. How it declined or fell # Assyria destroyed Israel in 722 BCE and deported its people; Babylon destroyed Judah and the Temple in 587 BCE and exiled its elite to Babylon. Legacy # The Hebrew Bible, ethical monotheism, the Sabbath and prophetic ideas of justice shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

d: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt.
x: Overview # Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt. Government and society # Kushite kings were chosen from the royal family with priestly approval; queen mothers and ruling queens (kandakes), such as Amanirenas who fought Rome, held great power. How people lived # Kushites farmed sorghum along the Nile and kept cattle, the main measure of wealth; Meroë was a major iron-smelting centre with workshops and slag heaps. Trade in gold, ivory, ebony and exotic animals with Egypt, Rome and Aksum enriched the elite. Queens (kandakes) and queen mothers held strong positions. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Kushites worshipped Egyptian gods like Amun alongside their own lion-headed war god Apedemak. Kings were buried in steep pyramids at El-Kurru, Nuri and Meroë. They developed the Meroitic script, still only partly understood. Food # Kushites grew sorghum, millet and barley along the Nile and kept large herds of cattle, which were symbols of wealth. They also ate fish, dates and dom palm fruit and drank sorghum beer. Construction and architecture # Over 200 steep pyramids at Meroë and Nuri, temples at Jebel Barkal and Naqa. Technology and knowledge # Meroë was a major iron-smelting centre with slag heaps still visible; Meroitic script (still only partly understood). How it rose # Kush grew south of Egypt and, under Piye, conquered Egypt around 744 BCE, ruling as the 25th dynasty. How it declined or fell # Assyrians drove them out of Egypt (~656 BCE); Kush continued at Meroë until Aksum conquered it around 350 CE. Legacy # One of Africa’s great early states; Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt.

d: Destroyed by Rome in the Third Punic War.
x: Overview # Destroyed by Rome in the Third Punic War. Government and society # A republic led by two annually elected suffetes, a council of elders and a popular assembly; Aristotle praised its constitution. How people lived # Carthage was a city of perhaps 400,000 at its peak, with tall houses, a harbour bustling with merchants and a hinterland of large estates worked by slaves and Libyan farmers. Wealthy families dominated politics and trade across the western Mediterranean. Carthage relied on mercenary armies from Africa, Spain and Gaul. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Carthaginians worshipped Baal Hammon and Tanit; tophet cemeteries of child burials suggest child sacrifice, though some scholars argue they were cemeteries for infants who died naturally. Their language, Punic, survived in North Africa until St Augustine’s time. Food # Carthaginians farmed wheat, barley, olives, grapes and pomegranates (the ‘Punic apple’) on rich estates, guided by Mago’s farming manual. They ate puls-like porridge, fish and garum, and Romans copied their recipe for placenta cake. Construction and architecture # A circular naval harbour sheltering ~220 warships and tall housing on Byrsa hill. Technology and knowledge # Shipbuilding with prefabricated, numbered parts, and agriculture described by Mago. How it rose # Founded by Phoenicians from Tyre around 814 BCE, it built a trading empire across North Africa, Spain, Sardinia and Sicily. How it declined or fell # It lost the three Punic Wars to Rome; in 146 BCE Rome destroyed the city. Legacy # Hannibal’s campaign remains a classic of military strategy.

d: At its height ruled ~44% of the world's population (estimates vary).
x: Overview # At its height ruled ~44% of the world’s population (estimates vary). Government and society # The ‘King of Kings’ ruled about 20 satrapies through satraps watched by royal inspectors (‘the king’s eyes and ears’). Darius I standardised taxes, coinage and laws, while respecting local religions and customs. How people lived # The empire included about 50 million people of many ethnicities. Workers on royal projects, recorded in the Persepolis tablets, received rations and wages, including women, who sometimes received maternity rations. Persian nobles valued horsemanship, archery and telling the truth; Herodotus says boys were taught ‘to ride, shoot the bow and speak the truth’. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The kings followed Zoroastrianism or a form of Mazda worship, but respected local religions, letting Jews rebuild the Temple. Persepolis reliefs show delegations from across the empire bringing tribute, symbolising harmony. Paradise gardens (pairidaeza) became a model for later gardens, including Mughal ones. Food # Persians ate wheat bread, rice in some regions, mutton, fruit such as pomegranates, apricots and pistachios, and drank wine. Greek writers marvelled at the royal table, which fed up to 15,000 people a day, and at desserts served throughout the meal. Construction and architecture # Persepolis with its Apadana audience hall of 72 columns and reliefs of tribute bearers; Pasargadae and Cyrus’s tomb. Technology and knowledge # The 2,700 km Royal Road with relay stations, qanat underground canals, the gold daric coin, and a canal linking the Nile and the Red Sea. How it rose # Cyrus the Great overthrew the Medes (550 BCE), conquered Lydia and Babylon (539 BCE), and his successors took Egypt and northwest India. How it declined or fell # Costly wars with Greece, palace intrigue and revolts weakened it; Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela (331 BCE). Legacy # A model of tolerant, multi-ethnic empire; the Cyrus Cylinder; Persian administrative practices adopted by later empires.

d: One of the four great powers of its time (according to Mani).
x: Overview # One of the four great powers of its time (according to Mani). Government and society # Aksumite ‘kings of kings’ ruled vassal states in Ethiopia, Eritrea and at times South Arabia. How people lived # Aksum’s people farmed teff, barley and wheat on terraces with ox-drawn ploughs and kept cattle. The port of Adulis traded ivory, gold and incense with Rome, Arabia and India. The Persian prophet Mani listed Aksum among the four great kingdoms of the world. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Aksum’s king Ezana converted to Christianity around 330, making Ethiopia one of the first Christian states; the Ethiopian Orthodox Church claims the Ark of the Covenant rests in Aksum. They wrote in Ge’ez and raised giant carved stelae over tombs. Food # Teff, the tiny grain used for injera flatbread, and barley were staples, with cattle, sheep and honey. Aksum also traded for spices and wine with India and Rome. Construction and architecture # Monolithic stelae up to 33 m tall; one was taken by Italy in 1937 and returned in 2005. Technology and knowledge # Own gold, silver and bronze coins; terraced farming; Ge’ez script with vowels. How it rose # Control of Red Sea trade between Rome, India and Africa made Aksum rich from the 1st century CE. How it declined or fell # Islamic control of Red Sea trade, soil exhaustion and climate change led to decline by the 10th century. Legacy # Ethiopian Christianity (from King Ezana, ~330s) and Ge’ez.

d: 'Land of gold' for Arab geographers.
x: Overview # ‘Land of gold’ for Arab geographers. Government and society # The king (ghana) ruled from Koumbi Saleh and taxed gold and salt trade; succession passed through the king’s sister’s son. How people lived # Ghana’s farmers grew millet and sorghum, while traders exchanged gold from southern fields for Saharan salt, copper and cloth carried by Berber camel caravans. The capital Koumbi Saleh had a royal town and a Muslim merchant town with 12 mosques. Al-Bakri (1068) described the king’s court with gold-adorned dogs and horses. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The rulers followed traditional Soninke religion while employing Muslim officials and scribes. Sacred groves near the palace were forbidden to outsiders. Oral traditions, including the legend of the snake Bida, explained the kingdom’s rise and fall. Food # People grew millet, sorghum and rice in the Sahel and herded cattle, sheep and goats. Salt, traded from Saharan mines, was so valuable it was exchanged weight for weight with gold in some accounts. Construction and architecture # A twin-town capital with a Muslim merchant quarter of stone houses and the royal town. Technology and knowledge # Organised trans-Saharan caravan trade with camels. How it rose # Soninke kings controlled trade between Saharan salt and gold fields of Bambuk from around 300 CE. How it declined or fell # Almoravid pressure, drought and shifting trade routes led to decline by 1200. Legacy # West Africa’s first great empire; the modern nation of Ghana took its name.

d: Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage spread gold through Cairo.
x: Overview # Mansa Musa’s 1324 pilgrimage spread gold through Cairo. Government and society # The mansa ruled with a council and provincial governors; the Kurukan Fuga charter (1236) traditionally organised clans and rights. How people lived # Mali’s people farmed millet and rice along the Niger, fished and traded gold, salt and kola nuts; Ibn Battuta (1352) praised the safety of travel and justice. Society was organised in clans and castes such as blacksmiths and griots (bards). Timbuktu, Djenné and Gao were trading and learning centres. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Mali’s rulers were Muslims who supported scholars and mosques, while many subjects kept traditional beliefs. Griots preserve the Epic of Sundiata. Timbuktu’s Sankore mosque and family libraries held manuscripts on law, astronomy and medicine. Food # Mali’s farmers grew millet, sorghum and African rice along the Niger, and used shea butter as cooking oil. Ibn Battuta (1352) described millet porridge, fish and baobab sauce. Construction and architecture # Mud-brick mosques such as Djinguereber in Timbuktu, designed by the architect Es-Saheli for Mansa Musa. Technology and knowledge # Manuscript libraries with works on astronomy, medicine and law. How it rose # Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru at Kirina (1235). How it declined or fell # Succession disputes, Tuareg raids and the rise of Songhai. Legacy # Timbuktu’s scholarship; the Sundiata epic.

d: Fell to Moroccan musketeers.
x: Overview # Fell to Moroccan musketeers. Government and society # Askia Muhammad organised provinces, a professional army and Islamic courts. How people lived # Songhai controlled the Niger bend and trade routes; Sorko fishermen, farmers and merchants lived along the river. Askia Muhammad created a standing army and standard weights and measures. Timbuktu had perhaps 100,000 people and many schools. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Askia Muhammad made the hajj and promoted Islamic scholarship; scholars such as Ahmed Baba wrote dozens of works. Local beliefs and Islam coexisted. Food # Songhai farmers grew rice, millet and sorghum in the Niger bend floodplain; Sorko fishermen supplied fish. Cattle-herding Fulani supplied milk and butter. Construction and architecture # The Tomb of Askia in Gao (UNESCO). Technology and knowledge # A river fleet on the Niger. How it rose # Sonni Ali (r. 1464–1492) captured Timbuktu and Djenné. How it declined or fell # Moroccan musketeers defeated Songhai at Tondibi in 1591. Legacy # Largest empire in West African history.

d: Gave its name to modern Zimbabwe.
x: Overview # Gave its name to modern Zimbabwe. Government and society # Kings ruled from the Hill Complex; a population of perhaps 10,000–18,000 lived around the stone enclosures. How people lived # Great Zimbabwe’s elite lived inside stone enclosures on the hill and valley, while ordinary people lived in daga (clay) huts around them. Cattle herding, farming and gold mining sustained the economy, and gold and ivory were traded to Swahili ports for Chinese porcelain and Indian beads. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Shona-speaking people venerated ancestors through spirit mediums. Carved soapstone birds found at the site are now Zimbabwe’s national emblem. Food # Cattle were the main wealth and source of meat and milk, with sorghum, finger millet and beans grown on hillsides. Construction and architecture # Walls up to 11 m high built of granite blocks without mortar, including the Great Enclosure and its conical tower. Technology and knowledge # Gold mining and trade with the Swahili coast. How it rose # Cattle wealth and gold trade from the 11th century. How it declined or fell # Overgrazing, depleted resources and shifting trade routes led to abandonment around 1450. Legacy # Colonial authorities long denied Africans built it; it became a symbol of Zimbabwe’s independence.

d: A blend of Bantu, Arab and Persian cultures.
x: Overview # A blend of Bantu, Arab and Persian cultures. Government and society # Each town had its own sultan and merchant elite. How people lived # Swahili towns like Kilwa, Mombasa, Lamu and Zanzibar had coral-stone houses for wealthy merchants and thatched houses for others. Merchants traded gold, ivory and enslaved people for cloth from Gujarat, porcelain from China and goods from Arabia. Ibn Battuta called Kilwa one of the most beautiful towns in the world. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Swahili culture blended Bantu African and Arab-Persian influences; Islam was the main religion, and Swahili poetry (utenzi) developed in Arabic script. Food # Swahili towns ate rice, millet, coconut, bananas, fish and spices traded across the Indian Ocean. Construction and architecture # Coral-stone mosques and palaces such as Husuni Kubwa at Kilwa. Technology and knowledge # Dhows sailing with the monsoon to Arabia, India and China. How it rose # Bantu coastal communities trading with Arab and Persian merchants from the 8th century. How it declined or fell # Portuguese attacks and the shift of trade after 1500. Legacy # The Swahili language, now spoken by about 200 million.

d: The British looted the bronzes in 1897; some are now being returned.
x: Overview # The British looted the bronzes in 1897; some are now being returned. Government and society # The Oba ruled with chiefs and guilds of artisans. How people lived # Benin City had wide streets, a royal palace and guilds of craftsmen who lived in their own wards. Farmers grew yams, and Benin traded pepper, ivory and cloth with the Portuguese from the 15th century, as well as slaves. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Oba was a sacred ruler. Royal brass casters made plaques and heads recording court history, now known as the Benin Bronzes; many looted in 1897 are being returned. Food # Yams were the central crop, eaten with palm-oil soups, plantains and bushmeat; kola nuts were shared in hospitality. Construction and architecture # Earthworks around Benin City estimated as among the largest built by people before the mechanical era. Technology and knowledge # Brass and bronze casting. How it rose # Emerged in the forests of southern Nigeria around the 12th century; expanded under Oba Ewuare (~1440). How it declined or fell # A British punitive expedition burned the city in 1897. Legacy # The Benin Bronzes, now being returned.

d: Lasted over six centuries.
x: Overview # Lasted over six centuries. Government and society # The sultan ruled with a grand vizier and the Imperial Council; the devshirme system recruited Christian boys to become janissaries and officials; non-Muslim communities (millets) governed their own religious affairs. How people lived # The Ottoman Empire ruled Turks, Arabs, Greeks, Armenians, Jews, Kurds and Slavs. Istanbul had perhaps 700,000 people in the 16th century — one of the world’s largest cities — with covered bazaars, coffee houses, public fountains and hamams endowed by charitable foundations (waqf). Peasants farmed land held by timariot cavalrymen in return for military service, while Christian boys taken through the devshirme could rise to grand vizier. Non-Muslim communities ran their own religious, educational and family-law affairs under the millet system. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ottoman culture blended Turkish, Persian, Arab and Byzantine traditions: calligraphy, miniature painting, Iznik tiles, carpets, Sufi music of the whirling Mevlevi dervishes, and poetry in Ottoman Turkish. Mimar Sinan’s mosques, such as the Süleymaniye and Selimiye, define its architecture. Coffee arrived from Yemen in the 1550s, and coffee houses became centres of conversation, chess and Karagöz shadow-puppet theatre, sometimes banned as hotbeds of dissent. Food # Ottoman palace kitchens at Topkapı fed up to 10,000 people a day; dishes included pilaf, kebabs, börek, dolma, yoghurt and baklava. Coffee houses spread from Istanbul in the 16th century. Construction and architecture # Mimar Sinan’s Süleymaniye and Selimiye mosques, Topkapı Palace and the Blue Mosque. Technology and knowledge # Large gunpowder artillery (the cannons that breached Constantinople), cartography (Piri Reis’s map) and an efficient postal system. How it rose # Osman I’s frontier principality in Anatolia expanded into the Balkans; Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453; Selim I took Egypt and Arabia; Suleiman reached Vienna (1529). How it declined or fell # Military defeats from 1683, nationalism in the Balkans, economic dependence on Europe and defeat in World War I led to its dissolution and the Turkish Republic (1923). Legacy # A multi-faith empire lasting six centuries; modern Middle Eastern and Balkan borders took shape from its collapse.

d: 'Isfahan is half the world.'
x: Overview # ‘Isfahan is half the world.’ Government and society # Shahs ruled with Qizilbash tribal elites; Shah Abbas I built a slave-soldier army to curb them. How people lived # Under Shah Abbas I, Isfahan grew to perhaps 600,000 people, with the vast Naqsh-e Jahan square used for polo, markets and ceremonies. He resettled thousands of Armenians in New Julfa to run Iran’s silk trade, which linked Iran to Europe and India. Craftsmen produced carpets, ceramics and textiles for export, and caravanserais lined the trade roads.
