Culture, beliefs and heritage # Shah Ismail I imposed Twelver Shia Islam, converting most Iranians and creating a lasting distinction from Sunni Ottomans and Mughals; the mourning of Muharram became central. Persian miniature painting peaked with masters like Reza Abbasi, and Persian poetry and architecture influenced the Mughal court, where many Iranian artists and administrators went. Food # Rice dishes (polow and chelow) with saffron, herbs and fruit, kebabs, flatbreads and sherbets; tea and coffee spread later. Construction and architecture # Isfahan’s Naqsh-e Jahan square, the Shah Mosque and the Si-o-se-pol bridge. Technology and knowledge # Silk and carpet industries organised for export. How it rose # Shah Ismail I founded the dynasty in 1501, making Shia Islam the state religion. How it declined or fell # Weak rulers and the Afghan sack of Isfahan in 1722. Legacy # Iran’s Shia identity and Persian art.

d: Its cities had some of the best urban drainage of the ancient world.
x: Overview # Its cities had some of the best urban drainage of the ancient world. Government and society # We do not know how the Indus cities were ruled because the script is undeciphered. There are no obvious royal palaces, royal tombs or monuments to rulers, and few weapons. The striking uniformity of brick sizes, weights, seals and city plans over a vast area suggests strong coordination, perhaps by merchant councils, priestly groups or competing elites rather than a single king. Some scholars think it may have been one of history’s more egalitarian early civilisations, though this is debated. How people lived # Indus cities like Mohenjo-daro had perhaps 40,000 people living in brick houses with bathrooms and wells, connected to covered street drains — a level of urban sanitation unmatched for millennia. Farmers grew wheat, barley, cotton and sesame; craftsmen made beads of carnelian, shell bangles, pottery and copper tools using standardised weights. Merchants traded with Mesopotamia, where Indus seals have been found. The absence of palaces, grand royal tombs or obvious weapons suggests a relatively egalitarian society. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Indus people used about 400 signs, the undeciphered Indus script, on seals with animals like the ‘unicorn’, bull and elephant. Figurines of a ‘Mother Goddess’, the ‘Priest-King’, the bronze ‘Dancing Girl’ and the ‘Pashupati’ seal suggest religious ideas some link to later Hinduism, such as possible yoga postures and reverence for the pipal tree. The Great Bath may have been used for ritual purification. Food # Indus farmers grew wheat, barley, millets, peas, lentils, sesame and cotton, and ate dates and mangoes; residues in pots show stews of meat and dairy. Cattle, buffalo, goat and fish were common, and grinding stones, ovens and large granaries suggest organised food storage. Construction and architecture # Cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan were laid out in grids, often with a raised ‘citadel’ and a lower town. Houses of standard-ratio baked bricks (4:2:1) had courtyards, private wells, bathing platforms and latrines connected to covered street drains with manholes. Mohenjo-daro had the Great Bath (12 × 7 m, waterproofed with bitumen), granary-like structures and around 700 wells. Dholavira carved huge rock reservoirs to store rain, and Lothal had a basin interpreted as a dock. Technology and knowledge # Harappans used a standardised system of cubic chert weights (in a binary-then-decimal series), precise measuring scales, the earliest known cotton cultivation and textiles, drilled carnelian beads with stone drills so fine they remain hard to replicate, bronze tools, wheel-thrown pottery, stoneware bangles, ploughed fields (Kalibangan), and seals carved with animals and script for trade. Dentistry at Mehrgarh, the ancestral site, goes back to ~7000 BCE. How it rose # The civ

d: Foundation of Hindu traditions.
x: Overview # Foundation of Hindu traditions. Government and society # Clans (jana) were led by a chief (rajan) whose power was checked by assemblies: the sabha (elders) and samiti (the wider tribe). Priests (purohitas) held great influence through ritual. Over time, clans merged into territorial kingdoms (janapadas) and society hardened into the four varnas. How people lived # Early Vedic people were semi-nomadic pastoralists who measured wealth in cattle; later they settled into villages of mud and thatch in the Ganga plain, farming barley and rice with iron ploughs. Society was organised in clans (jana) and families (kula) headed by men, but women like Gargi and Maitreyi took part in philosophical debates. Chariot races, gambling with dice and music were pastimes. Over time the varna system of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras became more rigid. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Religion centred on fire sacrifices (yajnas) to Agni, Indra, Varuna and Soma, with hymns preserved orally in the four Vedas. The Upanishads introduced ideas of Brahman, atman, karma and rebirth. The ashrama system described stages of life — student, householder, forest dweller and renunciant. Food # The Rigvedic diet was based on barley (yava), milk, curd, ghee and honey, with meat at sacrifices; later rice (vrihi) grew in the Ganga valley. Soma, a ritual drink, was praised in hymns. Construction and architecture # Early Vedic people built in wood, thatch and mud, so little survives; archaeologists link the period with Painted Grey Ware sites in the Ganga–Yamuna doab. Fire altars (vedi) were built of bricks to precise geometric plans described in the Shulba Sutras. Technology and knowledge # The Shulba Sutras (~800–200 BCE) contain geometry for altar construction, including statements of the Pythagorean theorem and approximations of √2. Horse-drawn chariots, iron ploughs in the later period, and an extraordinary oral technology of memorisation preserved the Vedas word-for-word for 3,000 years. How it rose # Indo-Aryan-speaking pastoralists, whose ancestry ancient DNA links partly to the steppe, settled in the Punjab (Sapta Sindhu) around 1500 BCE, mixing with local populations descended from Indus-era people. Over centuries they moved east into the Ganga plain, clearing forests with fire and later iron. How it declined or fell # The Vedic period did not ‘fall’ but transformed: by about 600 BCE the clans had become 16 mahajanapadas with cities, coins and kings, and new movements such as Buddhism and Jainism challenged Vedic ritualism. Legacy # The Vedas and Upanishads remain foundational for Hinduism; Sanskrit, ritual traditions, and the concepts of dharma, karma and moksha took shape.

d: Became the core of the Mauryan Empire.
x: Overview # Became the core of the Mauryan Empire. Government and society # Magadha’s kings, from the Haryanka Bimbisara onward, built a strong monarchy with officials, a standing army and land taxes collected directly. How people lived # Magadha’s people farmed wet rice in the fertile middle Ganga plain and mined iron from nearby hills. Cities like Rajagriha and Pataliputra grew with markets, guilds and punch-marked coins. Merchants and artisans formed guilds (shrenis). Culture, beliefs and heritage # Magadha was a centre of new religious movements: the Buddha and Mahavira preached there, and Ajivikas and Charvakas also debated. Many Buddhist sites, including Bodh Gaya, Rajgir and Nalanda, lie in Magadha. Food # Magadha’s wealth rested on wet rice cultivation in the Ganga plain, along with pulses, sugarcane and fish. Construction and architecture # Rajagriha (Rajgir) was ringed by 40 km of cyclopean stone walls; Pataliputra, founded by Ajatashatru’s successors at the Ganga–Son confluence, became the greatest city of India. Technology and knowledge # Rich iron mines in the Chota Nagpur region, war elephants from the eastern forests, and new siege weapons described in Buddhist texts gave Magadha a military edge. How it rose # Fertile rice land, iron, river trade and capable kings let Magadha conquer Anga, Kosala, Kashi and the Vajji confederacy in the 6th–5th centuries BCE. How it declined or fell # It did not fall but became the core of successive empires: the Nandas, Mauryas and Guptas. Legacy # The Buddha and Mahavira taught in Magadha; it was the seed of India’s first empire.

d: Ashoka turned to Buddhism after Kalinga (261 BCE).
x: Overview # Ashoka turned to Buddhism after Kalinga (261 BCE). Government and society # The Mauryas built one of the most centralised states of the ancient world. The emperor ruled from Pataliputra with a council of ministers (mantriparishad), with provinces under royal princes at Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri. The Arthashastra, attributed to Chanakya (Kautilya), describes departments for revenue, mines, trade, weights, forests, elephants and a network of spies. Megasthenes, the Seleucid ambassador, reported city boards managing trade, foreigners, births and deaths, and an army of perhaps 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants (likely exaggerated). Ashoka added dhamma-mahamattas, officials to promote ethics, welfare and religious harmony. How people lived # Megasthenes described seven classes in Mauryan society, from philosophers and farmers to soldiers and officials, and noted that India had no slaves (though the Arthashastra mentions them). Farmers paid about a quarter of their produce; the state ran mines, forests and workshops and maintained roads with milestones and rest houses. Pataliputra was a huge city with wooden walls, 570 towers and 64 gates. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ashoka’s dhamma promoted non-violence, tolerance among sects, respect for elders and kindness to animals, and he banned some animal sacrifices. Buddhism spread to Sri Lanka and Central Asia, while Jainism and Brahmanical religion also flourished. Mauryan art includes polished sandstone pillars with animal capitals and the Didarganj Yakshi. Food # People ate rice, wheat, barley, pulses, sugarcane, dairy and fruit; Megasthenes noted rice eaten from golden bowls. The Arthashastra set rules on storehouses, fair prices and famine relief. Construction and architecture # Pataliputra was protected by a timber palisade about 14 km long with 570 towers, and had a pillared palace hall at Kumrahar. Ashoka erected polished sandstone pillars topped with animal capitals, such as the Lion Capital of Sarnath (India’s national emblem), built thousands of stupas including the core of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, and cut the earliest rock-cut caves at Barabar for the Ajivika sect. Technology and knowledge # The Mauryas built a royal highway (Uttarapatha) from Taxila to Pataliputra and on toward Bengal, with trees, wells and rest houses that Ashoka describes in his edicts. They operated state mines, mints for punch-marked silver coins, irrigation such as the Sudarshana lake in Gujarat, shipbuilding and a polished stone-working technique (the ‘Mauryan polish’) that still gleams. Ashoka’s edicts were the first large body of written Indian texts, in Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts. How it rose # Chandragupta Maurya, advised by the Brahmin strategist Chanakya, overthrew the unpopular Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 322 BCE, after Alexander’s withdrawal from Punjab left a power vacuum in the northwest. In about 303 BCE he defeated or mad

d: Issued coins with kings' portraits.
x: Overview # Issued coins with kings’ portraits. Government and society # Kings ruled the Deccan through feudatories (maharathis) and queens sometimes acted as regents; inscriptions name kings with their mothers’ names (e.g. Gautamiputra Satakarni). How people lived # Satavahana society included farmers, guilds of artisans and merchants, and seafarers who traded with Rome through ports like Sopara and Kalyan. Inscriptions record donations to Buddhist monasteries by merchants, craftsmen and women. Kings used their mothers’ names, suggesting the importance of mothers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Satavahanas were Brahmanical but supported Buddhism generously; Prakrit literature such as the Gatha Saptashati, love poems attributed to King Hala, flourished. Amaravati and Karla show their art. Food # Rice in coastal areas, millets in the Deccan, pulses and dairy; pepper and textiles were exported to Rome. Construction and architecture # The chaitya hall at Karla, the caves at Nashik and Bhaja, and the richly carved stupa at Amaravati. Technology and knowledge # Coins with ships show maritime trade; they issued lead and potin coins and controlled ports for Roman trade. How it rose # After the Mauryas declined, Simuka founded the dynasty around the 1st century BCE in the western Deccan. How it declined or fell # Wars with the Western Kshatrapas and internal division split the realm into smaller kingdoms by the early 3rd century. Legacy # Linked north and south India; patrons of Prakrit literature such as the Gatha Saptashati and of Buddhist art.

d: Sangam poems describe love and war across five landscapes.
x: Overview # Sangam poems describe love and war across five landscapes. Government and society # Three crowned dynasties, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, ruled with numerous chieftains (velir); bards and poets were honoured at court and assemblies (manram) settled disputes. How people lived # Sangam poems describe five landscapes (tinai) — hills, forests, farmland, coast and desert — each with its people, occupations and moods of love. Farmers grew rice, fishermen worked the coast, and port cities like Muziris and Puhar traded pepper, pearls and muslin with Rome. Women poets such as Avvaiyar wrote, and Keeladi pottery inscriptions suggest widespread literacy. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Tamil culture celebrated love (akam) and war (puram) in poetry; warriors who died were honoured with hero stones. Murugan was the main deity, alongside Vedic, Buddhist and Jain influences. Food # Tamils ate rice, millet, fish, meat and fruit; Sangam poems describe five landscapes each with its own food. Black pepper was exported to Rome. Construction and architecture # Brick towns with drainage and wells at Keeladi, port cities such as Kaveripattinam and Muziris, and memorial hero-stones (natukal). Technology and knowledge # Iron smelting (iron furnaces and steel), a Tamil-Brahmi script found even on everyday pottery at Keeladi suggesting widespread literacy, and long-distance shipping to Rome and Southeast Asia. How it rose # Iron Age farming and port trade with the Romans and Greeks enriched the Tamil coast from about the 3rd century BCE. How it declined or fell # The obscure Kalabhra period (~3rd–6th century) displaced the three dynasties until the Pallavas and Pandyas revived. Legacy # Over 2,000 Sangam poems, the Tirukkural and the foundation of Tamil literary culture.

d: Spread Mahayana Buddhism to Central Asia.
x: Overview # Spread Mahayana Buddhism to Central Asia. Government and society # Kushan emperors such as Kanishka called themselves ‘son of heaven’ (devaputra) and ‘king of kings’, ruling through satraps from Bactria to the Ganga. How people lived # The Kushan Empire was a crossroads where Greek, Persian, Indian, Chinese and steppe peoples traded; caravans carried silk, spices, horses and Roman gold. Cities like Taxila, Peshawar and Mathura grew rich. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Kushan coins show Greek, Iranian and Indian gods, reflecting tolerance. Gandhara art produced the first human images of the Buddha, with Greek-style drapery, while Mathura art developed independently. Food # Wheat, barley, grapes, melons and wine in Bactria; rice and dairy in India. Construction and architecture # Buddhist stupas and monasteries of Gandhara and Mathura, and the giant Kanishka stupa at Peshawar. Technology and knowledge # They issued abundant gold coins and controlled the Silk Road’s southern branches, linking Rome, Persia, India and China. How it rose # The Yuezhi nomads, pushed from China’s frontier, conquered Bactria; Kujula Kadphises united them in the 1st century CE. How it declined or fell # Defeats by the Sasanians in the 3rd century and the rise of the Guptas in India reduced them to minor rulers. Legacy # Gandhara art made the first human images of the Buddha; Mahayana Buddhism spread along their trade routes to China.

d: Weakened by Huna invasions.
x: Overview # Weakened by Huna invasions. Government and society # The Guptas ruled the Ganga heartland directly but most of their empire through feudatories and tributary kings who acknowledged their supremacy. Kings took grand titles such as Maharajadhiraja. Land grants to Brahmins and temples, recorded on copper plates, began a process of decentralisation. Faxian, a Chinese monk who visited around 400 CE, described light taxes, few death penalties and rest houses and free hospitals in the towns. How people lived # Gupta India had rich towns with guilds, and a growing feudal system of land grants. Faxian (about 405) reported free hospitals, rest houses and that the ‘chandalas’ (untouchables) lived outside towns and had to announce their presence — evidence of caste discrimination. Women’s position declined, with child marriage and sati appearing in some texts. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Classical Hinduism developed with temple worship of Vishnu and Shiva and the Puranas. Kalidasa’s plays, the Kamasutra, the Panchatantra and the Natyashastra date from this era. Nalanda was founded, and Buddhist and Jain learning thrived. Food # Rice, wheat, pulses, milk products, sugar (crystallised sugar was an Indian invention) and spices; Faxian noted that many people avoided meat, onions and alcohol. Construction and architecture # Gupta builders made some of the earliest free-standing stone Hindu temples, such as the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh and the temple at Bhitargaon in brick, the Udayagiri caves with the great boar (Varaha) relief, Buddhist sculpture at Sarnath, and the paintings of Ajanta (under the contemporary Vakatakas). The Delhi Iron Pillar, over 7 m tall and nearly rust-free after 1,600 years, was made in this era. Technology and knowledge # Indian mathematics and astronomy reached a peak: Aryabhata (476–550) proposed that the Earth rotates on its axis, explained eclipses, calculated π as 3.1416 and used place value; the decimal system with zero was being developed (formalised by Brahmagupta in 628). Medicine (Sushruta and Charaka traditions), metallurgy, textile dyeing and Sanskrit grammar flourished. Nalanda university was founded under Kumaragupta I. How it rose # The Guptas began as a minor family in Magadha. Chandragupta I (r. ~320–335) married Kumaradevi, a princess of the powerful Licchavi clan, which raised his status. His son Samudragupta (r. ~335–375), celebrated in the Allahabad pillar inscription, conquered or subdued kings across northern India and received tribute from the south. Chandragupta II (r. ~375–415) defeated the Western Kshatrapas, gaining Gujarat’s sea trade. How it declined or fell # From around 460 CE the Alchon Huns (Hunas) invaded from Central Asia. Skandagupta repelled them at first, but later attacks under Toramana and Mihirakula devastated the northwest and drained the treasury. At the same time feudatories such as the Maukharis and Maitrakas became independent, trade with the

d: Spread Indian scripts to Southeast Asia.
x: Overview # Spread Indian scripts to Southeast Asia. Government and society # Pallava kings ruled from Kanchipuram with ministers and village assemblies, using Sanskrit and Tamil. How people lived # Pallava society centred on Kanchipuram, a city of temples and learning whose ghatika (college) drew students from across India; Xuanzang visited in the 7th century and found over 100 Buddhist monasteries alongside Hindu temples. Farmers in the Palar valley grew rice with tank irrigation, and village assemblies (sabha and ur) managed local affairs. The port of Mamallapuram linked Tamil merchants to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, carrying Pallava script and temple styles abroad. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Pallava kings were patrons of Shaivism and Vaishnavism during the rise of the Tamil Bhakti movement: the Nayanar poets (Appar, Sambandar) and Alvars (Andal, Nammalvar) sang devotional hymns in Tamil, challenging Buddhist and Jain influence. Mahendravarman I wrote the Sanskrit satire Mattavilasa Prahasana. The Mamallapuram reliefs, Shore Temple and Kailasanatha temple mark the birth of Dravidian architecture. Food # Rice, millets, coconuts, pepper and fish. Construction and architecture # The rock-cut monuments of Mamallapuram, including the Shore Temple, the Pancha Rathas and the giant relief ‘Arjuna’s Penance’, and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram. Technology and knowledge # Developed the Pallava–Grantha script, ancestor of many Southeast Asian scripts. How it rose # Rose in the 3rd–4th centuries around Kanchipuram after the Satavahanas. How it declined or fell # Defeated by the Cholas around 897. Legacy # The foundation of Dravidian temple architecture.

d: Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha.
x: Overview # Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha. Government and society # The Badami Chalukyas ruled the Deccan through feudatories; Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha on the Narmada around 618. How people lived # The Badami Chalukyas ruled an agrarian Deccan society of farming villages that grew millets, rice and cotton and paid taxes to the king’s feudatories. Aihole was home to the Ainnurruvar, a powerful guild of ‘500 merchants’ who traded across south India and overseas. Kings granted land to Brahmins and temples, which became centres of village life. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Chalukya patronage produced an extraordinary laboratory of temple styles at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal, mixing northern nagara and southern dravida forms; cave temples at Badami are carved with Shiva, Vishnu and Jain tirthankaras. Kannada inscriptions appear alongside Sanskrit, and the Jain poet Ravikirti composed the Aihole inscription in Sanskrit verse. Food # Millets (jowar, ragi), rice and pulses. Construction and architecture # Cave temples at Badami, the experimental temples of Aihole, and the UNESCO group at Pattadakal blending northern and southern styles. Technology and knowledge # Advanced stone carving and temple engineering. How it rose # Pulakeshin I founded Badami as capital in 543. How it declined or fell # The Rashtrakutas overthrew them in 753; a later branch ruled from Kalyani. Legacy # The Vesara temple style and Kannada inscriptions.

d: Arab travellers ranked its king among the world's four greatest.
x: Overview # Arab travellers ranked its king among the world’s four greatest. Government and society # A powerful Deccan monarchy; Arab traveller Sulaiman listed its king among the four great rulers of the world. How people lived # The Rashtrakuta capital Manyakheta was a wealthy city, and Arab travellers like Sulaiman and al-Masudi described the kingdom as one of the world’s four great powers, friendly to Muslim merchants on the west coast. Agriculture, cotton textiles and coastal trade sustained the economy, with feudatories collecting revenue. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Rashtrakutas patronised Shaivism, Vaishnavism and especially Jainism; Amoghavarsha I is said to have become a Jain monk. They sponsored Kannada classics such as Kavirajamarga and Adikavi Pampa’s works, Sanskrit mathematics (Mahavira’s Ganitasarasangraha), and the monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora, where Hindu, Buddhist and Jain caves stand side by side. Food # Jowar and other millets, rice, pulses and dairy. Construction and architecture # The Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved from a single rock by removing about 200,000 tonnes of stone. Technology and knowledge # Masterful rock-cut engineering. How it rose # Dantidurga overthrew the Chalukyas in 753. How it declined or fell # Western Chalukyas defeated them in 982. Legacy # Kannada literature (Kavirajamarga) and Ellora.

d: Rajendra I raided Srivijaya in 1025.
x: Overview # Rajendra I raided Srivijaya in 1025. Government and society # The Chola king ruled through a hierarchy of provinces (mandalams), districts (valanadus) and village groups (nadus), but villages enjoyed remarkable self-government. Inscriptions at Uttaramerur (~919–921 CE) describe village assemblies (sabhas) choosing committee members by lottery (kudavolai, ‘pot ticket’) from qualified candidates, with rules disqualifying the corrupt and their relatives. Temples were economic hubs, employing hundreds of people and lending money. How people lived # Chola villages were self-governing: inscriptions at Uttaramerur describe election by lot (kudavolai) of committees for tanks, gardens and justice. Temples were the centres of economic life, employing dancers, musicians, cooks and accountants and lending money. Merchant guilds like the Ainnurruvar traded across Southeast Asia and China. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Cholas were devoted Shaivas who built the Brihadeeswarar and Gangaikonda Cholapuram temples. Chola bronze sculptures, especially Nataraja, are masterpieces. Bharatanatyam’s ancestor, temple dance, flourished, and Kamban wrote his Tamil Ramayana. Food # Rice from the Kaveri delta, coconut, tamarind, pepper and fish; temple kitchens served thousands. Construction and architecture # The Cholas built some of India’s greatest temples: the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur (1010), whose granite tower rises about 66 m and is crowned by an 80-tonne capstone; the temple of Gangaikonda Cholapuram; and Airavatesvara at Darasuram, all UNESCO World Heritage sites. They also built tanks, irrigation channels and maintained the ancient Kallanai dam on the Kaveri. Technology and knowledge # Chola artisans perfected lost-wax bronze casting, producing the iconic Nataraja (Shiva as cosmic dancer). Engineers moved and raised enormous granite blocks, built irrigation systems in the Kaveri delta, and the navy mastered the monsoon winds to sail to Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Southeast Asia. Land surveys under Rajaraja I recorded tax for every village. How it rose # The early Cholas appear in Sangam literature, but the Imperial Cholas began when Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars around 848. Rajaraja I (985–1014) conquered the Cheras, Pandyas, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives; his son Rajendra I (1014–1044) marched to the Ganga, founding Gangaikonda Cholapuram (‘city of the Chola who conquered the Ganga’), and sent a naval expedition against the Srivijaya empire in 1025. How it declined or fell # Long wars with the Western Chalukyas drained resources. In the 12th–13th centuries, provincial chiefs grew powerful, the Pandyas revived in the south and the Hoysalas in the west. The last Chola king, Rajendra III, was defeated by the Pandya Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan around 1279. Legacy # Dravidian temple architecture, Chola bronzes, the spread of Tamil culture and Hindu-Buddhist influence to Southeast Asia,

d: Last great Buddhist empire in India.
x: Overview # Last great Buddhist empire in India. Government and society # Founded by Gopala, elected by local chiefs to end anarchy (matsyanyaya, ‘law of the fishes’); later kings were Buddhist patrons with feudatory chiefs. How people lived # Pala Bengal and Bihar were rich rice-growing lands with river trade to the Bay of Bengal and Southeast Asia. Land grants inscribed on copper plates record villages, ponds, fields and boundaries, giving a picture of rural life; many villagers were farmers, fishermen and weavers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Palas were the last great royal patrons of Buddhism in India, supporting Nalanda and founding Vikramashila and Somapura. Scholars such as Atisha Dipankara travelled to Tibet, shaping Tibetan Buddhism. Pala bronzes and palm-leaf manuscript paintings influenced Nepal, Tibet and Southeast Asia, and Bengali language began to emerge in the Charyapada songs. Food # Rice, fish, pulses and sweets made from milk. Construction and architecture # The Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur (Bangladesh), one of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalaya. Technology and knowledge # Pala bronze and stone sculpture and palm-leaf manuscript painting. How it rose # Gopala’s election around 750; Dharmapala and Devapala expanded the realm across north India. How it declined or fell # Weakened by Pratihara and Rashtrakuta wars, they were overthrown by the Senas in the 12th century. Legacy # Nalanda and Vikramashila universities; Pala art shaped Tibetan Buddhism.

d: Razia Sultan was its only woman ruler.
x: Overview # Razia Sultan was its only woman ruler. Government and society # Sultans ruled with Turkic, Afghan and later Indian nobles who received iqtas (revenue assignments) in return for military service. Alauddin Khalji controlled market prices, measured land and built a large standing army to repel Mongols; Muhammad bin Tughlaq experimented boldly with token copper currency and moving the capital to Daulatabad, with disastrous results. How people lived # Delhi grew into one of the largest cities in the Islamic world, with markets, mosques and madrasas. Peasants paid land revenue to iqtadars; Alauddin’s price controls kept grain cheap for soldiers. Slaves could rise to power (the Mamluk sultans were former slaves). Culture, beliefs and heritage # Persian became the court language, and Hindustani emerged from mixing. Sufi saints like Nizamuddin Auliya attracted followers of all faiths; Amir Khusrau developed qawwali. Indo-Islamic architecture produced the Qutub Minar. Food # Wheat bread, rice, meat dishes such as samosa (sanbusa) and pilaf, and sweets; Persian cuisine mixed with Indian. Construction and architecture # The Sultanate introduced the true arch and dome to India: the Qutub Minar (72.5 m), the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Alai Darwaza, the fortress cities of Tughlaqabad and Siri, and the tombs of the Lodis in Delhi. Technology and knowledge # Paper, the Persian wheel for irrigation, the spinning wheel, gunpowder (late), and new building techniques arrived or spread; Persian became the language of administration. How it rose # Muhammad of Ghor defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain (1192); after his death his slave general Qutb ud-Din Aibak ruled from Delhi (1206). Five dynasties followed: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi. How it declined or fell # Overexpansion, rebellions in Bengal and the Deccan, the founding of the Bahmani and Vijayanagara states, Timur’s devastating sack of Delhi (1398), and finally Babur’s victory over Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat (1526). Legacy # Indo-Islamic architecture, the Hindustani language, Sufi orders, and repelling the Mongols from India.

d: Defeated at Talikota (1565).
x: Overview # Defeated at Talikota (1565). Government and society # Kings ruled through nayakas, military chiefs given territory (amaram) in return for troops, a system later continued by the Nayaka kingdoms of Madurai and Thanjavur. Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529) was a great general, administrator and poet. How people lived # Hampi had perhaps 500,000 people, with markets selling diamonds, horses and spices; travellers like Domingo Paes and Niccolò de’ Conti described it as a city as large as Rome. Brahmins, warriors, merchants, artisans and devadasis made up society; nayakas controlled villages. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Vijayanagara patronised temple festivals, Carnatic music (Purandara Dasa), and Telugu, Kannada and Sanskrit literature. The Mahanavami festival displayed royal power. Food # Rice, ragi, pulses and spices; Domingo Paes described markets full of food. Construction and architecture # The capital Hampi had massive walls, the Virupaksha and Vittala temples (with musical pillars and the stone chariot), the Lotus Mahal, elephant stables, stepped tanks and aqueducts across a landscape of giant granite boulders. Technology and knowledge # Advanced water engineering with tanks, canals and aqueducts; large armies using cavalry and later firearms; a busy trade in diamonds, spices and horses. How it rose # Brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family founded the empire in 1336 to resist the Delhi Sultanate’s raids into the south. How it declined or fell # An alliance of the Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565; Hampi was sacked for months. The dynasty continued weakly until 1646. Legacy # Carnatic music (Purandara Dasa), Telugu and Kannada literature and the UNESCO ruins of Hampi.

d: Lasted nearly 600 years.
x: Overview # Lasted nearly 600 years. Government and society # The Ahom king (swargadeo) ruled with great ministers (gohains) and the paik system, in which every adult male owed labour or military service in rotation. How people lived # Under the paik system, every adult man was a paik who served the state for part of the year — as soldier, labourer or craftsman — in return for land; groups of paiks (khels) were managed by officers. Farmers grew wet rice in the Brahmaputra valley, fished and raised silk (muga and eri); villages managed embankments and roads. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ahom kings arrived as Tai Buddhists and animists, gradually adopting Hinduism and Assamese culture, while keeping Tai rituals. They wrote detailed court chronicles called Buranjis, first in Tai Ahom and later in Assamese — rare historical records in South Asia. Bihu festivals and Sattriya dance, from Sankardev’s Vaishnava monasteries (sattras), flourished. Food # Rice, fish, bamboo shoots and rice beer. Construction and architecture # Rang Ghar, Asia’s oldest surviving amphitheatre pavilion, the Talatal Ghar palace and the maidam burial mounds of Charaideo (UNESCO, 2024). Technology and knowledge # Gunpowder and cannon, river naval warfare, and embankments along the Brahmaputra. How it rose # The Tai prince Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills in 1228 and united local peoples. How it declined or fell # Civil war, Burmese invasions (1817–1826) and British annexation after the Treaty of Yandabo (1826). Legacy # Repelled the Mughals at Saraighat (1671); Assamese identity and the Buranji chronicles.

d: Ended after the 1857 uprising.
x: Overview # Ended after the 1857 uprising. Government and society # The emperor held absolute power, supported by the mansabdari system: nobles (mansabdars) held numbered ranks determining their salary and the cavalry they must supply, and were paid through revenue assignments (jagirs) that were regularly transferred to prevent local power bases. Akbar’s finance minister Raja Todar Mal measured land and fixed tax as a share of average produce (the zabt system). Akbar also abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, took Rajput nobles into high office and promoted sulh-i-kul, ‘peace with all’. How people lived # Mughal India produced about a quarter of the world’s manufacturing, mainly textiles. Peasants paid a third or more of their produce in revenue to mansabdars, while artisans in karkhanas produced luxury goods. Cities like Agra, Delhi and Lahore were among the world’s largest, with bazaars, caravanserais and gardens. European travellers like Bernier described both splendour and peasant poverty. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Mughal culture blended Persian, Central Asian and Indian traditions: miniature painting, Mughal gardens (charbagh), the Taj Mahal, Hindustani music (Tansen), Urdu poetry, and cuisine like biryani and kebabs. Akbar’s policy of sulh-i-kul promoted tolerance, while Aurangzeb was more orthodox. Food # Mughal kitchens blended Persian, Central Asian and Indian cooking: biryani, pulao, kebabs, kormas, naan and kulfi. Babur missed Kabul’s melons; ordinary people ate khichdi, roti and dal. Construction and architecture # Mughal architecture blended Persian, Timurid and Indian traditions: Humayun’s Tomb (1570) with its charbagh garden; Akbar’s red sandstone city of Fatehpur Sikri and Agra Fort; Jahangir’s gardens in Kashmir; and under Shah Jahan, the white-marble Taj Mahal (1632–1653), the Red Fort and Jama Masjid of Delhi. Pietra dura inlay, domes, arches, minarets and symmetrical gardens defined the style. Technology and knowledge # The Mughals used gunpowder artillery and matchlock muskets (Babur won at Panipat with Ottoman-style tactics), built a road network with sarais, minted high-quality silver rupees (a standard introduced by Sher Shah Suri), and supported astronomy and the production of world-leading textiles. The Mughal economy produced roughly a quarter of world output around 1700 by Angus Maddison’s estimates. How it rose # Babur, a Timurid prince from Fergana descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded India and defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527). His son Humayun lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri (1540) and regained it in 1555. Akbar (r. 1556–1605) won the Second Battle of Panipat and built a stable empire through conquest, alliances and reforms. How it declined or fell # Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707) expanded the empire to its largest extent but spent 25 years at war in the Deccan against the Ma

d: Became the dominant Indian power in the 18th century.
x: Overview # Became the dominant Indian power in the 18th century. Government and society # Shivaji created a council of eight ministers (Ashta Pradhan), paid soldiers in cash rather than land grants, and collected chauth (a quarter of revenue) and sardeshmukhi from neighbouring territories. Under the Peshwas (prime ministers) from 1713, power shifted to Pune, and great chiefs (Holkar, Scindia, Gaekwad, Bhonsle) formed a confederacy. How people lived # Most Marathas were peasant farmers of the Deccan plateau who also served as cavalry. Shivaji paid soldiers in cash, regulated revenue and protected peasants from plunder by his own troops. Later the Peshwas’ Pune was a growing city of bankers, merchants and Brahmin administrators, while armies raised chauth across India. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Maratha identity drew on the Bhakti tradition of saints like Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath and Tukaram, whose abhangs are sung on the annual wari pilgrimage to Pandharpur. Shivaji used Marathi in administration and created the Rajavyavahara Kosha, a dictionary to replace Persian terms. Powadas (ballads) celebrated warriors. Food # Bhakri of jowar or bajra, dal, onion and chillies — a portable diet for fast cavalry. Construction and architecture # Hundreds of hill and sea forts such as Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad and Sindhudurg; the Peshwas’ Shaniwar Wada in Pune; and temples and ghats across India restored by Ahilyabai Holkar. Technology and knowledge # Guerrilla tactics (ganimi kava) suited to mountains; a navy under Kanhoji Angre that challenged the British and Portuguese; and later European-trained artillery under Mahadji Scindia. How it rose # Shivaji (1630–1680) built a state in the Western Ghats by seizing Bijapur forts, defeated Afzal Khan (1659), escaped from Aurangzeb’s custody at Agra (1666) and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. After Aurangzeb’s death the Marathas expanded across India under Peshwa Bajirao I. How it declined or fell # Defeat by Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) cost a generation of leaders. Internal rivalries let the British win three Anglo-Maratha Wars; the confederacy ended in 1818. Legacy # A powerful symbol of regional pride and resistance; the Maratha navy, Marathi culture and much of central India’s princely history.

d: Annexed by the East India Company in 1849.
x: Overview # Annexed by the East India Company in 1849. Government and society # Maharaja Ranjit Singh ruled a secular state in which Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims served in high office; his Khalsa army was modernised by European officers. How people lived # Ranjit Singh’s Punjab was a fertile farming land; he reduced oppressive taxes in some areas and encouraged trade, and Lahore and Amritsar became busy commercial centres. His army recruited Sikhs, Hindus, Muslims and even European officers, providing many jobs. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The empire was rooted in Sikh teachings of one God, equality and service, expressed in langar (community kitchen) and the Khalsa. Ranjit Singh gilded the Harmandir Sahib, but also gave to Hindu temples and mosques. Punjabi poetry, such as Waris Shah’s Heer (1766), and miniature painting from the hill states flourished. Food # Wheat roti, dairy, and the langar community kitchen that fed everyone equally. Construction and architecture # He gilded the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple), and built Lahore’s palaces and the gurdwara at the Guru’s birthplace. Technology and knowledge # A modern artillery corps and infantry trained on European lines. How it rose # Ranjit Singh unified the Sikh misls and captured Lahore in 1799, then Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar. How it declined or fell # After his death in 1839, court intrigue and assassinations weakened the state; the British won the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–46, 1848–49) and annexed Punjab. Legacy # The memory of Sikh sovereignty and the Golden Temple’s golden dome; the Koh-i-Noor was taken to Britain.

d: Tipu's Mysorean rockets influenced British rocketry.
x: Overview # Tipu’s Mysorean rockets influenced British rocketry. Government and society # Ruled by the Wodeyar family from 1399; Hyder Ali, a commander, took power in 1761, and his son Tipu Sultan modernised revenue, trade and the army. How people lived # Mysore’s farmers grew ragi, rice, sugarcane and coconut, irrigated by tanks and the Kaveri; Tipu Sultan promoted sericulture, introducing silkworms from China, and built the foundation of the Kannambadi dam. Sandalwood was a royal monopoly. Tipu’s state also built factories for guns and rockets. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Wodeyars made Mysore Dasara a grand royal festival with an elephant procession and patronised Carnatic music and Kannada literature; Tipu’s court used Persian. The Mysore painting style, with gold leaf, developed under the Wodeyars. Food # Ragi balls (ragi mudde), rice and sambar. Construction and architecture # Srirangapatna fort, Tipu’s Daria Daulat Bagh summer palace and later the Mysore Palace. Technology and knowledge # Iron-cased Mysorean rockets used against the British, which inspired the British Congreve rocket; silk farming introduced by Tipu. How it rose # Hyder Ali seized power from the Wodeyars and expanded Mysore across the south. How it declined or fell # Four Anglo-Mysore Wars; Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, and the British restored the Wodeyars as subordinate rulers. Legacy # Rocketry and Mysore Dasara.

d: A private company ruled India with its own army of ~260,000.
x: Overview # A private company ruled India with its own army of ~260,000. Government and society # A joint-stock company governed by directors in London, supervised from 1773 by Parliament, ruled through a Governor-General in Calcutta and presidencies in Madras and Bombay, with a private army of Indian sepoys. How people lived # Under Company rule, peasants faced heavy revenue demands through the Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems, and many lost land to moneylenders. Bengal’s famous weavers were forced to sell cloth cheaply to Company agents, and later British machine-made textiles ruined them. Famines such as Bengal’s in 1770 killed millions. Culture, beliefs and heritage # British orientalists founded the Asiatic Society (1784), translated Sanskrit texts and promoted study of India’s past, while Christian missionaries and reformers like Ram Mohan Roy debated sati, caste and education. Macaulay’s 1835 Minute pushed English education, creating a new educated class. Food # Indians ate traditional grains and pulses, but Company revenue demands contributed to famines such as the Bengal famine of 1770, which killed about a third of the province’s people. Construction and architecture # Fort William in Calcutta, Fort St George in Madras and neo-classical government buildings. Technology and knowledge # Surveys such as the Great Trigonometrical Survey (from 1802), which later measured Everest; steamships and the first telegraph lines. How it rose # Victory at Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) turned the Company into a territorial power; wars against Mysore, the Marathas and Sikhs extended its rule. How it declined or fell # The 1857 uprising led Parliament to abolish Company rule in 1858. Legacy # Colonial administration, the drain of wealth, and the deindustrialisation of Indian textiles.

d: Ended with Independence and Partition in 1947.
x: Overview # Ended with Independence and Partition in 1947. Government and society # India was ruled by a Viceroy responsible to the Secretary of State in London; about 1,000 Indian Civil Service officers governed 300 million people. About 560 princely states remained under indirect rule. Limited reforms (1909, 1919, 1935) gave Indians some elected seats. How people lived # Most Indians remained poor farmers; famines in 1876–78, 1896–1902 and 1943 killed tens of millions. Railways and ports moved raw cotton, jute and wheat to Britain, while new industrial cities like Bombay and Calcutta grew with textile mills and slums. A Western-educated middle class of lawyers, teachers and clerks emerged and led the national movement. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Raj saw the Bengal Renaissance, social reform movements (Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Aligarh movement), and literature in Indian languages from Tagore and Premchand. The national movement developed its own culture of khadi, songs like ‘Vande Mataram’, and mass protest. Food # Most Indians ate rice or wheat, pulses and vegetables; famines in 1876–78, 1896–1902 and 1943 killed tens of millions while grain was exported. Construction and architecture # New Delhi by Lutyens and Baker, Indo-Saracenic buildings such as Victoria Terminus (Mumbai) and the Victoria Memorial (Kolkata), hill stations and cantonments. Technology and knowledge # About 67,000 km of railways, telegraph, canals in Punjab, and the census; but designed largely to serve British commercial and military needs. How it rose # After 1857 the British Crown took direct control (1858); Victoria became Empress of India in 1877. How it declined or fell # The mass freedom movement led by Gandhi, Nehru, Bose, Patel and many others, the 1946 naval mutiny, Britain’s exhaustion after WWII, and the end of Indian soldiers’ loyalty led to independence and Partition on 15 August 1947. Legacy # Parliamentary institutions, English as a link language and railways, but also famines, poverty, communal division and Partition.

d: The earliest Chinese writing on oracle bones.
x: Overview # The earliest Chinese writing on oracle bones. Government and society # Shang kings ruled with the help of ancestors, consulted through divination; they led armies, performed sacrifices (including human sacrifice) and controlled bronze production. How people lived # Millet farmers, bronze casters and diviners lived around royal centres. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ancestor worship and oracle-bone divination. Food # Millet in the north and rice in the south, plus pigs, dogs and fermented alcoholic drinks made in bronze vessels. Construction and architecture # The capital Yin (Anyang) had rammed-earth palace foundations and royal tombs; Erlitou (possibly Xia) had the earliest palaces in China. Technology and knowledge # Sophisticated bronze casting with piece-moulds, horse-drawn chariots, silk and the oracle-bone script, ancestor of Chinese characters. How it rose # The Shang overthrew the semi-legendary Xia around 1600 BCE according to tradition. How it declined or fell # The last Shang king, remembered as a tyrant, was defeated by the Zhou around 1046 BCE. Legacy # Writing, bronze art and ancestor veneration that shaped Chinese civilisation.

d: China's longest dynasty.
x: Overview # China’s longest dynasty. Government and society # The Western Zhou kings granted land to relatives and allies in a feudal system, justified by the Mandate of Heaven: heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from tyrants. After 771 BCE royal power faded and states competed in the Spring and Autumn (770–476) and Warring States (475–221) periods. How people lived # Peasants worked land for lords under a feudal order. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Confucian rites, the Book of Songs and Taoist ideas. Food # Millet, wheat, soybeans, vegetables and meat for nobles; elaborate ritual banquets were described in the Book of Rites. Construction and architecture # Walled cities, ancestral temples and elaborate ritual bronze vessels with long inscriptions. Technology and knowledge # Iron tools and casting, the crossbow, cavalry, and large irrigation works such as Dujiangyan (256 BCE), still in use. How it rose # King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king at Muye around 1046 BCE. How it declined or fell # Nomad attacks and rebellion forced the move east in 771 BCE; afterwards the Zhou kings were figureheads until Qin extinguished them in 256 BCE. Legacy # Confucius, Laozi, Mencius and Sunzi lived in the Zhou era, the classical age of Chinese philosophy.

d: Gave China its name.
x: Overview # Gave China its name. Government and society # Qin Shi Huang ruled by Legalist principles: strict laws, harsh punishments, collective responsibility, and abolition of feudal fiefs in favour of 36 commanderies run by appointed officials. How people lived # Peasants were conscripted for armies and huge building projects. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Standardised writing and legalist philosophy. Food # Millet and wheat, with state granaries feeding armies. Construction and architecture # The emperor’s tomb near Xi’an, guarded by about 8,000 life-size terracotta soldiers, horses and chariots; the first connected Great Wall; and the vast Epang Palace. Technology and knowledge # The Qin standardised script, coins, weights, measures and axle widths, built about 6,800 km of roads and the Lingqu canal linking the Yangtze and Pearl river systems, and mass-produced crossbows with interchangeable parts. How it rose # Qin, a western state, became powerful after Shang Yang’s Legalist reforms (4th century BCE). King Ying Zheng conquered the other six Warring States by 221 BCE and named himself First Emperor. How it declined or fell # Massive forced labour, harsh laws and book burning provoked hatred. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, the Chen Sheng–Wu Guang uprising and other rebellions brought down the dynasty by 206 BCE. Legacy # The name ‘China’ probably comes from Qin; the unified written language and centralised state lasted two millennia.

d: Han is still the name of China's majority people.
x: Overview # Han is still the name of China’s majority people. Government and society # The Han combined Qin centralisation with Confucian ideals. Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BCE) made Confucianism the state ideology and founded an Imperial Academy; officials were recommended for virtue and tested on the classics. Commanderies and counties were run by appointed officials, with state monopolies on salt and iron to raise revenue. How people lived # Peasant families farmed with iron ploughs; officials studied Confucian classics. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Silk, lacquer, paper and the historian Sima Qian. Food # Millet, wheat (as noodles), rice, soybeans and tofu (traditionally Han), plus pork and tea. Construction and architecture # Han cities such as Chang’an and Luoyang had walled palaces and markets; tombs held clay models of houses, watchtowers and farms showing everyday buildings. The Han extended the Great Wall west into the Gansu corridor to protect Silk Road trade. Technology and knowledge # Cai Lun refined papermaking around 105 CE; Zhang Heng built a seismoscope (132 CE) and a water-powered armillary sphere; the Han also developed the wheelbarrow, blast furnaces producing cast iron, the rudder, the horse collar and acupuncture texts. How it rose # Liu Bang, a peasant-born official, rebelled after the Qin collapse and defeated the aristocrat Xiang Yu in 202 BCE, founding the Han. He softened Qin’s harsh laws while keeping its centralised structure. How it declined or fell # Land concentration, court intrigue between eunuchs and consort families, and natural disasters led to the Yellow Turban rebellion (184 CE). Warlords who suppressed it carved up China; in 220 the last Han emperor abdicated, beginning the Three Kingdoms. Legacy # The Han defined Chinese identity; the majority ethnic group still calls itself Han. Paper, the Silk Road and the Confucian civil service were its lasting gifts.

d: A golden age of Chinese culture.
x: Overview # A golden age of Chinese culture. Government and society # The Tang emperor ruled through the Three Departments and Six Ministries: a Secretariat drafted edicts, a Chancellery reviewed them, and the Department of State Affairs carried them out through ministries of personnel, revenue, rites, war, justice and works. Officials were increasingly chosen by competitive imperial examinations on the Confucian classics and poetry. The ‘equal-field’ system allotted land to peasant households in return for taxes in grain and cloth and labour service, and the Tang Code (624) became the model for law across East Asia. Wu Zetian (r. 690–705) became China’s only woman emperor in her own name. How people lived # Chang’an was a cosmopolitan city of about a million. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Poetry of Li Bai and Du Fu, tea culture and Buddhist art. Food # Rice, wheat cakes, mutton and tea, which became a national drink; foreign foods such as grapes and sesame cakes were popular in Chang’an. Construction and architecture # Chang’an, the capital, was the largest city in the world (~1 million people), laid out on a strict grid of 108 walled wards around a central avenue 150 m wide, with two great markets where Persians, Sogdians, Arabs and Indians traded. The Tang built the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda to house sutras brought from India by Xuanzang, the vast Daming Palace, Buddhist cave temples at Longmen and Dunhuang, and wooden halls that influenced Japanese temples like those of Nara. Technology and knowledge # The Tang produced the world’s oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra (868), by woodblock printing; early porcelain and sancai three-colour glazed ceramics; mechanical clocks with water-driven escapements; advances in medicine (Sun Simiao’s encyclopaedias), cartography and astronomy (Yi Xing measured the meridian). Alchemists experimenting with saltpetre and sulphur took the first steps toward gunpowder. How it rose # After the short Sui dynasty reunified China (581) but exhausted it with huge canal projects and failed wars in Korea, rebellions broke out. Li Yuan, a Sui general, and his son Li Shimin captured Chang’an and founded the Tang in 618. Li Shimin, as Emperor Taizong (r. 626–649), defeated the Eastern Turks, extended control along the Silk Road into Central Asia, and governed so effectively his reign became a byword for good rule. How it declined or fell # In 751 the Tang lost to the Abbasids at the Battle of Talas, ending expansion westward. In 755 the general An Lushan rebelled; the eight-year An Lushan rebellion devastated the north and may have cost millions of lives. Afterwards provincial military governors (jiedushi) became semi-independent, eunuchs dominated the court, and the equal-field system collapsed. The Huang Chao rebellion (874–884) sacked Chang’an, and in 907 the warlord Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor, opening the Five Dynasties period. Legacy # The

d: The world's most advanced economy of its time.
x: Overview # The world’s most advanced economy of its time. Government and society # The Song placed civilian scholar-officials above generals, recruiting them through greatly expanded examinations. Reformers like Wang Anshi tried state loans to farmers and new taxes; Neo-Confucian thinkers like Zhu Xi reshaped education. How people lived # Commercial towns, rice farmers and scholar-officials. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Landscape painting, printed books and the tea house. Food # Champa rice, tea, restaurants and teahouses in cities; the first known restaurant menus. Construction and architecture # Song builders wrote the Yingzao Fashi construction manual (1103), built tall pagodas and covered bridges, and laid out bustling commercial cities like Kaifeng, shown in the scroll ‘Along the River During the Qingming Festival’. Technology and knowledge # The Song had the world’s most advanced economy: gunpowder weapons and fire lances, the magnetic compass for navigation, movable type (Bi Sheng, ~1040), the first government paper money (jiaozi), large ocean-going junks with watertight bulkheads, and new rice varieties from Champa that doubled harvests. How it rose # General Zhao Kuangyin was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 960 and reunified most of China, ending the Five Dynasties chaos. How it declined or fell # The Song lost the north to the Jurchen Jin in 1127 and moved its capital to Hangzhou. The Mongols conquered the Jin, then besieged Song cities for decades; the last Song emperor died at the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279. Legacy # Printing, the compass and gunpowder spread from Song China to the world; Song landscape painting and porcelain set lasting standards.

d: Founded by Genghis Khan's grandson.
x: Overview # Founded by Genghis Khan’s grandson. Government and society # Kublai Khan ruled China as Great Khan and Emperor, dividing society into four ranks: Mongols, Semu (Central Asians and others), northern Chinese and southern Chinese. The examination system was suspended until 1315 and many officials were foreigners, among them Persians, Uyghurs and, by his own account, Marco Polo. How people lived # Mongol, Chinese and foreign populations under a layered order. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Yuan drama and blue-and-white porcelain. Food # Mongol mutton, dairy and soups combined with Chinese rice dishes. Construction and architecture # The new capital Dadu (Khanbaliq, today’s Beijing) was laid out on a classical grid with palaces, lakes and the White Pagoda, built by the Nepali architect Araniko. Technology and knowledge # Paper money circulated empire-wide. The Grand Canal was extended to Beijing. Guo Shoujing built observatories and calculated the year to within 26 seconds. Postal relay stations (yam) linked China to Persia. How it rose # Genghis Khan’s Mongols attacked the Jin from 1211. His grandson Kublai declared the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and destroyed the Southern Song in 1279, the first time a non-Chinese people ruled all of China. How it declined or fell # Failed invasions of Japan (1274, 1281) and Java drained the treasury, and paper-money inflation and Yellow River floods followed. Plague and ethnic discrimination fuelled the Red Turban revolts. Zhu Yuanzhang took Dadu in 1368 and the Mongols withdrew to the steppe. Legacy # It reunified China after centuries of division and opened the age of Silk Road contact with Europe described by Marco Polo. It also produced zaju drama.

d: Rebuilt the Great Wall in stone.
x: Overview # Rebuilt the Great Wall in stone. Government and society # The founding emperor Hongwu abolished the post of chancellor and ruled personally through ministries, with a secret police (the Embroidered Uniform Guard). Later emperors relied heavily on eunuchs. The examination system and the eight-legged essay dominated elite life. How people lived # A large farming population and busy market towns. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Porcelain, Ming novels and the Forbidden City. Food # Rice and new American crops: maize, sweet potatoes and chillies. Construction and architecture # The Ming built the Forbidden City in Beijing (1406–1420), the Temple of Heaven, the Ming tombs and rebuilt the Great Wall in brick and stone into the form seen today. Technology and knowledge # Zheng He’s treasure fleets (1405–1433) sailed ships far larger than European vessels to India, Arabia and East Africa. The Ming produced famous blue-and-white porcelain, encyclopaedias like the Yongle Encyclopedia, and adopted New World crops such as maize and sweet potatoes. How it rose # Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant orphan and former monk, led the Red Turban rebellion against the Mongol Yuan and founded the Ming in 1368. How it declined or fell # Bureaucratic paralysis, eunuch corruption, costly wars in Korea against Japan, silver shortages, Little Ice Age famines and epidemics led to peasant revolts. Rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing in 1644; the last emperor hanged himself, and the Manchus swept in as the Qing. Legacy # The Forbidden City, the Great Wall in its famous form, porcelain trade with the world and classic novels like Journey to the West.

d: China's last imperial dynasty.
x: Overview # China’s last imperial dynasty. Government and society # The Manchu Qing ruled with a dual Manchu–Han bureaucracy and the Eight Banners military system. Emperors Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong (1661–1796) presided over a long era of prosperity and territorial expansion into Tibet, Xinjiang and Mongolia. How people lived # A population boom to about 400 million farmers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Peking opera and Qing literature. Food # Rice, maize and the Manchu–Han imperial feast. Construction and architecture # The Qing expanded the Summer Palace and Old Summer Palace (destroyed by British and French troops in 1860), and the Potala-style temples at Chengde. Technology and knowledge # Qing China adopted Jesuit astronomy and cartography, but by the 19th century fell behind Europe’s industrial technology. How it rose # The Manchus, unified by Nurhaci, took Beijing in 1644 after the Ming collapse. How it declined or fell # Population pressure, corruption, the Opium Wars (1839–42, 1856–60), the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) and other revolts, unequal treaties, defeat by Japan (1895), and the Boxer Rebellion (1900) undermined the dynasty. The 1911 Xinhai Revolution ended over 2,000 years of imperial rule. Legacy # Modern China’s borders largely reflect Qing conquests.

d: Silla's capital Gyeongju had an observatory (Cheomseongdae).
x: Overview # Silla’s capital Gyeongju had an observatory (Cheomseongdae). Government and society # In the Three Kingdoms period, Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla were monarchies ruled with powerful aristocracies. Silla used the ‘bone-rank’ system: birth into ‘sacred bone’ or ‘true bone’ lineages decided who could hold office. How people lived # Farmers and aristocratic elites. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Buddhist temples such as Bulguksa. Food # Rice, barley and fermented vegetables. Construction and architecture # Goguryeo left painted tombs and mountain fortresses. Baekje’s Mireuksa temple pagoda and Silla’s capital Gyeongju (Cheomseongdae observatory, Bulguksa temple, Seokguram grotto) survive. Technology and knowledge # Silla’s Cheomseongdae (7th century) is among the oldest surviving observatories in East Asia. Baekje transmitted writing, Buddhism and craftsmen to Japan. All three produced superb gold crowns and metalwork. How it rose # The kingdoms took shape from the 1st century BCE to the 4th century CE. Goguryeo grew to rule much of Manchuria under Gwanggaeto the Great (r. 391–413). How it declined or fell # Silla allied with Tang China to conquer Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668), then expelled the Tang by 676 to unify most of the peninsula. Unified Silla later split amid noble revolts and gave way to Goryeo in 935. Legacy # The first unification of Korea, Korean Buddhist art and the transmission of continental culture to Japan.

d: King Sejong created Hangul.
x: Overview # King Sejong created Hangul. Government and society # Joseon was a Neo-Confucian monarchy run by scholar-officials (yangban) chosen by civil service examinations. Royal records (the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty) were kept with such independence that even kings could not read them. How people lived # Confucian society of yangban, farmers and artisans. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Hangul, pansori and kimchi culture. Food # Rice, kimchi (chilli was added in the 18th century) and many banchan side dishes. Construction and architecture # Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces in Seoul, Jongmyo royal shrine and the Hwaseong fortress at Suwon. Technology and knowledge # King Sejong (r. 1418–1450) commissioned Hangul (1443), a phonetic alphabet designed so ordinary people could read. His scholars also built rain gauges, water clocks and sundials. Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s ironclad ‘turtle ships’ defeated Japanese fleets in the 1590s. How it rose # General Yi Seong-gye overthrew the Goryeo dynasty in 1392 and moved the capital to Hanyang (Seoul). How it declined or fell # Japanese (1592–98) and Manchu (1627, 1636) invasions devastated the country. Factional strife and isolation as the ‘Hermit Kingdom’ followed. Japan forced open its ports (1876), made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910. Legacy # Hangul, Confucian family culture and one of the world’s longest-ruling dynasties (518 years).

d: The world's first novel by Murasaki Shikibu.
x: Overview # The world’s first novel by Murasaki Shikibu. Government and society # The emperor reigned in Heian-kyō (Kyoto), but real power passed to the Fujiwara clan, who ruled as regents by marrying daughters into the imperial family. Later, retired emperors ruled ‘from the cloister’ (insei). How people lived # Aristocrats in Kyoto; peasants farmed rice. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Tale of Genji and waka poetry. Food # Rice, fish and vegetables; Buddhism discouraged meat. Construction and architecture # Kyoto was laid out on a grid modelled on Chang’an. Byōdō-in’s Phoenix Hall and shinden-style aristocratic mansions with gardens and ponds also survive. Technology and knowledge # The kana syllabaries developed, letting writers, many of them court women, write Japanese phonetically. How it rose # Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō in 794 to escape the power of Nara’s Buddhist monasteries. How it declined or fell # Provincial warrior clans grew strong. The Genpei War (1180–85) between the Taira and Minamoto ended with Minamoto no Yoritomo founding the Kamakura shogunate in 1185. Legacy # Murasaki Shikibu’s The Tale of Genji (~1010), often called the world’s first novel, and Sei Shōnagon’s Pillow Book.

d: Edo became one of the largest cities.
x: Overview # Edo became one of the largest cities. Government and society # The shogun ruled from Edo, while about 260 daimyo governed their domains. The ‘alternate attendance’ system (sankin-kōtai) made daimyo spend every other year in Edo and leave families there as hostages. Society was ranked as samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. How people lived # Samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Kabuki, haiku (Bashō) and ukiyo-e prints. Food # Rice, miso, tofu; sushi and tempura stalls in Edo. Construction and architecture # Edo Castle, Himeji Castle (completed 1609), Nikkō’s Tōshō-gū shrine and merchant townhouses. Technology and knowledge # Japan was largely closed to foreigners (sakoku) except the Dutch at Dejima, through whom ‘Dutch learning’ (rangaku) brought European medicine and science. Literacy was high and woodblock printing (ukiyo-e) became a mass art. How it rose # Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara (1600) and became shogun in 1603, ending a century of civil war. How it declined or fell # Commodore Perry’s US ships (1853) forced Japan open. Unequal treaties and domestic unrest followed, and samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū overthrew the shogunate in the Meiji Restoration (1868). Legacy # Two and a half centuries of peace, haiku (Bashō), kabuki, Hokusai’s woodblock prints and the foundations of modern Japan.

d: An early Southeast Asian state.
x: Overview # An early Southeast Asian state. Government and society # Funan, known from Chinese records, was ruled by kings, said to descend from the marriage of an Indian Brahmin named Kaundinya and a local queen named Soma. How people lived # Farmers and port traders. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Hindu and Buddhist worship. Food # Rice from the Mekong delta and fish. Construction and architecture # Óc Eo, its port in the Mekong delta, had canals linking it to inland cities, brick buildings and workshops. Technology and knowledge # Canals for drainage and transport. Roman, Indian and Chinese goods have been found at Óc Eo. How it rose # It grew from about the 1st century CE as a stop on the sea route between India and China. How it declined or fell # Shifts in shipping routes through the Strait of Malacca weakened it, and by the 7th century Chenla had absorbed it. Legacy # The earliest Indianised state of mainland Southeast Asia.

d: Studied by Chinese pilgrim Yijing.
x: Overview # Studied by Chinese pilgrim Yijing. Government and society # A thalassocracy: maharajas at Palembang controlled the Strait of Malacca and Sunda Strait through allied ports and the loyalty of sea peoples (orang laut). How people lived # Sailors and traders around Palembang. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Buddhist learning centres. Food # Rice, sago, fish and spices. Construction and architecture # Little survives at Palembang. Related monuments include Muara Takus and, in Java, the Sailendra dynasty’s Borobudur. Technology and knowledge # Navigation with monsoon winds and control of shipping and taxes on the China–India sea trade. How it rose # Srivijaya emerged around 650 CE in Sumatra. The Chinese monk Yijing (671) found over a thousand monks studying there. How it declined or fell # The Chola king Rajendra I raided its ports in 1025. Later, Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit took over its role. Legacy # A major centre of Buddhist learning; Old Malay inscriptions are the ancestors of Malay and Indonesian.

d: Angkor may have been the largest pre-industrial city.
x: Overview # Angkor may have been the largest pre-industrial city. Government and society # The god-king (devaraja) cult linked the Khmer king to Shiva or Vishnu. The king ruled a vast network of provinces through officials and temple foundations. How people lived # Rice farmers supporting temple cities. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Apsara dance and Angkor’s reliefs. Food # Rice, fish (prahok paste) and fruit. Construction and architecture # Angkor Wat (early 12th century, built by Suryavarman II) is the largest religious monument in the world. Angkor Thom, the faces of the Bayon, and Ta Prohm (built by Jayavarman VII) also survive. Technology and knowledge # A huge hydraulic system of barays (reservoirs), canals and moats. Lidar shows Angkor was a sprawling low-density city of perhaps 750,000–900,000 people. How it rose # Jayavarman II declared independence from Java and himself universal monarch in 802 at Phnom Kulen. How it declined or fell # Overstretched water infrastructure, alternating mega-droughts and floods in the 14th–15th centuries, a shift to Theravada Buddhism and maritime trade, and attacks by Ayutthaya (1431) led the capital to move south. Legacy # Angkor Wat is on Cambodia’s flag. Khmer architecture influenced all of mainland Southeast Asia.

d: Inspired Indonesian nationalism.
x: Overview # Inspired Indonesian nationalism. Government and society # Kings ruled from Trowulan in East Java with powerful ministers, most famously Gajah Mada, who swore the Palapa oath not to rest until the archipelago was united. How people lived # Farmers and traders across Java. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Wayang shadow puppetry and Old Javanese poetry. Food # Rice, spices and coconut. Construction and architecture # Red-brick temples (candi) and gates such as Bajang Ratu, with the canals of Trowulan. Technology and knowledge # Rice irrigation, a large fleet and the spice trade. How it rose # Raden Wijaya used a Mongol invasion force to defeat his rival in 1293, then drove the Mongols out. How it declined or fell # Succession wars, the rise of Muslim port states such as Demak and Malacca, and Demak’s conquest around 1527. Legacy # A symbol of Indonesian unity; the Nagarakretagama poem. Bali preserves its Hindu culture.

d: Spread across the largest area of any pre-modern culture.
x: Overview # Spread across the largest area of any pre-modern culture. Government and society # Chiefs (ariki) of ranked lineages, tracing descent from gods and founding canoe voyagers, led island societies. Hawai’i and Tonga developed paramount kingships. How people lived # Settled Hawaii, New Zealand, Easter Island Culture, beliefs and heritage # Tattooing, navigation lore and oral genealogies. Food # Voyagers carried ‘canoe plants’ — taro, breadfruit, yam, banana, sugarcane, coconut and later sweet potato — plus pigs, dogs and chickens. Fish and shellfish provided protein. Construction and architecture # Marae temples, Tonga’s Ha’amonga trilithon, Rapa Nui’s moai statues and Hawai’i’s heiau and fishponds. Technology and knowledge # Double-hulled voyaging canoes navigated without instruments, using star paths, ocean swells, birds and clouds. The Hōkūleʻa voyages since 1976 proved such journeys possible. How it rose # Lapita ancestors reached Tonga and Samoa by about 800 BCE. Their descendants settled East Polynesia, Hawai’i, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa (~1250 CE). How it declined or fell # European contact from the 18th century brought diseases that killed many, missionaries, plantations and colonial annexation. Legacy # The most widespread human migration before modern times, across a third of the globe’s surface.

d: Weakened by the Thera eruption.
x: Overview # Weakened by the Thera eruption. Government and society # Minoan Crete was organised around large ‘palaces’ at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, which acted as administrative, religious and storage centres, collecting and redistributing oil, wine and grain recorded in Linear A. Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, Minoan art shows no images of a mighty warrior-king, and towns lacked strong walls, suggesting a relatively peaceful society under priestly or elite rule, perhaps with prominent priestesses. How people lived # People farmed olives, grapes and grain, raised sheep for wool, fished, and worked as potters and metalworkers. Women appear prominently in religious scenes. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Religion centred on goddesses, sacred horns, the double axe (labrys) and peak sanctuaries; bull-leaping was a ritual sport. Food # Olives, wine, honey, barley, legumes and fish; storage jars (pithoi) filled palace magazines. Construction and architecture # Knossos covered about 20,000 m² with multi-storey wings around a central court, columns tapering downward, light wells, grand staircases, and painted frescoes of dolphins, bull-leaping and processions. It had clay pipes for water and drainage, and some of the earliest flushing toilets. Its maze-like plan may have inspired the labyrinth myth. Technology and knowledge # Minoans were skilled sailors who traded across the Aegean, Egypt and the Levant. They made fine pottery like Kamares ware, gold jewellery and seal stones, and wrote Linear A (undeciphered) and Cretan hieroglyphs. The Phaistos Disc is the earliest stamped text. How it rose # Neolithic farmers settled Crete around 7000 BCE. By about 2000 BCE wealth from olive oil, wine and sea trade allowed palaces to rise. After an earthquake destroyed them around 1700 BCE, even grander ‘new palaces’ were built. How it declined or fell # The eruption of Thera around 1600 BCE devastated Minoan towns and trade. Around 1450 BCE most palaces were burned, and Mycenaean Greeks took over Knossos, writing in Linear B. Minoan culture faded by about 1100 BCE. Legacy # Arthur Evans named the civilisation after the mythical King Minos when he excavated Knossos (from 1900). Minoan art and myths of the Minotaur, Daedalus and Icarus shaped European imagination.

d: Fell in the Bronze Age collapse.
x: Overview # Fell in the Bronze Age collapse. Government and society # Mycenaean Greece was a set of palace kingdoms — Mycenae, Pylos, Tiryns, Thebes — each ruled by a wanax (king) with officials like the lawagetas (military leader). Linear B tablets from Pylos record taxes, rations, land holdings, bronze smiths and slaves, showing a centralised palace economy. How people lived # Most people farmed, raised livestock and worked for palaces as craftsmen or labourers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # They worshipped gods like Zeus, Poseidon and Dionysus, recorded in Linear B. Food # Barley, wheat, olive oil, figs and wine; Linear B tablets record rations. Construction and architecture # Massive ‘Cyclopean’ walls made of huge stones (Greeks later thought giants built them), the Lion Gate of Mycenae (about 1250 BCE), megaron throne halls and beehive tholos tombs like the Treasury of Atreus. Technology and knowledge # Bronze weapons and armour, chariots, and Linear B — the earliest form of Greek, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952. Their ships traded across the Mediterranean. How it rose # Mainland Greek chiefdoms grew rich from about 1650 BCE, as shown by the gold death masks of Mycenae’s Shaft Graves (including the ‘Mask of Agamemnon’). They absorbed Minoan culture and took over Crete around 1450 BCE. How it declined or fell # Around 1200 BCE palaces were burned and abandoned in the Bronze Age collapse. Causes included drought, earthquakes, internal revolts and attacks; Greece entered a ‘Dark Age’ without writing. Legacy # Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey preserve memories of the Mycenaean world; heroes like Agamemnon, Achilles and Odysseus are set in it.

d: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Parthenon.
x: Overview # Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Parthenon. Government and society # Hundreds of city-states (poleis) had different constitutions. Athens built a direct democracy in which citizen men voted in the Assembly and juries were chosen by lot after Cleisthenes’ reforms (508 BCE). Sparta was a militarised oligarchy with two kings. How people lived # Citizens farmed, traded and served as soldiers; women managed households with limited rights in Athens but more in Sparta; slaves did much labour. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Greeks worshipped the Olympian gods and held festivals like the Panathenaia and Dionysia, with theatre. Food # Bread or barley porridge, olives, cheese, figs and wine mixed with water; meat came mainly from sacrifices. Spartans ate a notorious black broth. Construction and architecture # Greek architects developed the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders. The Parthenon (447–432 BCE) used subtle curves to look perfectly straight; theatres like Epidaurus had remarkable acoustics; and cities had an agora, stoas, temples and gymnasia. Technology and knowledge # Greeks developed the trireme warship, advances in geometry (Pythagoras, Euclid), astronomy (Aristarchus proposed a Sun-centred model), medicine (Hippocrates) and engineering, including the Antikythera mechanism, an analogue astronomical computer from the Hellenistic period. How it rose # After the Greek Dark Ages, city-states revived from the 8th century BCE with the alphabet, colonies and the Olympic Games (776 BCE). They defeated Persia at Marathon (490), Salamis (480) and Plataea (479). How it declined or fell # The Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) exhausted Athens and Sparta. Thebes briefly dominated, then Philip II of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea (338 BCE). Rome conquered Greece in 146 BCE. Legacy # Democracy, philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle), drama (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Aristophanes), history (Herodotus, Thucydides), the Olympic Games, mathematics and science all shaped Western and world civilisation.

d: Reached the Beas River in Punjab (326 BCE).
