Weakening monsoons and shifting rivers led to de-urbanisation.

d: 282 laws carved on a stele.
x: What happened # 282 laws carved on a stele. Causes, course and consequences # Around 1754 BCE King Hammurabi of Babylon placed 282 laws on a basalt stele, topped with an image of him receiving authority from Shamash. Laws covered trade, wages, divorce and medicine, with punishments that depended on class. The stele was taken to Susa and found there in 1901.

d: A massive eruption buried Akrotiri.
x: What happened # A massive eruption buried Akrotiri. Causes, course and consequences # The Minoan eruption of Thera (Santorini) around 1600 BCE was one of the largest in the past 10,000 years, burying Akrotiri under metres of ash. It produced tsunamis that struck Crete. Its exact date is debated, with radiocarbon and archaeology pointing to slightly different times.

d: Ahmose I drove out Asian rulers.
x: What happened # Ahmose I drove out Asian rulers. Causes, course and consequences # The Hyksos, West Asian rulers who introduced horses, chariots and composite bows, controlled northern Egypt from about 1650 BCE. Kings of Thebes fought back; Ahmose I captured their capital Avaris around 1550 BCE. Egypt then built an empire in the Levant and Nubia, the New Kingdom.

d: A pharaoh promoted a single sun-disc god.
x: What happened # A pharaoh promoted a single sun-disc god. Causes, course and consequences # Amenhotep IV renamed himself Akhenaten, promoting the Aten, the sun disc, as Egypt’s supreme god, closing other temples and building a new capital, Amarna. Art became naturalistic. After his death, the old gods returned under Tutankhamun, and Akhenaten’s name was erased.

d: Excavations at Hisarlik show a destroyed city around this time.
x: What happened # Excavations at Hisarlik show a destroyed city around this time. Causes, course and consequences # Homer’s Iliad tells of Greeks besieging Troy to recover Helen. Excavations at Hisarlik in Turkey by Schliemann and later teams found a city destroyed around 1180 BCE. Hittite records mention ‘Wilusa’, likely Troy. Whether the war happened as told is debated.

d: Cheap iron tools made farming and armies larger.
x: What happened # Cheap iron tools made farming and armies larger. Causes, course and consequences # Iron requires hotter furnaces and forging but iron ore is more common than tin. After the Bronze Age collapse disrupted tin trade around 1200 BCE, iron spread across the Near East and Mediterranean. In India, iron appears at sites in the Ganga valley and south India by 1800–1500 BCE; in Africa, Nok and Meroë became iron centres.

d: Hymns preserved orally for millennia.
x: What happened # Hymns preserved orally for millennia. Causes, course and consequences # Between about 1500 and 1200 BCE, poet-priests in the Punjab composed over 1,000 hymns to Agni, Indra, Soma and others. They were memorised exactly using techniques such as pada and ghana recitation, and written down only around 1000 CE. UNESCO lists Vedic chanting as intangible heritage.

d: Held every four years for over 1,000 years.
x: What happened # Held every four years for over 1,000 years. Causes, course and consequences # In 776 BCE, according to tradition, the first Olympic Games were held at Olympia in honour of Zeus, with a single footrace. Held every four years, they grew to include wrestling, chariot races and the pankration; a sacred truce allowed athletes to travel. Theodosius I may have ended them around 393 CE; Pierre de Coubertin revived them in 1896.

d: Romulus and Remus legend.
x: What happened # Romulus and Remus legend. Causes, course and consequences # Roman tradition held that Romulus and Remus, twin sons of the god Mars and the princess Rhea Silvia, were abandoned on the Tiber, suckled by a she-wolf and raised by a shepherd. Romulus founded the city on the Palatine on 21 April 753 BCE, killing Remus in a quarrel, and populated it by welcoming outlaws and seizing Sabine women. Archaeology shows Iron Age villages from around 1000 BCE merging into a city by the 7th century BCE, ruled by kings until about 509 BCE.

d: Babylonians and Medes destroyed the Assyrian capital.
x: What happened # Babylonians and Medes destroyed the Assyrian capital. Causes, course and consequences # After the death of Ashurbanipal (c. 631 BCE), the Assyrian Empire fell into civil war. The Babylonian Nabopolassar and the Median king Cyaxares allied and besieged Nineveh, which fell in 612 BCE after a three-month siege; flooding of the Khosr river may have breached walls. Assyria’s last king held out at Harran until 609 BCE. Ashurbanipal’s buried library preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh.

d: Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the First Temple.
x: What happened # Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the First Temple. Causes, course and consequences # After Judah rebelled, Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem, deporting King Jehoiachin and elites in 597 BCE, then destroyed the city and Solomon’s Temple in 587/586 BCE. In Babylon, exiled Jews kept their identity through the Sabbath, scripture and synagogue-like gatherings; much of the Hebrew Bible was edited then. When Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE he allowed them to return and rebuild the Temple.

d: Cyrus freed the exiled Jews.
x: What happened # Cyrus freed the exiled Jews. Causes, course and consequences # The Babylonian king Nabonidus had alienated Marduk’s priests by favouring the moon god Sin and spending years in Arabia. In October 539 BCE, after defeating the Babylonian army at Opis, Cyrus’s forces entered Babylon with little resistance. The Cyrus Cylinder presents him as chosen by Marduk, restoring temples and returning deported peoples, which the Bible echoes for the Jews.

d: Cleisthenes' reforms.
x: What happened # Cleisthenes’ reforms. Causes, course and consequences # After the tyrant Hippias was expelled, Cleisthenes in 508 BCE reorganised Athenian citizens into ten tribes mixing different regions, and created a Council of 500 chosen by lot. Under Ephialtes and Pericles, the Assembly of all adult male citizens voted on laws and war, juries of hundreds judged cases, and officials were paid so poor citizens could serve. Women, slaves and resident foreigners — most of the population — were excluded.

d: The legend of the runner.
x: What happened # The legend of the runner. Causes, course and consequences # In 490 BCE Darius I sent a fleet to punish Athens for supporting the Ionian revolt. At Marathon, about 10,000 Athenian and 1,000 Plataean hoplites under Miltiades charged the Persians, strengthening their wings to envelop the enemy. Herodotus counts 6,400 Persian and 192 Athenian dead. The legend of a runner carrying news to Athens inspired the modern marathon.

d: Recorded by Thucydides.
x: What happened # Recorded by Thucydides. Causes, course and consequences # Fear of Athens’ growing empire led Sparta and its allies to war in 431 BCE. Pericles kept Athenians behind their walls, but plague killed a quarter of them, including him. Athens’ disastrous Sicilian Expedition (415–413 BCE) lost its fleet; Sparta, funded by Persia, destroyed Athens’ navy at Aegospotami (405) and starved it into surrender in 404 BCE. Thucydides wrote its history.

d: Condemned for impiety.
x: What happened # Condemned for impiety. Causes, course and consequences # Socrates questioned Athenians about justice and virtue, angering powerful men. In 399 BCE, after the defeat in the Peloponnesian War and the rule of the Thirty Tyrants (some his former pupils), he was tried for impiety and corrupting the young. Found guilty, he refused to flee and drank hemlock; Plato’s Apology and Phaedo record his defence and last hours.

d: Alexander defeated Darius III.
x: What happened # Alexander defeated Darius III. Causes, course and consequences # Crossing the Hellespont in 334 BCE with about 40,000 men, Alexander won at the Granicus, then at Issus (333 BCE) where Darius III fled. He took Tyre after a seven-month siege and Egypt without a fight, then crushed Darius at Gaugamela (331 BCE). He took Babylon, Susa and Persepolis, which burned; Darius was murdered by his own nobles in 330 BCE.

d: Seleucus traded lands for 500 war elephants.
x: What happened # Seleucus traded lands for 500 war elephants. Causes, course and consequences # Seleucus I tried to reclaim Alexander’s Indian provinces around 305 BCE but came to terms with Chandragupta Maurya. Seleucus ceded Arachosia, Gedrosia and Paropamisadae (parts of Afghanistan and Baluchistan) in exchange for 500 war elephants, which helped him win at Ipsus (301 BCE). A marriage alliance and the embassy of Megasthenes to Pataliputra followed.

d: Rock edicts in Brahmi and Kharosthi.
x: What happened # Rock edicts in Brahmi and Kharosthi. Causes, course and consequences # From about 260 BCE Ashoka had his messages carved on rocks and polished pillars across his empire, mostly in Prakrit in Brahmi script, but in Greek and Aramaic in Afghanistan. They speak of his remorse after Kalinga, tolerance for all sects, medical care for people and animals, and officials (dhamma-mahamattas) to spread welfare. James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837, recovering Ashoka for history.

d: Earlier walls joined under Qin Shi Huang.
x: What happened # Earlier walls joined under Qin Shi Huang. Causes, course and consequences # After 221 BCE, Qin Shi Huang sent General Meng Tian with 300,000 men to drive back the Xiongnu and link older state walls of rammed earth into a frontier wall. Many forced labourers died. The famous brick-and-stone Great Wall seen today was mostly built by the Ming dynasty.

d: Han envoy Zhang Qian reached Bactria.
x: What happened # Han envoy Zhang Qian reached Bactria. Causes, course and consequences # Han Emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian west in 138 BCE to find allies against the Xiongnu; captured for ten years, he escaped and reached Bactria. His reports opened official contact with Central Asia. Silk, horses, paper, Buddhism, spices and ideas soon flowed along routes linking China, India, Persia and Rome.

d: Crushed by Crassus.
x: What happened # Crushed by Crassus. Causes, course and consequences # In 73 BCE Spartacus, a Thracian gladiator, escaped from a school in Capua with about 70 others and hid on Vesuvius. Slaves joined him, building an army of perhaps 70,000–120,000 that defeated several Roman armies. Marcus Crassus finally defeated him in 71 BCE, and 6,000 captured slaves were crucified along the Appian Way.

d: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra.
x: What happened # Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra. Causes, course and consequences # Mark Antony and Cleopatra controlled the eastern Roman provinces; Octavian declared war on Cleopatra. On 2 September 31 BCE, off Actium in western Greece, Agrippa’s fleet defeated them; Cleopatra’s ships fled and Antony followed. Both took their own lives in Alexandria in 30 BCE. Octavian became sole ruler and, in 27 BCE, Augustus.

d: Three legions destroyed by Arminius.
x: What happened # Three legions destroyed by Arminius. Causes, course and consequences # In 9 CE Arminius, a Cheruscan chief who had served as a Roman officer, led the governor Varus’s three legions into an ambush in the Teutoburg Forest. Over three days in rain, about 15,000–20,000 Romans were killed. Augustus reportedly cried ‘Varus, give me back my legions!’ Rome gave up conquering Germany, keeping the Rhine as the frontier.

d: Kushan patronage.
x: What happened # Kushan patronage. Causes, course and consequences # Kanishka the Kushan emperor convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir, around the 1st–2nd century CE, under Vasumitra and Ashvaghosha. Scholars compiled the Mahavibhasha commentaries of the Sarvastivada school. The council marked the rise of Mahayana Buddhism and the use of Sanskrit for Buddhist texts, which spread to Central Asia and China.

d: Peasant revolt led to warlordism and the Three Kingdoms.
x: What happened # Peasant revolt led to warlordism and the Three Kingdoms. Causes, course and consequences # In 184 CE, after famine, land concentration and court corruption, the Daoist healer Zhang Jue led hundreds of thousands of peasants, wearing yellow headbands, against the Han, proclaiming a new ‘Yellow Heaven’. The rebellion was crushed within a year, but the generals who suppressed it — Dong Zhuo, Cao Cao, Liu Bei, Sun Jian — became warlords, ending the Han and creating the Three Kingdoms.

d: Over 20 emperors in 50 years.
x: What happened # Over 20 emperors in 50 years. Causes, course and consequences # Between 235 and 284 CE Rome had around 26 emperors, most murdered or killed in battle. Persian and Gothic invasions, plague, and silver-debased coinage caused inflation. The Persian king Shapur I captured Emperor Valerian (260), and the empire split into the Gallic Empire, Palmyrene Empire under Queen Zenobia, and Rome. Aurelian reunited it, and Diocletian reformed it into a tetrarchy.

d: Edict of Milan.
x: What happened # Edict of Milan. Causes, course and consequences # Christians faced persecution, especially under Diocletian (303). Constantine, after attributing his victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) to the Christian God, issued with Licinius the Edict of Milan (313), granting religious tolerance. He funded churches, called the Council of Nicaea (325) and was baptised on his deathbed. Theodosius I made Christianity the state religion in 380.

d: Alaric's army sacked Rome.
x: What happened # Alaric’s army sacked Rome. Causes, course and consequences # Alaric, king of the Visigoths, besieged Rome three times after the emperor refused his demands for land and titles. On 24 August 410 his troops entered and looted the city for three days, though they spared churches. It was the first sack in 800 years, shocking the Roman world; Augustine wrote City of God to defend Christianity against blame.

d: Toramana and Mihirakula attacked northern India.
x: What happened # Toramana and Mihirakula attacked northern India. Causes, course and consequences # The Alchon Huns, a branch of the ‘White Huns’, invaded north-west India from about 460 CE; Skandagupta repelled them, but under Toramana and Mihirakula they took Punjab, Gandhara and Malwa. Xuanzang later reported Mihirakula destroyed Buddhist monasteries. The Aulikara king Yashodharman defeated Mihirakula around 528, but the invasions weakened Gupta power and trade.

d: Muslims defeated the Meccans.
x: What happened # Muslims defeated the Meccans. Causes, course and consequences # In March 624 about 313 Muslims from Medina intercepted a Meccan caravan and fought a Quraysh army roughly three times larger at the wells of Badr. The Muslim victory, seen as divine support (the Quran refers to angels), killed several Meccan leaders including Abu Jahl. It established Muhammad as a political and military leader and strengthened the community in Medina.

d: Arab armies defeated the Persians.
x: What happened # Arab armies defeated the Persians. Causes, course and consequences # In 636 an Arab army under Sa’d ibn Abi Waqqas met the Sasanian Persian army led by Rustam near Kufa in Iraq. After three or four days of fighting, including against Persian war elephants, Rustam was killed. The victory opened Mesopotamia, and the capital Ctesiphon fell in 637; Persia gradually converted to Islam while keeping its language and culture.

d: Studied at Nalanda and brought texts to China.
x: What happened # Studied at Nalanda and brought texts to China. Causes, course and consequences # Defying a travel ban, the monk Xuanzang left Chang’an in 629 and crossed the Taklamakan desert and the Pamirs to reach India. He studied for years at Nalanda under Shilabhadra, debated at Harsha’s court, and returned in 645 with 657 texts, which he spent his life translating. His ‘Great Tang Records on the Western Regions’ describes Indian cities, customs and rulers and guided archaeologists to sites like Nalanda.

d: Songtsen Gampo's successors rivalled the Tang.
x: What happened # Songtsen Gampo’s successors rivalled the Tang. Causes, course and consequences # Under Songtsen Gampo, Tibet became an empire in the 7th century; he married a Chinese princess (Wencheng) and a Nepali princess, bringing Buddhism. Tibet and Tang China fought for the Tarim basin’s Silk Road oasis cities for two centuries. In 763, when the Tang was weakened by the An Lushan rebellion, Tibetan armies briefly occupied Chang’an; a treaty pillar of 821–822 in Lhasa records peace.

d: One of the deadliest conflicts of pre-modern times.
x: What happened # One of the deadliest conflicts of pre-modern times. Causes, course and consequences # An Lushan, a general of Sogdian–Turkic descent who commanded border armies, rebelled in 755, capturing Luoyang and Chang’an. Emperor Xuanzong fled, and his beloved consort Yang Guifei was executed by his own troops. The war lasted until 763 with help from Uyghur mercenaries; census numbers dropped sharply, and the Tang never fully recovered central control.

d: Crowned by Pope Leo III.
x: What happened # Crowned by Pope Leo III. Causes, course and consequences # Charlemagne, king of the Franks, had conquered the Lombards and Saxons and protected Pope Leo III from Roman enemies. On Christmas Day 800, Leo crowned him ‘Emperor of the Romans’ in St Peter’s. The title, rejected by Byzantium, laid the basis for the Holy Roman Empire and long rivalry between popes and emperors.

d: Monks massacred at a famous monastery.
x: What happened # Monks massacred at a famous monastery. Causes, course and consequences # On 8 June 793 Norse raiders attacked the island monastery of Lindisfarne off Northumberland, killing monks and seizing treasures. The scholar Alcuin wrote that such terror had never appeared in Britain. It marks the start of the Viking Age, when Scandinavians raided, traded and settled from Ireland to Russia.

d: Seljuks defeated Byzantium.
x: What happened # Seljuks defeated Byzantium. Causes, course and consequences # On 26 August 1071 the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine army in eastern Anatolia and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes, after some Byzantine units deserted. Civil war at Constantinople followed, and Turkish groups poured into Anatolia, which became ‘Turkey’. The Byzantine plea for help led to the First Crusade.

d: One of 17 raids into India.
x: What happened # One of 17 raids into India. Causes, course and consequences # Mahmud, ruler of Ghazni in Afghanistan, raided north India about 17 times between 1000 and 1027, looting temple wealth from Mathura, Kannauj and Thanesar. In 1025–26 he plundered the Somnath temple in Gujarat. Al-Biruni accompanied his court and wrote a study of India; the temple was rebuilt many times, most recently in 1951.

d: Built by Suryavarman II.
x: What happened # Built by Suryavarman II. Causes, course and consequences # Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat between about 1113 and 1150 as a temple to Vishnu and probably his own mausoleum, facing west. Its five towers represent Mount Meru, and 800 metres of bas-reliefs show the churning of the ocean of milk and battles from the Mahabharata and Ramayana. It later became a Buddhist site and is now on Cambodia’s flag.

d: After the Battle of Hattin.
x: What happened # After the Battle of Hattin. Causes, course and consequences # Saladin united Egypt and Syria and, on 4 July 1187, destroyed the crusader army at the Horns of Hattin. He took Jerusalem in October after negotiations, allowing many Christians to ransom themselves, in contrast to the 1099 massacre. The Third Crusade under Richard the Lionheart failed to retake it.

d: Crusaders attacked a Christian city.
x: What happened # Crusaders attacked a Christian city. Causes, course and consequences # Crusaders, indebted to Venice for ships, were diverted to Constantinople to back a Byzantine claimant. In April 1204 they stormed and sacked the city, looting churches and taking the bronze horses now in Venice. A Latin Empire ruled until 1261, permanently weakening Byzantium and the relationship between Catholic and Orthodox churches.

d: Mamluks defeated the Mongols.
x: What happened # Mamluks defeated the Mongols. Causes, course and consequences # On 3 September 1260 the Mamluks of Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol army in Galilee, the first major check on Mongol expansion. Hulagu had withdrawn much of his army after the Great Khan’s death. Baybars soon killed Qutuz and became sultan.

d: His book inspired Columbus.
x: What happened # His book inspired Columbus. Causes, course and consequences # The Venetian Marco Polo travelled with his father and uncle along the Silk Road, reaching Kublai Khan around 1275 and serving him for 17 years. Imprisoned in Genoa after returning, he dictated his travels to Rustichello. His book described paper money, coal and great cities, and inspired Columbus.

d: Typhoons wrecked Kublai's fleets.
x: What happened # Typhoons wrecked Kublai’s fleets. Causes, course and consequences # Kublai Khan demanded Japan’s submission; when refused, he sent a fleet in 1274 and a much larger one, possibly 140,000 men, in 1281. Samurai fought fiercely and built a stone wall at Hakata Bay, and typhoons — the kamikaze or ‘divine winds’ — destroyed the fleets. The failure strained the Kamakura shogunate.

d: Rain-ruined harvests at the start of the Little Ice Age.
x: What happened # Rain-ruined harvests at the start of the Little Ice Age. Causes, course and consequences # Torrential rains from 1315 to 1317 rotted crops across northern Europe, followed by livestock disease. Perhaps 5–12% of the population died, and there were reports of cannibalism. It marked the end of medieval population growth, just before the Black Death.

d: Joan of Arc; the longbow at Agincourt.
x: What happened # Joan of Arc; the longbow at Agincourt. Causes, course and consequences # English kings claimed the French throne; the war (1337–1453) saw English longbow victories at Crécy, Poitiers and Agincourt. Joan of Arc helped lift the siege of Orléans (1429), and France eventually drove the English out except from Calais. The war strengthened national identities and the use of cannon.

d: Tens of thousands killed.
x: What happened # Tens of thousands killed. Causes, course and consequences # Timur invaded India in 1398, defeated Sultan Nasir-ud-din Mahmud Tughlaq, and sacked Delhi in December. He massacred about 100,000 prisoners before the battle and took artisans to build Samarkand. The Tughlaq state collapsed; his descendant Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

d: Treasure fleets reached Calicut and East Africa.
x: What happened # Treasure fleets reached Calicut and East Africa. Causes, course and consequences # Between 1405 and 1433, the Muslim eunuch admiral Zheng He led seven Ming fleets of up to 300 ships and 27,000 men to Southeast Asia, Calicut, Hormuz, Arabia and East Africa. They brought back tributes, including a giraffe from Malindi. After 1433 the Ming stopped the voyages and turned inward.

d: One of medieval Europe's largest battles.
x: What happened # One of medieval Europe’s largest battles. Causes, course and consequences # The Teutonic Knights, a crusading order, ruled Prussia and fought Christian Lithuania and Poland. On 15 July 1410 King Władysław II Jagiełło and Grand Duke Vytautas led about 30,000 Poles, Lithuanians, Ruthenians and Tatars against the Order; the Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen was killed. It broke the Order’s power and remains a symbol of Polish and Lithuanian pride.

d: Expulsion of Jews followed.
x: What happened # Expulsion of Jews followed. Causes, course and consequences # The Christian reconquest of Iberia from Muslim rulers took over 700 years. Ferdinand and Isabella besieged Granada, the last Nasrid kingdom, which surrendered on 2 January 1492. That year Jews were expelled, Muslims were later forced to convert, and Columbus sailed under the same monarchs.

d: Afonso de Albuquerque captured it.
x: What happened # Afonso de Albuquerque captured it. Causes, course and consequences # Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate in 1510, with help from local ally Timmayya. Goa became the capital of Portugal’s Asian empire and a centre of Catholic missions, including the Inquisition (1560). It remained Portuguese until India took it in 1961.

d: Luther's 95 theses.
x: What happened # Luther’s 95 theses. Causes, course and consequences # Martin Luther, a German monk, attacked the sale of indulgences in his Ninety-five Theses (1517), arguing salvation came through faith alone. Printing spread his ideas; Zwingli, Calvin and Henry VIII’s break with Rome followed. Wars of religion and the Catholic Counter-Reformation reshaped Europe.

d: Babur defeated Rana Sanga.
x: What happened # Babur defeated Rana Sanga. Causes, course and consequences # After Panipat, the Rajput leader Rana Sanga of Mewar, allied with Afghan chiefs, gathered an army of perhaps 100,000 to drive Babur out. On 17 March 1527, near Fatehpur Sikri, Babur rallied his troops by renouncing wine and declaring the war a jihad, then used artillery and cavalry flanking. The Rajputs were defeated and Sanga died soon after, securing Mughal power.

d: Hemu defeated.
x: What happened # Hemu defeated. Causes, course and consequences # After Humayun’s death, Hemu, a Hindu general of the Suri dynasty, took Delhi and proclaimed himself Raja Vikramaditya. On 5 November 1556 Akbar’s army under Bairam Khan fought him; an arrow struck Hemu’s eye, his army broke, and he was executed. Akbar’s long reign began.

d: Maharana Pratap fought Akbar's army.
x: What happened # Maharana Pratap fought Akbar’s army. Causes, course and consequences # Maharana Pratap of Mewar refused to accept Mughal overlordship. On 18 June 1576, at a narrow pass near Gogunda, his army of about 3,000 cavalry and Bhil archers fought a larger Mughal army led by Raja Man Singh of Amber. Pratap escaped on his horse Chetak, which died after carrying him to safety. He waged guerrilla war for 20 years and recovered most of Mewar except Chittor.

d: Storms and fireships scattered the fleet.
x: What happened # Storms and fireships scattered the fleet. Causes, course and consequences # Philip II of Spain, angered by English raids and the execution of Mary Queen of Scots, sent an Armada of about 130 ships in 1588 to escort an invasion army from the Netherlands. English ships harassed it in the Channel, and fireships broke its formation off Calais, followed by battle at Gravelines. Storms wrecked many ships as they sailed around Scotland and Ireland.

d: Admiral Yi's turtle ships.
x: What happened # Admiral Yi’s turtle ships. Causes, course and consequences # Toyotomi Hideyoshi, having unified Japan, invaded Korea in 1592 with about 158,000 troops armed with muskets, capturing Seoul in weeks. Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s turtle ships destroyed Japanese supply fleets at Hansan and Myeongnyang, and Ming China sent armies. After Hideyoshi’s death in 1598, Japan withdrew; Korea lost perhaps a million people.

d: Decided Japan's unification.
x: What happened # Decided Japan’s unification. Causes, course and consequences # After Hideyoshi’s death, regents competed for power. On 21 October 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu’s Eastern Army of about 75,000 fought Ishida Mitsunari’s Western Army at Sekigahara; Kobayakawa Hideaki’s defection decided the battle. Ieyasu became shogun in 1603, founding the Tokugawa shogunate that ruled until 1868.

d: Monopoly on Asian spice trade.
x: What happened # Monopoly on Asian spice trade. Causes, course and consequences # Founded in 1602, the VOC was the first company to issue public shares on a stock exchange (Amsterdam). With power to wage war and make treaties, it seized the Spice Islands, based itself in Batavia (Jakarta), and controlled the nutmeg and clove trade through violence, including the massacre of Banda islanders (1621).

d: First permanent English colony.
x: What happened # First permanent English colony. Causes, course and consequences # In 1607 the Virginia Company founded Jamestown, the first permanent English colony in America. Many settlers starved; tobacco became the cash crop, and in 1619 the first enslaved Africans arrived in Virginia. Relations with the Powhatan Confederacy included Pocahontas’s marriage to John Rolfe.

d: Charles I beheaded (1649).
x: What happened # Charles I beheaded (1649). Causes, course and consequences # Charles I ruled without Parliament for 11 years and imposed religious reforms. War began in 1642 between Royalists and Parliamentarians; Oliver Cromwell’s New Model Army won at Naseby (1645). Charles was tried and beheaded in 1649, England became a republic, and Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector. The monarchy returned in 1660 under Charles II.

d: Ming collapsed after Li Zicheng's revolt.
x: What happened # Ming collapsed after Li Zicheng’s revolt. Causes, course and consequences # Rebels under Li Zicheng took Beijing in April 1644, and the last Ming emperor hanged himself. General Wu Sangui opened the Shanhai Pass to the Manchus, who defeated Li and took Beijing, proclaiming the Qing dynasty. Ming loyalists resisted in the south for decades, and Taiwan fell only in 1683; Han men were forced to adopt the Manchu queue.

d: Crowned Chhatrapati.
x: What happened # Crowned Chhatrapati. Causes, course and consequences # Shivaji had built a state from Bijapur and Mughal lands, but needed formal kingship to treat with other rulers as an equal. On 6 June 1674 at Raigad fort, the scholar Gaga Bhatt crowned him Chhatrapati with Vedic rites; he took the title Haindava Dharmoddharak and began a new era (Rajyabhishek Shaka). He issued coins and established the Ashta Pradhan council.

d: Bill of Rights (1689).
x: What happened # Bill of Rights (1689). Causes, course and consequences # James II, a Catholic, angered Parliament, especially when his son was born in 1688, raising the prospect of a Catholic dynasty. Leading nobles invited the Dutch William of Orange, married to James’s Protestant daughter Mary; William landed in November and James fled. The Bill of Rights (1689) limited royal power, establishing parliamentary sovereignty.

d: Succession wars followed.
x: What happened # Succession wars followed. Causes, course and consequences # Aurangzeb ruled the Mughal Empire at its largest extent but spent his last 25 years fighting Marathas in the Deccan. He reimposed jizya and alienated Rajputs and Sikhs. He died at Ahmednagar in 1707, aged 88. Wars of succession followed, governors in Bengal, Hyderabad and Awadh became independent, and Maratha power expanded.

d: A massacre in Delhi.
x: What happened # A massacre in Delhi. Causes, course and consequences # Nadir Shah, ruler of Persia, invaded India in 1738–39, defeating Emperor Muhammad Shah’s army at Karnal. In Delhi, after a rumour of his death sparked attacks on his troops, he ordered a massacre on 22 March 1739 that killed about 20,000–30,000 people. He carried off the Peacock Throne, the Koh-i-Noor and vast treasure, exposing Mughal weakness.

d: Called the first world war.
x: What happened # Called the first world war. Causes, course and consequences # From 1756 to 1763 Britain and Prussia fought France, Austria and Russia in Europe, North America, the Caribbean and India — often called the first world war. In India, Clive’s victory at Plassey and Eyre Coote’s at Wandiwash (1760) ended French ambitions. Britain gained Canada and dominance in India, but its war debts led to taxes on American colonies.

d: A disputed incident used in British propaganda.
x: What happened # A disputed incident used in British propaganda. Causes, course and consequences # After Siraj ud-Daulah captured Fort William in June 1756, British prisoners were held overnight in a small guardroom. John Holwell claimed 123 of 146 died of suffocation; historians think the numbers were exaggerated. The story was used to justify the British counter-attack leading to Plassey.

d: The Company became Bengal's tax collector.
x: What happened # The Company became Bengal’s tax collector. Causes, course and consequences # Signed in August 1765 after Buxar, it gave the East India Company the diwani — the right to collect revenue — of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha from Mughal emperor Shah Alam II, in return for an annual tribute. This ‘dual government’ made the Company a territorial power.

d: Efficient steam power for factories.
x: What happened # Efficient steam power for factories. Causes, course and consequences # Newcomen’s 1712 steam engine pumped water from mines but wasted fuel. James Watt, an instrument maker at Glasgow University, added a separate condenser in 1769 and later a rotary motion mechanism. With Matthew Boulton, he sold engines that powered cotton mills, foundries and later locomotives — the heart of the Industrial Revolution.

d: Fixed land revenue.
x: What happened # Fixed land revenue. Causes, course and consequences # In 1793 Governor-General Cornwallis fixed land revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha permanently, making zamindars owners of land if they paid on time. The revenue fixed was high, and estates of defaulters were auctioned, creating new landlords from merchants. Peasants lost customary rights and faced rack-renting, while the Company gained a stable income.

d: British control of the south.
x: What happened # British control of the south. Causes, course and consequences # After Tipu Sultan sought French alliance, Governor-General Wellesley launched the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War. In May 1799 British and Hyderabadi forces stormed Srirangapatna’s walls; Tipu died fighting near a gate. Mysore was given back to the Wodeyar dynasty as a subsidiary ally, and much of Tipu’s territory was annexed.

d: Wellington and Blücher won.
x: What happened # Wellington and Blücher won. Causes, course and consequences # Escaping exile on Elba, Napoleon returned to power in 1815 for the ‘Hundred Days’. On 18 June near Waterloo in Belgium, he attacked the Duke of Wellington’s Anglo-allied army; the arrival of Blücher’s Prussians in the afternoon decided the battle. Napoleon abdicated and was exiled to St Helena, ending 23 years of war.

d: Bolívar and San Martín led wars of independence.
x: What happened # Bolívar and San Martín led wars of independence. Causes, course and consequences # Napoleon’s invasion of Spain (1808) set off independence movements. Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led armies that liberated most of Spanish South America by 1825; Mexico won independence in 1821 and Brazil in 1822. New republics faced inequality and military rule.

d: Campaign led by Ram Mohan Roy.
x: What happened # Campaign led by Ram Mohan Roy. Causes, course and consequences # Sati, the burning of widows on their husband’s pyre, was practised among some communities, with hundreds of cases a year recorded in Bengal. Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against it, quoting scriptures. In 1829 Governor-General Bentinck’s Regulation XVII made sati illegal, and the Privy Council rejected an appeal by orthodox groups in 1832.

d: Created an English-educated class.
x: What happened # Created an English-educated class. Causes, course and consequences # In February 1835 Thomas Babington Macaulay argued that government money should fund English education rather than Sanskrit and Arabic, claiming ‘a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India’. Bentinck adopted it in the English Education Act. It created an English-educated middle class that later led the freedom movement.

d: Potato blight and British policy.
x: What happened # Potato blight and British policy. Causes, course and consequences # Potato blight (Phytophthora infestans) struck in 1845, destroying the staple food of Ireland’s poor. British relief was limited and food exports continued. About 1 million people died and another million emigrated, many to America. Ireland’s population fell from 8.5 million to about 6.5 million.

d: A wave across Europe.
x: What happened # A wave across Europe. Causes, course and consequences # Economic crisis and demands for constitutions and national unity sparked revolts in France, the German and Italian states, Austria and Hungary in 1848. The French monarchy fell and a republic was declared; Metternich fled Vienna. Most revolts were crushed by 1849, but serfdom was abolished in Austria, and that year Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto.

d: 34 km run.
x: What happened # 34 km run. Causes, course and consequences # On 16 April 1853 a train with 14 carriages and three locomotives ran 34 km from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane. Lord Dalhousie promoted railways for trade and military use; by 1900 India had about 40,000 km. Railways also helped unify Indians and moved famine grain — but freight rates favoured British exports.

d: Led by a man claiming to be Jesus's brother.
x: What happened # Led by a man claiming to be Jesus’s brother. Causes, course and consequences # Hong Xiuquan, a failed examination candidate, believed after a vision that he was Jesus’s younger brother. His Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, promising land equality and banning opium and foot-binding, captured Nanjing in 1853. Qing armies, led by Zeng Guofan and aided by Western-led forces, crushed it by 1864. About 20–30 million died.

d: End of the shogunate.
x: What happened # End of the shogunate. Causes, course and consequences # After Commodore Perry forced Japan open (1853–54), samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū rebelled against the Tokugawa shogunate and restored power to the young Emperor Meiji in 1868. The new government abolished feudal domains and the samurai class, adopted Western technology, built railways and a modern army and navy, and drafted a constitution (1889). Japan defeated China (1895) and Russia (1905).

d: Cut sailing distance by ~7,000 km.
x: What happened # Cut sailing distance by ~7,000 km. Causes, course and consequences # The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps obtained a concession from Egypt’s ruler and built the 164 km canal between 1859 and 1869, using forced labour; thousands died. It opened on 17 November 1869, cutting the London–Bombay sea voyage by about 7,000 km. Britain bought Egypt’s shares in 1875 and occupied Egypt in 1882.

d: Bismarck's wars.
x: What happened # Bismarck’s wars. Causes, course and consequences # Otto von Bismarck, Prussia’s minister-president, used ‘blood and iron’. Prussia defeated Denmark (1864) over Schleswig-Holstein, Austria (1866) to exclude it from Germany, and France (1870–71). On 18 January 1871, William I was proclaimed German Emperor in Versailles’ Hall of Mirrors, and France lost Alsace-Lorraine.

d: No Africans were invited.
x: What happened # No Africans were invited. Causes, course and consequences # From November 1884 to February 1885, convened by Bismarck, 14 powers met to regulate colonisation in Africa. They agreed that claims required ‘effective occupation’ and recognised King Leopold II’s Congo Free State. No African was invited. Within 30 years, Europeans controlled 90% of Africa.

d: Menelik II defeated Italy.
x: What happened # Menelik II defeated Italy. Causes, course and consequences # Italy claimed a protectorate over Ethiopia based on a disputed treaty. On 1 March 1896 Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu’s army of about 100,000, armed with modern rifles, defeated about 17,000 Italian troops at Adwa. Italy recognised Ethiopian independence, making Ethiopia a symbol of African freedom.

d: 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk.
x: What happened # 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk. Causes, course and consequences # Bicycle makers Orville and Wilbur Wright studied gliders and built a wind tunnel to test wings. On 17 December 1903 at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville flew the Wright Flyer for 12 seconds and 37 m; Wilbur later flew 260 m. Within 15 years aircraft were used in World War I.

d: Inspired anti-colonial movements.
x: What happened # Inspired anti-colonial movements. Causes, course and consequences # Russia and Japan clashed over Manchuria and Korea. Japan attacked Port Arthur in February 1904, won at Mukden, and destroyed Russia’s Baltic Fleet at Tsushima (May 1905). The Treaty of Portsmouth gave Japan Korea and southern Manchuria. Asia’s first modern victory over a European power inspired nationalists from India to Egypt.

d: Sun Yat-sen's republic.
x: What happened # Sun Yat-sen’s republic. Causes, course and consequences # The Qing dynasty faced foreign humiliation and reform demands. On 10 October 1911 an army uprising at Wuchang spread across provinces; Sun Yat-sen was elected provisional president. The child emperor Puyi abdicated in February 1912, ending over 2,000 years of imperial rule, but China soon fell into warlord division.

d: Against forced indigo farming.
x: What happened # Against forced indigo farming. Causes, course and consequences # Under the tinkathia system, farmers in Champaran, Bihar, had to grow indigo on 3/20 of their land for European planters. In 1917, at the request of farmer Raj Kumar Shukla, Gandhi went there, defied an order to leave, and recorded farmers’ testimonies. The government formed an inquiry and abolished the system — Gandhi’s first successful satyagraha in India.

d: Atatürk's reforms.
x: What happened # Atatürk’s reforms. Causes, course and consequences # After the Ottoman defeat in World War I, the Allies planned to partition Anatolia. Mustafa Kemal led the Turkish War of Independence (1919–22) against Greek, Armenian and Allied forces. The Treaty of Lausanne (1923) recognised Turkey, and the Republic was proclaimed on 29 October 1923; Atatürk abolished the caliphate, adopted the Latin alphabet and secularised the state.

d: Long March (1934–35).
x: What happened # Long March (1934–35). Causes, course and consequences # The Nationalists (Kuomintang) under Chiang Kai-shek turned on their Communist allies in 1927. Mao Zedong’s Red Army survived the Long March (1934–35) and grew during the war against Japan. Civil war resumed in 1946; the Communists won and Chiang retreated to Taiwan in 1949.

d: Rehearsal for WWII.
x: What happened # Rehearsal for WWII. Causes, course and consequences # In July 1936 army generals led by Francisco Franco rebelled against Spain’s elected Popular Front government. Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy aided Franco, while the Soviet Union and International Brigades backed the Republic. The bombing of Guernica (1937), painted by Picasso, became a symbol of horror. Franco won in 1939 and ruled until 1975.

d: Nearly 2 million casualties.
x: What happened # Nearly 2 million casualties. Causes, course and consequences # In the summer of 1942 Germany’s Sixth Army attacked Stalingrad on the Volga. Brutal street fighting followed; in November the Soviets launched Operation Uranus, encircling the Germans. Field Marshal Paulus surrendered on 2 February 1943; total casualties reached about 2 million. It marked the turning point on the Eastern Front.

d: Called Britain's greatest battle.
x: What happened # Called Britain’s greatest battle. Causes, course and consequences # In March 1944 Japan, with Bose’s Indian National Army, invaded Manipur and Nagaland aiming to reach India. British and Indian troops, supplied by air, held Imphal and fought at close quarters at Kohima’s tennis court. Japan lost about 55,000 men, its largest defeat on land; in 2013 the battles were voted Britain’s greatest battle.

d: India was a founding member.
x: What happened # India was a founding member. Causes, course and consequences # The League of Nations failed to prevent World War II. In April–June 1945, 50 nations met in San Francisco and signed the UN Charter on 26 June; it came into force on 24 October 1945. The Security Council has five permanent members with vetoes. India was a founding member, and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights followed in 1948.

d: Sukarno declared independence.
x: What happened # Sukarno declared independence. Causes, course and consequences # After Japan’s surrender, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta declared independence on 17 August 1945. The Dutch returned and fought a four-year war with ‘police actions’. Under UN and US pressure, the Netherlands recognised Indonesia’s sovereignty in December 1949.

t: Creation of Israel and the Nakba
d: Arab–Israeli war followed.
x: What happened # Arab–Israeli war followed. Causes, course and consequences # After the Holocaust, the UN voted in November 1947 to partition Palestine. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, and neighbouring Arab states attacked. Israel won; about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled — the Nakba (‘catastrophe’), creating a refugee problem that persists.

d: Killed by Nathuram Godse.
x: What happened # Killed by Nathuram Godse. Causes, course and consequences # On 30 January 1948, at Birla House in Delhi, Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who blamed Gandhi for Partition and concessions to Pakistan, shot him three times. Gandhi died aged 78. Godse and Narayan Apte were hanged in 1949. The government briefly banned the RSS.

d: An armistice, never a peace treaty.
x: What happened # An armistice, never a peace treaty. Causes, course and consequences # Korea was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945. On 25 June 1950 North Korea invaded the South; UN forces led by the US drove north to the Chinese border, then Chinese troops pushed them back. After about 3 million deaths, an armistice in July 1953 restored a border near the 38th parallel. India chaired the commission for prisoner repatriation.

d: Kwame Nkrumah.
x: What happened # Kwame Nkrumah. Causes, course and consequences # The Gold Coast’s Convention People’s Party, led by Kwame Nkrumah, campaigned for self-government with strikes and boycotts. On 6 March 1957 Ghana became independent, the first sub-Saharan colony to do so. Nkrumah championed Pan-Africanism, inspiring independence movements across the continent.

d: China won a short war.
x: What happened # China won a short war. Causes, course and consequences # Disputes over the McMahon Line and Aksai Chin, India’s ‘forward policy’ and China’s anger over the Dalai Lama’s asylum led China to attack on 20 October 1962. Chinese forces advanced in Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh and then declared a ceasefire, withdrawing in the east. India’s defeat led to military modernisation.

d: Thirteen days.
x: What happened # Thirteen days. Causes, course and consequences # In October 1962 US spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. Kennedy imposed a naval ‘quarantine’, and the world came closer to nuclear war than ever before. Khrushchev withdrew the missiles in exchange for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and the secret removal of US missiles from Turkey.

d: High-yield wheat and rice.
x: What happened # High-yield wheat and rice. Causes, course and consequences # After droughts in 1965–66 forced India to import food, scientists M. S. Swaminathan and Norman Borlaug introduced high-yield dwarf wheat and rice. With irrigation, fertilisers and support prices, Punjab and Haryana’s output soared and India became self-sufficient. It also caused groundwater depletion and soil problems.

d: Indira Gandhi's rule by decree.
x: What happened # Indira Gandhi’s rule by decree. Causes, course and consequences # After a court voided her election and opposition protests grew, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency on 25 June 1975. Opposition leaders were jailed, the press censored, and forced sterilisation campaigns were run. She lost the 1977 election to the Janata Party.

d: Shah overthrown.
x: What happened # Shah overthrown. Causes, course and consequences # Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi’s autocratic modernisation and secret police (SAVAK) provoked protests by clerics, students and workers. The Shah fled in January 1979, and Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile to found an Islamic Republic. US embassy staff were held hostage for 444 days.

d: The worst industrial disaster.
x: What happened # The worst industrial disaster. Causes, course and consequences # On the night of 2–3 December 1984 about 40 tonnes of methyl isocyanate leaked from Union Carbide’s pesticide plant in Bhopal. Thousands died within days and estimates of total deaths reach 15,000–20,000, with hundreds of thousands injured. It is the world’s worst industrial disaster.

d: A reactor exploded.
x: What happened # A reactor exploded. Causes, course and consequences # On 26 April 1986 a safety test went wrong at Reactor 4 of the Chernobyl plant in Soviet Ukraine, causing an explosion and fire. Radioactive fallout spread over Europe, 350,000 people were relocated, and an exclusion zone remains. Soviet secrecy damaged trust and helped glasnost.

d: Mandela elected.
x: What happened # Mandela elected. Causes, course and consequences # Apartheid, enforced from 1948, segregated South Africa by race. Under internal resistance and international sanctions, President F. W. de Klerk released Nelson Mandela in 1990. Negotiations led to the first democratic elections in April 1994, and Mandela became president.

d: In about 100 days.
x: What happened # In about 100 days. Causes, course and consequences # After the president’s plane was shot down on 6 April 1994, Hutu extremist militias and soldiers killed about 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in about 100 days, often with machetes, encouraged by radio broadcasts. The UN failed to intervene. The Tutsi-led RPF ended the genocide in July.

d: Mortgage collapse.
x: What happened # Mortgage collapse. Causes, course and consequences # Low interest rates and lax regulation fuelled risky subprime mortgages bundled into complex securities. When US house prices fell in 2007, losses spread; Lehman Brothers collapsed on 15 September 2008. Governments bailed out banks and central banks slashed rates. The Great Recession followed, with millions losing jobs and homes.

d: Started in Tunisia.
x: What happened # Started in Tunisia. Causes, course and consequences # In December 2010 the self-immolation of Tunisian street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi sparked protests that toppled Tunisia’s Ben Ali. Uprisings spread to Egypt, Libya, Yemen, Bahrain and Syria. Tunisia briefly democratised, Egypt returned to military rule, and Syria, Libya and Yemen fell into civil wars.

d: Overtook China.
x: What happened # Overtook China. Causes, course and consequences # In April 2023, according to UN estimates, India overtook China with about 1.43 billion people, while China’s population had begun to decline. India’s population is young, with a median age under 30. The shift has implications for jobs, resources and global influence.

d: A small population of Homo sapiens left Africa, probably across the Bab-el-Mandeb strait or through Sinai, and spread along the southern coasts of Arabia and India to Southeast Asia and Australia within about 15,000 years. They met and interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans, which is why most people outside Africa carry about 2% Neanderthal DNA. Ancient DNA and stone tools from sites such as Jwalapuram in India help map the route.
x: What happened # A small population of Homo sapiens left Africa, probably across the Bab-el-Mandeb strait or through Sinai, and spread along the southern coasts of Arabia and India to Southeast Asia and Australia within about 15,000 years. They met and interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans, which is why most people outside Africa carry about 2% Neanderthal DNA. Ancient DNA and stone tools from sites such as Jwalapuram in India help map the route. Causes, course and consequences # Fossils from Misliya and Apidima show early Homo sapiens groups left Africa as early as 180,000–210,000 years ago, but these populations left little genetic trace. Genetic studies of living people show that all non-Africans descend mainly from a population that left about 60,000–50,000 years ago, possibly when climate opened green corridors across Arabia. Moving along coasts and river valleys, they reached South Asia, Australia by about 50,000 years ago and Europe by 45,000 years ago. On the way they interbred with Neanderthals in western Asia and with Denisovans further east, inheriting genes that still affect immunity, skin and altitude adaptation. Mitochondrial DNA shows India was one of the earliest regions settled, and Indians today carry some of the deepest non-African lineages.

d: When sea levels were low in the Ice Age, Beringia linked Siberia and Alaska. People crossed and moved south along the Pacific coast or through an ice-free corridor; footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, suggest presence by about 21,000 years ago, and Monte Verde in Chile was occupied by 14,500 years ago. Within a few thousand years humans reached Tierra del Fuego.
x: What happened # When sea levels were low in the Ice Age, Beringia linked Siberia and Alaska. People crossed and moved south along the Pacific coast or through an ice-free corridor; footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, suggest presence by about 21,000 years ago, and Monte Verde in Chile was occupied by 14,500 years ago. Within a few thousand years humans reached Tierra del Fuego. Causes, course and consequences # During the Last Glacial Maximum, sea levels dropped and created Beringia, a land bridge up to 1,000 km wide. Ancient DNA shows Native Americans descend from a population that mixed Siberian and East Asian ancestry and lived isolated in Beringia for thousands of years (the ‘Beringian standstill’). They entered the Americas probably along the Pacific coast by boat, reaching Monte Verde in Chile by 14,500 years ago; White Sands footprints suggest people were in New Mexico by 21,000–23,000 years ago. Clovis hunters spread across North America about 13,000 years ago, and later migrations brought the ancestors of Na-Dene and Inuit peoples.

d: Farmers speaking Bantu languages spread from the Cameroon–Nigeria borderlands across central, eastern and southern Africa over 2,000 years, carrying yams, sorghum, cattle and, later, ironworking. Today about 350 million people speak some 500 Bantu languages, including Swahili, Zulu and Kikongo, and genetic studies trace the movement.
x: What happened # Farmers speaking Bantu languages spread from the Cameroon–Nigeria borderlands across central, eastern and southern Africa over 2,000 years, carrying yams, sorghum, cattle and, later, ironworking. Today about 350 million people speak some 500 Bantu languages, including Swahili, Zulu and Kikongo, and genetic studies trace the movement. Causes, course and consequences # About 5,000–4,000 years ago, farmers speaking Bantu languages began moving out of the region on the Nigeria–Cameroon border. One stream went through the rainforest to Central Africa, and another east to the Great Lakes, where they adopted cattle and ironworking around 500 BCE, then south to southern Africa by 300 CE. They displaced or absorbed hunter-gatherers such as the ancestors of the Batwa and Khoisan, whose click sounds entered Xhosa and Zulu. Linguistic, archaeological and genetic evidence agree on this spread, which explains why over 500 related Bantu languages are spoken by about 350 million people from Cameroon to South Africa.

d: Austronesian-speaking farmers sailed out of Taiwan to the Philippines and Indonesia, then east into the Pacific as the Lapita culture and west to Madagascar, using outrigger canoes. They carried rice, pigs, chickens and taro. Their languages, from Malagasy to Hawaiian, now span half the globe's longitudes.
x: What happened # Austronesian-speaking farmers sailed out of Taiwan to the Philippines and Indonesia, then east into the Pacific as the Lapita culture and west to Madagascar, using outrigger canoes. They carried rice, pigs, chickens and taro. Their languages, from Malagasy to Hawaiian, now span half the globe’s longitudes. Causes, course and consequences # Austronesian-speaking rice farmers from southern China settled Taiwan about 5,500 years ago. Around 4,000 years ago they sailed to the Philippines and Indonesia using outrigger canoes and sails, then east as the Lapita culture to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by 800 BCE. Polynesian descendants reached Hawai’i, Rapa Nui and finally New Zealand around 1250 CE, and westward voyagers settled Madagascar around 500 CE. Austronesian languages (about 1,250 of them, including Malay, Tagalog, Malagasy and Hawaiian) are spoken across more than half the globe’s longitudes, and they spread rice, pigs, chickens, taro, breadfruit and navigation knowledge.

d: Ancient DNA shows that pastoralists of the Yamnaya culture, using wagons and horses, moved into Europe around 3000 BCE, and related steppe groups reached Central Asia and later South Asia around 2000–1500 BCE, mixing with local populations. The spread explains why Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, Persian and English share many words.
x: What happened # Ancient DNA shows that pastoralists of the Yamnaya culture, using wagons and horses, moved into Europe around 3000 BCE, and related steppe groups reached Central Asia and later South Asia around 2000–1500 BCE, mixing with local populations. The spread explains why Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, Persian and English share many words. Causes, course and consequences # Linguists reconstructed Proto-Indo-European from shared words like those for ‘father’, ‘horse’ and ‘wheel’. Ancient DNA studies since 2015 showed that Yamnaya herders of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, with wagons and horses, moved into Europe about 5,000 years ago, contributing much ancestry to Corded Ware peoples. Related steppe groups (Sintashta, Andronovo) spread east, and around 2000–1500 BCE some moved into South Asia, mixing with Indus-related populations; this ancestry is higher among some north Indian groups and Brahmins. The process was gradual migration and mixing, not a single ‘invasion’, and remains debated in India.

d: Coalitions of seafaring raiders attacked Anatolia, Cyprus, the Levant and Egypt; Ramesses III recorded his victory over them at Medinet Habu around 1175 BCE. Their identity is still debated. Along with drought, earthquakes and rebellions, they helped bring down the Hittite empire, Ugarit and Mycenaean palaces.
x: What happened # Coalitions of seafaring raiders attacked Anatolia, Cyprus, the Levant and Egypt; Ramesses III recorded his victory over them at Medinet Habu around 1175 BCE. Their identity is still debated. Along with drought, earthquakes and rebellions, they helped bring down the Hittite empire, Ugarit and Mycenaean palaces. Causes, course and consequences # Egyptian records at Medinet Habu name groups such as the Peleset (Philistines), Sherden, Shekelesh and Denyen, who attacked by land and sea with families and ox-carts around 1177 BCE. The rich trading city of Ugarit in Syria fell; its last tablets plead for help against enemy ships. The Hittite Empire, Mycenaean palaces and many Levantine cities collapsed around the same time. Modern historians see the Sea Peoples as both cause and symptom of a wider ‘systems collapse’ driven by drought, famine, earthquakes and broken trade networks. Some settled in Canaan, becoming the Philistines.

d: Clans became 16 mahajanapadas, kingdoms and republics such as Magadha, Kosala, Vajji and Gandhara, with cities, coins and armies. Republics (ganas) like the Vajji were governed by assemblies. This was the world the Buddha and Mahavira lived in.
x: What happened # Clans became 16 mahajanapadas, kingdoms and republics such as Magadha, Kosala, Vajji and Gandhara, with cities, coins and armies. Republics (ganas) like the Vajji were governed by assemblies. This was the world the Buddha and Mahavira lived in. Causes, course and consequences # By about 600 BCE, iron tools and rice farming in the Ganga plain supported growing towns, and Vedic tribes had become 16 great states (mahajanapadas) listed in Buddhist texts: Kashi, Kosala, Anga, Magadha, Vajji, Malla, Chedi, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Matsya, Surasena, Assaka, Avanti, Gandhara and Kamboja. Some were monarchies; others, like the Vajji and Malla, were republics (ganas) governed by assemblies of clan elders. Punch-marked silver coins, fortified cities like Rajagriha and Ujjain, and long-distance trade appeared. Magadha gradually conquered its rivals, laying the foundation for the Maurya Empire. Tradition places the Mahabharata war at Kurukshetra in this region.

d: Ashoka sponsored a council and sent missionaries, including his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka, where the Pali Canon was later written down. Buddhism then spread along trade routes to Central Asia, China and Southeast Asia.
x: What happened # Ashoka sponsored a council and sent missionaries, including his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka, where the Pali Canon was later written down. Buddhism then spread along trade routes to Central Asia, China and Southeast Asia. Causes, course and consequences # About 250 BCE Ashoka sponsored a council at Pataliputra under the monk Moggaliputta Tissa to purify the sangha and compile the Abhidhamma. Afterwards missionaries were sent to Gandhara, Kashmir, the Himalayas, Suvarnabhumi (Southeast Asia) and Sri Lanka, where Ashoka’s son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta, who carried a branch of the Bodhi tree, converted King Devanampiya Tissa. In Sri Lanka the Pali Canon was written down in the 1st century BCE. Ashoka’s edicts also mention envoys to Greek kings in the west. These missions turned Buddhism into a world religion.

d: Emperor Constantine called about 300 bishops to settle the Arian controversy over the nature of Christ; they issued the Nicene Creed, still recited by most Christians, and set the method of dating Easter.
x: What happened # Emperor Constantine called about 300 bishops to settle the Arian controversy over the nature of Christ; they issued the Nicene Creed, still recited by most Christians, and set the method of dating Easter. Causes, course and consequences # Arius, a priest of Alexandria, taught that Christ was created by the Father and was not equally divine, causing bitter disputes. Emperor Constantine, wanting church unity, convened about 250–318 bishops at Nicaea (İznik, Turkey) in 325, the first ecumenical council. It condemned Arius and adopted the Nicene Creed, declaring the Son ‘of one substance’ (homoousios) with the Father, set a common date for Easter, and issued church laws. Arianism remained powerful for decades, especially among Goths. The creed is still recited by Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant churches.

d: Founded under the Gupta king Kumaragupta I, Nalanda grew to host thousands of students and teachers in Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar, medicine and astronomy; Xuanzang and Yijing studied there. It flourished for 700 years until destroyed around 1193.
x: What happened # Founded under the Gupta king Kumaragupta I, Nalanda grew to host thousands of students and teachers in Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar, medicine and astronomy; Xuanzang and Yijing studied there. It flourished for 700 years until destroyed around 1193. Causes, course and consequences # Nalanda was founded around 427 CE under Gupta king Kumaragupta I near Rajagriha, and expanded by Harsha, the Palas and donors from Sumatra’s Sailendra kings. At its height it housed perhaps 10,000 students and 2,000 teachers in monasteries, temples and a nine-storey library called Dharmaganja. Entry required passing an oral examination by gatekeeper scholars. It taught Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar, medicine, astronomy and mathematics, and scholars like Nagarjuna, Dharmakirti and Shantarakshita are associated with it. Xuanzang and Yijing studied there. It was sacked around 1193, and its ruins became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

t: Spread of Islam to India via Kerala
d: Arab traders had long visited the Malabar coast for pepper; tradition dates the Cheraman Juma mosque at Kodungallur to 629 CE. Islam spread peacefully among coastal communities, forming the Mappila Muslims, long before conquests in the north.
x: What happened # Arab traders had long visited the Malabar coast for pepper; tradition dates the Cheraman Juma mosque at Kodungallur to 629 CE. Islam spread peacefully among coastal communities, forming the Mappila Muslims, long before conquests in the north. Causes, course and consequences # Arab traders had sailed to Kerala’s pepper ports for centuries before Islam. According to tradition, a Chera king, Cheraman Perumal, converted and travelled to Arabia, and Malik ibn Dinar founded the Cheraman Juma Mosque at Kodungallur around 629, though historians debate the date. Muslim traders married local women, forming the Mappila community, and Islam spread peacefully along the coast to Kerala, Konkan, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu. The Zamorins of Calicut protected Muslim merchants, who dominated Indian Ocean trade until the Portuguese arrived.

d: After the Battle of Talas, papermaking spread to Samarkand and then Baghdad (794), replacing papyrus and parchment, enabling the Islamic Golden Age's books and later Europe's printing.
x: What happened # After the Battle of Talas, papermaking spread to Samarkand and then Baghdad (794), replacing papyrus and parchment, enabling the Islamic Golden Age’s books and later Europe’s printing. Causes, course and consequences # Paper was invented in China, refined by Cai Lun around 105 CE. Tradition says that after the Battle of Talas (751), Chinese prisoners taught papermaking in Samarkand; whatever the exact route, by 794 a paper mill operated in Baghdad. Paper was much cheaper than papyrus or parchment, enabling an explosion of books, libraries, government records and translations in the Islamic world. Papermaking spread to Egypt, Morocco and Islamic Spain (Xàtiva, about 1150), then to Christian Europe, where it later made Gutenberg’s printing possible.

t: Founding of Baghdad and the House of Wisdom
d: Caliph al-Mansur founded the Round City of Baghdad; under al-Mamun the House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian works, and scholars such as al-Khwarizmi developed algebra and adopted Indian numerals.
x: What happened # Caliph al-Mansur founded the Round City of Baghdad; under al-Mamun the House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian works, and scholars such as al-Khwarizmi developed algebra and adopted Indian numerals. Causes, course and consequences # In 762 Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the Tigris as a perfectly round city about 2 km across, with the caliph’s palace and mosque at the centre. It grew into perhaps the world’s largest city, with over a million people by the 10th century, linked by trade to China, India and Africa. Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Mamun, the House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) translated Greek, Persian, Syriac and Sanskrit works; Indian astronomical texts were translated around 771. Scholars including al-Khwarizmi, al-Kindi and the Banu Musa brothers made advances in algebra, optics and engineering. It was destroyed by the Mongols in 1258.

d: Leif Erikson's Norse settlers built a camp at L'Anse aux Meadows, confirmed by excavation in the 1960s; tree rings date woodcutting there to 1021.
x: What happened # Leif Erikson’s Norse settlers built a camp at L’Anse aux Meadows, confirmed by excavation in the 1960s; tree rings date woodcutting there to 1021. Causes, course and consequences # Norse settlers from Iceland founded colonies in Greenland around 985 under Erik the Red. According to the Icelandic sagas, Bjarni Herjólfsson sighted land to the west, and Erik’s son Leif Erikson sailed there around 1000, naming regions Helluland, Markland and Vinland. In 1960 Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found the remains of a Norse settlement at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, and tree-ring evidence from cut wood dates activity there to exactly 1021. Conflict with Indigenous people, called skrælings, and long distances ended the attempts, almost 500 years before Columbus.

d: Rajendra I marched to the Ganga and built Gangaikonda Cholapuram, then sent a fleet to raid Srivijaya's ports (1025), the most ambitious overseas campaign by an Indian state.
x: What happened # Rajendra I marched to the Ganga and built Gangaikonda Cholapuram, then sent a fleet to raid Srivijaya’s ports (1025), the most ambitious overseas campaign by an Indian state. Causes, course and consequences # Rajendra I (r. 1014–1044), son of Rajaraja, sent an army north around 1019–1023 through Kalinga to the Ganga, defeating the Pala king Mahipala of Bengal. He brought back Ganga water in golden pots, took the title Gangaikonda (‘conqueror of the Ganga’), and founded a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, with a great temple and a huge tank called the Chola Gangam. In 1025 his navy raided Srivijaya in Southeast Asia. These campaigns made the Chola Empire the dominant power of South Asia and the Indian Ocean.

d: Great Zimbabwe's stone enclosures housed perhaps 18,000 people, trading gold to the coast for Chinese porcelain and Persian glass.
x: What happened # Great Zimbabwe’s stone enclosures housed perhaps 18,000 people, trading gold to the coast for Chinese porcelain and Persian glass. Causes, course and consequences # Between about 1200 and 1450, Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a Shona kingdom in the southern African plateau. Its Hill Complex, Great Enclosure with walls up to 11 m high and 250 m long, and conical tower were built of granite blocks without mortar. Wealth came from cattle and from gold mined in the region and traded through Sofala to Kilwa and the Indian Ocean; Chinese celadon, Persian pottery and Indian beads have been found there. Colonial authorities claimed foreigners built it, but archaeology proved its African origins; it gave its name to Zimbabwe at independence in 1980.

d: Mansa Musa travelled with thousands of attendants and camels laden with gold; his gifts in Cairo reportedly depressed gold's value for years. The 1375 Catalan Atlas shows him holding a gold nugget.
x: What happened # Mansa Musa travelled with thousands of attendants and camels laden with gold; his gifts in Cairo reportedly depressed gold’s value for years. The 1375 Catalan Atlas shows him holding a gold nugget. Causes, course and consequences # In 1324 Mansa Musa travelled from Mali to Mecca with a caravan reported to include 60,000 people, 12,000 slaves carrying gold bars, and 80 camels each carrying up to 300 pounds of gold dust. In Cairo he gave so much gold to officials and the poor that its value fell for about 12 years, according to the historian al-Umari. He returned with scholars, the Andalusian architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, and books, building mosques in Timbuktu and Gao. The journey put Mali on European maps; the 1375 Catalan Atlas depicts him seated on a throne with a golden orb.

d: According to legend, the Mexica found an eagle on a cactus on an island in Lake Texcoco and founded their city there; it is now Mexico City.
x: What happened # According to legend, the Mexica found an eagle on a cactus on an island in Lake Texcoco and founded their city there; it is now Mexico City. Causes, course and consequences # The Mexica, migrants from a legendary northern homeland called Aztlan, arrived in the Valley of Mexico around the 13th century as poor mercenaries. Their god Huitzilopochtli had told them to settle where they saw an eagle perched on a cactus eating a snake; in 1325 they saw this on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco. They built Tenochtitlan with causeways, canals and chinampas, and within two centuries it became a city of about 200,000, one of the largest in the world. The eagle-and-cactus symbol is on Mexico’s flag today.

d: Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Vienna in 1529 but withdrew; a second siege in 1683 was broken by Jan Sobieski's Polish cavalry, beginning Ottoman retreat.
x: What happened # Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Vienna in 1529 but withdrew; a second siege in 1683 was broken by Jan Sobieski’s Polish cavalry, beginning Ottoman retreat. Causes, course and consequences # After crushing Hungary at Mohács (1526), Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Vienna in September 1529 with about 120,000 men. Heavy rains forced him to leave his heavy artillery behind, the city’s defenders held out, and with winter approaching he withdrew in October. A second siege by Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa in 1683 was broken on 12 September by a relief army under King Jan III Sobieski of Poland, whose winged hussars made the largest cavalry charge in history. The defeat began the Ottoman retreat from central Europe; legend says the croissant was created to celebrate it.

d: Potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies and cacao went to the Old World; wheat, horses, cattle and diseases went to the Americas, where epidemics killed most of the indigenous population.
x: What happened # Potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies and cacao went to the Old World; wheat, horses, cattle and diseases went to the Americas, where epidemics killed most of the indigenous population. Causes, course and consequences # After 1492, plants, animals, people and diseases moved between the Americas and the rest of the world. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, cassava, peanuts, cacao and tobacco reached Europe, Africa and Asia; chillies arrived in India with the Portuguese, and potatoes helped Europe’s population boom. Wheat, rice, sugarcane, coffee, horses, cattle, pigs and sheep transformed the Americas. Smallpox, measles and influenza killed perhaps 50–90% of Indigenous Americans. To work new plantations, Europeans enslaved millions of Africans. The historian Alfred Crosby coined the term in 1972.

d: Ended the Thirty Years' War and the Eighty Years' War, recognising state sovereignty and religious coexistence.
x: What happened # Ended the Thirty Years’ War and the Eighty Years’ War, recognising state sovereignty and religious coexistence. Causes, course and consequences # The Peace of Westphalia, signed at Osnabrück and Münster in 1648, ended the Thirty Years’ War in the Holy Roman Empire and the Eighty Years’ War between Spain and the Netherlands. It confirmed the right of rulers to choose their state’s religion (Catholic, Lutheran or Calvinist), recognised Dutch and Swiss independence, and gave German princes near-sovereignty, weakening the emperor. It is often seen as the origin of the modern system of sovereign states that do not interfere in each other’s internal affairs, though historians debate this.

d: Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan fought four wars against the East India Company, using rockets; Tipu died at Srirangapatna in 1799.
x: What happened # Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan fought four wars against the East India Company, using rockets; Tipu died at Srirangapatna in 1799. Causes, course and consequences # Hyder Ali of Mysore fought the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767–69), reaching the outskirts of Madras and forcing a treaty. In the Second (1780–84), Hyder and his son Tipu destroyed a British force at Pollilur, using rockets; Hyder died during the war. In the Third (1790–92), Lord Cornwallis, allied with the Marathas and Nizam, took half of Tipu’s kingdom and two of his sons as hostages. In the Fourth (1799), Governor-General Wellesley stormed Srirangapatna, where Tipu died. Captured Mysorean rockets inspired William Congreve’s rockets used against Napoleon.

d: Brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu led about 60,000 Santhals against landlords, moneylenders and British officials; the rebellion was crushed but led to the Santhal Parganas district.
x: What happened # Brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu led about 60,000 Santhals against landlords, moneylenders and British officials; the rebellion was crushed but led to the Santhal Parganas district. Causes, course and consequences # Santhal farmers who had cleared forests in the Damin-i-Koh area (Rajmahal hills) were exploited by moneylenders, zamindars and police who charged huge interest and seized land. On 30 June 1855 the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu, with brothers Chand and Bhairav and sisters Phulo and Jhano, gathered about 10,000 Santhals at Bhognadih and declared rebellion. With bows and arrows they attacked moneylenders and Company posts. The army crushed the Hul by 1856, killing about 15,000. The Santhal Parganas district was created, and 30 June is celebrated as Hul Diwas.

t: Partition of Africa and the Congo Free State
d: King Leopold II's personal colony forced rubber collection with mutilation and terror; deaths are estimated at millions.
x: What happened # King Leopold II’s personal colony forced rubber collection with mutilation and terror; deaths are estimated at millions. Causes, course and consequences # At the Berlin Conference (1884–85), King Leopold II won recognition of the Congo Free State as his personal property, promising free trade and to end the slave trade. Instead his agents forced Congolese to collect wild rubber, then in high demand for bicycle and car tyres; soldiers of the Force Publique took women hostage, burned villages and cut off hands to prove bullets weren’t wasted. Millions died from violence, famine and disease. Journalists, missionaries and activists like E. D. Morel, Roger Casement, George Washington Williams and Mark Twain exposed the atrocities, and Belgium annexed the Congo in 1908.

d: Ottoman authorities deported and massacred Armenians during World War I.
x: What happened # Ottoman authorities deported and massacred Armenians during World War I. Causes, course and consequences # During World War I, the Committee of Union and Progress government of the Ottoman Empire accused Armenians of siding with Russia. On 24 April 1915 hundreds of Armenian intellectuals were arrested in Constantinople and later killed; then Armenian men were massacred and women, children and the elderly were deported on death marches into the Syrian desert. About 1 million to 1.5 million Armenians died. Assyrians and Greeks also suffered. Turkey denies it was genocide, but many countries and historians recognise it; the jurist Raphael Lemkin cited it when coining the word ‘genocide’.

d: Soviet collectivisation and grain requisitions caused a famine in Ukraine that killed about 3.5–5 million people.
x: What happened # Soviet collectivisation and grain requisitions caused a famine in Ukraine that killed about 3.5–5 million people. Causes, course and consequences # In 1932–33 Stalin’s forced collectivisation, impossible grain quotas, confiscation of food, and blacklisting of villages caused a famine in Ukraine. Peasants were banned from leaving to find food. About 3.5–5 million Ukrainians died, along with victims in Kazakhstan (where about 1.5 million died) and Russia. The Soviet government denied the famine, and some Western journalists like Walter Duranty helped cover it up, while Gareth Jones exposed it. Ukraine and many countries recognise it as a genocide.

d: Mao's forced collectivisation and steel campaigns caused famine killing perhaps 15–45 million.
x: What happened # Mao’s forced collectivisation and steel campaigns caused famine killing perhaps 15–45 million. Causes, course and consequences # In 1958 Mao launched the Great Leap Forward to overtake Britain’s industry within 15 years. Peasants were forced into huge communes, private cooking was banned, millions were sent to make useless steel in backyard furnaces, and pseudoscientific farming methods were imposed. Officials reported fake record harvests, so the state took grain for cities and export while villagers starved. Between 1959 and 1961 an estimated 15–45 million people died. The famine was hidden for decades; historians like Yang Jisheng and Frank Dikötter documented it.

t: Invention of the World Wide Web
d: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the web in 1989; the first website went live in 1991.
x: What happened # Tim Berners-Lee proposed the web in 1989; the first website went live in 1991. Causes, course and consequences # In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist at CERN in Switzerland, proposed a system to share documents across computers using hypertext.
