By 1990 he had written HTTP, HTML and the first web browser and server on a NeXT computer, and the first website went online in 1991. CERN made the technology royalty-free in 1993, and the Mosaic browser that year made it popular. The web, running over the internet, which grew from ARPANET, transformed communication, commerce and media.

d: An international project sequenced the human genome; ancient DNA later rewrote prehistory.
x: What happened # An international project sequenced the human genome; ancient DNA later rewrote prehistory. Causes, course and consequences # Launched in 1990 by the US and partners in Britain, Japan, France, Germany and China, the Human Genome Project aimed to sequence all 3 billion DNA letters of the human genome. A private company, Celera, led by Craig Venter, raced it. A draft was announced in 2000 and the project declared complete in 2003 at a cost of about $2.7 billion; a truly complete sequence came in 2022. It found humans have only about 20,000 protein-coding genes. Cheaper sequencing since then enabled ancient DNA research that rewrote human prehistory.

d: Alexander Graham Bell spoke the first words over a telephone to his assistant: 'Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.'
x: What happened # Alexander Graham Bell spoke the first words over a telephone to his assistant: ‘Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.’ Causes, course and consequences # Three days earlier Bell had received his patent, filed hours before Elisha Gray’s caveat. Bell’s transmitter in this test used a liquid (acid water) design similar to Gray’s, fuelling claims that he had seen Gray’s papers. Bell demonstrated the phone at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition, where Emperor Pedro II of Brazil exclaimed ‘My God, it talks!’. By 1886 over 150,000 Americans had phones.

t: Edison's light and Pearl Street station
d: Edison's team demonstrated long-lasting light bulbs at Menlo Park on New Year's Eve 1879, and opened the Pearl Street power station in 1882.
x: What happened # Edison’s team demonstrated long-lasting light bulbs at Menlo Park on New Year’s Eve 1879, and opened the Pearl Street power station in 1882. Causes, course and consequences # Pearl Street, in Manhattan’s financial district, supplied direct current to 82 customers and 400 lamps at first, including the New York Times and J. P. Morgan’s offices. DC could only travel about a mile, limiting the system. Swan’s competing bulbs lit London’s Savoy Theatre in 1881.

d: The Adams Power Plant at Niagara Falls began generating AC electricity using Tesla's polyphase system.
x: What happened # The Adams Power Plant at Niagara Falls began generating AC electricity using Tesla’s polyphase system. Causes, course and consequences # In 1896 power was sent 42 km to Buffalo, proving long-distance AC transmission. It ended the ‘war of the currents’, and Tesla’s statue now stands at Niagara Falls on both the US and Canadian sides.

d: The Lumière brothers screened ten short films to a paying audience at the Grand Café in Paris.
x: What happened # The Lumière brothers screened ten short films to a paying audience at the Grand Café in Paris. Causes, course and consequences # The films included workers leaving their factory; a legend says audiences fled from a film of an arriving train. In July 1896 the Lumières’ agents screened films at Watson’s Hotel in Bombay, India’s first cinema show. Within a decade nickelodeons spread across America.

d: Guglielmo Marconi received the Morse letter 'S' sent from Cornwall to St John's, Newfoundland.
x: What happened # Guglielmo Marconi received the Morse letter ‘S’ sent from Cornwall to St John’s, Newfoundland. Causes, course and consequences # Some scientists doubted it, since he used a kite antenna and noisy reception. His detector used a mercury coherer likely based on J. C. Bose’s design. In 1912 wireless messages from the sinking Titanic saved 700 lives.

d: Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria in a petri dish at St Mary's Hospital.
x: What happened # Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria in a petri dish at St Mary’s Hospital. Causes, course and consequences # Fleming’s 1929 paper attracted little interest. In 1940 Florey and Chain showed penicillin cured infections in mice; mass production in the US enabled treating soldiers at D-Day. Before antibiotics, a scratch could kill.

d: John Logie Baird demonstrated television in 1926, and the BBC launched the world's first regular high-definition service in 1936.
x: What happened # John Logie Baird demonstrated television in 1926, and the BBC launched the world’s first regular high-definition service in 1936. Causes, course and consequences # The 1936 Berlin Olympics were broadcast in Germany as Nazi propaganda. Television spread rapidly after WWII; Doordarshan started in Delhi in 1959.

d: The US launched a secret project to build an atomic bomb, after Einstein's 1939 letter warned of German research.
x: What happened # The US launched a secret project to build an atomic bomb, after Einstein’s 1939 letter warned of German research. Causes, course and consequences # Under General Leslie Groves and J. Robert Oppenheimer, 130,000 people worked at Los Alamos, Oak Ridge and Hanford, most without knowing their purpose. Enrico Fermi achieved the first chain reaction in Chicago on 2 December 1942. Soviet spies infiltrated the project.

d: The first atomic bomb, 'the Gadget', exploded in the desert with the force of about 25,000 tonnes of TNT.
x: What happened # The first atomic bomb, ‘the Gadget’, exploded in the desert with the force of about 25,000 tonnes of TNT. Causes, course and consequences # The flash was seen 300 km away. Scientists had bet on whether it would ignite the atmosphere. Local residents, many Hispanic and Native American, were not warned and were exposed to fallout; they have never been fully compensated.

t: Discovery of the DNA double helix
d: Watson and Crick published the double helix model of DNA, based partly on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data.
x: What happened # Watson and Crick published the double helix model of DNA, based partly on Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray data. Causes, course and consequences # Their one-page paper noted that base pairing ‘immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism’. Franklin’s role was minimised for decades.

d: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.
x: What happened # The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite. Causes, course and consequences # Its beeping signal shocked the US, leading to NASA’s founding (1958), more science education funding and DARPA, which later created ARPANET. Laika, a stray dog, became the first animal in orbit on Sputnik 2 but died within hours.

d: Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth once in Vostok 1, in 108 minutes.
x: What happened # Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth once in Vostok 1, in 108 minutes. Causes, course and consequences # He ejected from the capsule and parachuted separately, a fact hidden for years because records required landing in the spacecraft. He died in a training jet crash in 1968.

t: India's first rocket launch from Thumba
d: A US-made Nike-Apache sounding rocket launched from Thumba, near Thiruvananthapuram.
x: What happened # A US-made Nike-Apache sounding rocket launched from Thumba, near Thiruvananthapuram. Causes, course and consequences # Rocket parts were carried on bicycles and a bullock cart, and a church served as the office. Vikram Sarabhai and young engineers like A. P. J. Abdul Kalam worked there; ISRO was founded in 1969.

d: Charley Kline at UCLA tried to type 'LOGIN' to Stanford; the system crashed after 'LO'.
x: What happened # Charley Kline at UCLA tried to type ‘LOGIN’ to Stanford; the system crashed after ‘LO’. Causes, course and consequences # The network grew to connect universities and military sites, and TCP/IP (1983) created the modern internet.

d: India tested a nuclear device it called a 'peaceful nuclear explosion'.
x: What happened # India tested a nuclear device it called a ‘peaceful nuclear explosion’. Causes, course and consequences # The test, led by Raja Ramanna, led to the creation of the Nuclear Suppliers Group to restrict nuclear trade. In 1998 India conducted five more tests (Operation Shakti), followed by Pakistan.

d: India's first satellite, named after the mathematician, was launched on a Soviet rocket.
x: What happened # India’s first satellite, named after the mathematician, was launched on a Soviet rocket. Causes, course and consequences # Built by ISRO at Peenya, Bangalore, it was featured on the ₹2 note. India launched its own satellite with SLV-3 in 1980.

d: Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone, combining a phone, internet and touchscreen.
x: What happened # Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone, combining a phone, internet and touchscreen. Causes, course and consequences # The App Store (2008) created a new economy; Android spread cheaper smartphones worldwide, bringing internet access to billions in India and Africa.

d: The National Payments Corporation of India launched the Unified Payments Interface.
x: What happened # The National Payments Corporation of India launched the Unified Payments Interface. Causes, course and consequences # UPI processes billions of transactions a month, with India accounting for nearly half of the world’s real-time digital payments.

d: OpenAI released ChatGPT, reaching 100 million users in two months.
x: What happened # OpenAI released ChatGPT, reaching 100 million users in two months. Causes, course and consequences # It sparked a global race in large language models and debates about jobs, education and safety.

d: Edward Snowden leaked NSA documents revealing global surveillance.
x: What happened # Edward Snowden leaked NSA documents revealing global surveillance. Causes, course and consequences # Programmes like PRISM collected data from internet companies, and allies’ leaders’ phones were tapped. Snowden fled to Russia.

t: Attila's invasion of Gaul and Italy
d: Attila, ruler of the Hunnic Empire stretching from the Caspian to the Rhine, invaded Gaul in 451 and Italy in 452.
x: What happened # Attila, ruler of the Hunnic Empire stretching from the Caspian to the Rhine, invaded Gaul in 451 and Italy in 452. Causes, course and consequences # The Huns, nomadic horse archers from the steppe, had driven the Goths into the Roman Empire around 376, setting off the migrations that helped bring down the West. In 451 a Roman–Visigothic army under Flavius Aetius fought Attila to a standstill at the Catalaunian Plains. In 452 Attila sacked Aquileia and northern Italian cities — refugees founded settlements in the lagoons that became Venice — but withdrew after meeting Pope Leo I, probably because of plague and famine in his army. He died in 453 on his wedding night, and his empire collapsed.

d: A Muslim army of Berbers and Arabs under Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Morocco and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic.
x: What happened # A Muslim army of Berbers and Arabs under Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Morocco and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic. Causes, course and consequences # Tariq landed at the rock named after him, Jabal Tariq (Gibraltar), in 711 and won the Battle of Guadalete, after which most Visigothic cities surrendered within a few years. Al-Andalus became a centre of learning: Córdoba under Abd al-Rahman III was one of Europe’s largest and most cultured cities, where Muslims, Christians and Jews translated science and philosophy. The Christian Reconquista ended with the fall of Granada in 1492.

d: Batu Khan's Mongol armies conquered the Russian principalities and destroyed Kiev in 1240.
x: What happened # Batu Khan’s Mongol armies conquered the Russian principalities and destroyed Kiev in 1240. Causes, course and consequences # Attacking in winter, when frozen rivers served as roads, the Mongols took Ryazan, Vladimir and Moscow and annihilated Kiev, which a papal envoy described years later as a field of skulls. The principalities became vassals of the Golden Horde, paying tribute through princes of Moscow, who grew powerful as tax collectors. In 1480 Ivan III ended tribute after the Great Stand on the Ugra River.

d: Mongol armies raided India repeatedly but were defeated by the Delhi Sultanate.
x: What happened # Mongol armies raided India repeatedly but were defeated by the Delhi Sultanate. Causes, course and consequences # Genghis Khan chased the Khwarazmian prince Jalal ad-Din to the Indus in 1221 but turned back. Later Chagatai Mongol armies besieged Delhi itself in 1299 and 1303; Alauddin Khalji defeated them at Kili, Amroha and Ravi, building the fort of Siri and a large standing army funded by market controls. India was one of the few major regions that resisted Mongol conquest, and Indian rulers welcomed refugees fleeing the Mongols, including scholars from Persia.

d: Napoleon invaded Russia with about 600,000 troops; fewer than 100,000 returned.
x: What happened # Napoleon invaded Russia with about 600,000 troops; fewer than 100,000 returned. Causes, course and consequences # Russia withdrew east, burning crops (a ‘scorched earth’ policy). After the bloody Battle of Borodino, Napoleon entered Moscow, but fires destroyed the city and the tsar refused to negotiate. The retreat in a brutal winter, with typhus, starvation and Cossack attacks, destroyed the army. Tolstoy’s War and Peace and Tchaikovsky’s 1812 Overture remember it.

t: Japanese invasion of China and the Nanjing Massacre
d: Japan launched a full-scale invasion of China in July 1937.
x: What happened # Japan launched a full-scale invasion of China in July 1937. Causes, course and consequences # After the Marco Polo Bridge incident, Japanese forces took Shanghai and the Nationalist capital Nanjing, where soldiers massacred tens of thousands to about 300,000 civilians and prisoners and committed mass rape over six weeks. Japan also used chemical and biological weapons, including Unit 731’s plague attacks. About 15–20 million Chinese died in the war. Japanese denial of the massacre still strains relations.

d: Germany invaded Poland using blitzkrieg tactics; the Soviet Union invaded from the east on 17 September.
x: What happened # Germany invaded Poland using blitzkrieg tactics; the Soviet Union invaded from the east on 17 September. Causes, course and consequences # Hitler staged a fake Polish attack on a German radio station at Gleiwitz as a pretext. Britain and France declared war on 3 September. Poland was divided under the secret Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact; both occupiers murdered Polish elites, including the Soviet massacre of about 22,000 officers at Katyn. About 6 million Polish citizens, half of them Jews, died during the war.

d: Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union with about 3.8 million soldiers.
x: What happened # Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union with about 3.8 million soldiers. Causes, course and consequences # Stalin ignored warnings, including from spy Richard Sorge. Germans encircled huge Soviet armies and reached the outskirts of Moscow by December, but winter, Soviet reserves from Siberia and overstretched supply lines stopped them. Behind the front, Einsatzgruppen murdered over a million Jews, beginning the Holocaust by bullets. The war in the east caused most of WWII’s military deaths.

d: Japanese forces conquered Malaya and Singapore, capturing about 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops.
x: What happened # Japanese forces conquered Malaya and Singapore, capturing about 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops. Causes, course and consequences # Japan advanced down the Malay Peninsula on bicycles, and Singapore’s guns, mostly facing the sea, could not stop them. Churchill called it the ‘worst disaster’ in British military history. Many Indian prisoners joined the Indian National Army, later led by Subhas Chandra Bose.

d: Allied forces landed about 156,000 soldiers on five beaches in Normandy.
x: What happened # Allied forces landed about 156,000 soldiers on five beaches in Normandy. Causes, course and consequences # Operation Overlord was the largest seaborne invasion in history, using artificial Mulberry harbours and deception (Operation Fortitude) to make Germany expect a landing at Calais. Paris was liberated in August.

d: The Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to support its communist government.
x: What happened # The Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to support its communist government. Causes, course and consequences # The US, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia armed mujahideen fighters, including Stinger missiles. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers and up to 2 million Afghans died, and millions fled. Soviet withdrawal in 1989 contributed to the USSR’s collapse; the war’s aftermath helped give rise to the Taliban and al-Qaeda.

t: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and Gulf War
d: Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990; a US-led coalition expelled Iraq in early 1991.
x: What happened # Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990; a US-led coalition expelled Iraq in early 1991. Causes, course and consequences # Retreating Iraqi forces set fire to over 600 oil wells. India carried out the largest civilian airlift in history, evacuating about 170,000 Indians from Kuwait.

d: A US-led coalition invaded Iraq, claiming it had weapons of mass destruction.
x: What happened # A US-led coalition invaded Iraq, claiming it had weapons of mass destruction. Causes, course and consequences # No WMD were found. The occupation, sectarian civil war and the rise of ISIS killed hundreds of thousands.

d: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, following its 2014 annexation of Crimea.
x: What happened # Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, following its 2014 annexation of Crimea. Causes, course and consequences # Ukraine resisted the attempt to take Kyiv. The war has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.

d: Sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon (r. c. 1792–1750 BCE), he turned a small city-state into an empire covering most of Mesopotamia through diplomacy and war against Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari. Late in his reign he set up stone stelae carrying 282 laws, framed as given by the sun god Shamash, so that 'the strong may not oppress the weak'. His letters show a king closely involved in canals, taxes and court cases.

d: The 'Great Ancestor' of later pharaohs, Ramesses II reigned for 66 years (c. 1279–1213 BCE). He fought the Hittites at Kadesh (c. 1274 BCE), proclaimed it a victory, and later signed the world's oldest surviving peace treaty with them. He built Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum and a new capital, Pi-Ramesses, and fathered over a hundred children.

d: Daughter of Thutmose I, Hatshepsut ruled first as regent for her stepson Thutmose III and then as pharaoh (c. 1479–1458 BCE), depicted with the royal false beard. Her reign was peaceful and prosperous: she sent an expedition to the land of Punt for incense and built the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari. After her death her images were chiselled away, perhaps to secure Thutmose III's line.

d: Founder of the Achaemenid Persian Empire (r. c. 559–530 BCE), Cyrus overthrew the Medes, conquered Lydia and took Babylon in 539 BCE almost without a fight. The Cyrus Cylinder records that he returned deported peoples and restored their temples; the Bible praises him for letting the Jews return to Jerusalem. He died campaigning in Central Asia and was buried in a simple tomb at Pasargadae.

d: King of Macedon at 20, Alexander (356–323 BCE) was taught by Aristotle and in 11 years conquered the Persian Empire, Egypt and lands to the Indus, never losing a major battle. At the Hydaspes (326 BCE) he defeated Porus, but his exhausted army refused to go beyond the Beas. He founded cities, mixed Greek and Persian elites and spread Greek culture, but died in Babylon at 32, and his empire split among his generals.

He defeated Seleucus I, who ceded the northwest in exchange for 500 elephants. Jain tradition says he abdicated, became a monk under Bhadrabahu and fasted to death at Shravanabelagola.

d: Grandson of Chandragupta, Ashoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) conquered Kalinga in a war that his own edict says killed 100,000 and deported 150,000. Filled with remorse, he embraced Buddhism and dhamma — non-violence, tolerance and welfare — building hospitals, wells and rest houses and sending missions abroad. His lion capital at Sarnath is India's national emblem and his wheel is on its flag.

d: King Ying Zheng of Qin conquered the six rival Warring States and in 221 BCE proclaimed himself First Emperor. He standardised script, coins, weights and roads, joined border walls into an early Great Wall, and ordered the burning of books and the persecution of scholars. Obsessed with immortality, he died in 210 BCE and was buried with the Terracotta Army.

d: A Roman general and politician (100–44 BCE), Caesar conquered Gaul, crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE to start a civil war, and became dictator. He reformed the calendar (the Julian calendar) and expanded the Senate. Senators who feared he would become king stabbed him on the Ides of March, 44 BCE; his heir Octavian became Rome's first emperor.

d: Born Octavian, Caesar's adopted heir defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BCE) and in 27 BCE became Augustus, the first Roman emperor. He kept republican forms while holding real power, began 200 years of the Pax Romana, built roads and temples, and said he found Rome brick and left it marble. The month of August is named after him.

d: Cleopatra VII Philopator (69–30 BCE) was the last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt and the only member of her Macedonian Greek dynasty to learn Egyptian; Plutarch says she spoke about nine languages. Driven from power by her brother Ptolemy XIII, she allied with Julius Caesar, who restored her to the throne in 47 BCE; she bore him a son, Caesarion. After Caesar's murder she allied with Mark Antony, bearing three children and ruling the eastern Mediterranean with him. Octavian declared war on her, and after defeat at Actium (31 BCE) both she and Antony took their own lives in Alexandria in 30 BCE — tradition says by the bite of an asp — and Egypt became a Roman province. Roman propaganda painted her as a seductress, but ancient sources also show a shrewd, educated ruler who kept Egypt independent for two decades.

d: Kanishka I (reigned about 127–150 CE) was the greatest ruler of the Kushan Empire, descended from Yuezhi nomads who had migrated from China's frontier to Bactria. His realm stretched from Central Asia and Afghanistan to the Ganga plain, with capitals at Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura, controlling key Silk Road routes. The Rabatak inscription, found in Afghanistan in 1993, lists his conquests and shows that he used Bactrian rather than Greek on his coins. He is remembered in Buddhist tradition for convening the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir and building a giant stupa at Peshawar, though his coins also show Greek, Persian and Hindu gods like Shiva, Mithra and Helios. His reign saw the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art produce some of the first images of the Buddha in human form.

d: Samudragupta (reigned about 335–375 CE), son of Chandragupta I and the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi, built the Gupta Empire through conquest. The Allahabad Pillar inscription, composed by his court poet Harishena on an Ashokan pillar, lists the kings he 'violently uprooted' in the Ganga valley, the southern rulers he defeated and then reinstated as tributaries, and frontier states and forest kingdoms that paid homage. He performed the ashvamedha horse sacrifice to proclaim universal sovereignty. His gold coins show him playing the veena, and the inscription praises him as a poet and music lover. The historian Vincent Smith later called him 'the Napoleon of India'.

d: Justinian I (reigned 527–565), a peasant's son from the Balkans who rose through his uncle Justin I, was the last Byzantine emperor whose first language was Latin. With his wife Theodora, a former actress who became a powerful empress, he survived the Nika riots of 532, which nearly toppled him and burned much of Constantinople; Theodora reportedly declared that 'royalty is a good burial shroud'. He rebuilt the city, including Hagia Sophia (537), and his generals Belisarius and Narses reconquered North Africa from the Vandals and Italy from the Ostrogoths. His Corpus Juris Civilis codified Roman law and later shaped European legal systems. His reign was also struck by the Plague of Justinian (541), which he survived, and his wars drained the empire.

d: Harshavardhana (reigned 606–647) of the Pushyabhuti family of Thanesar took power at 16 after his elder brother was murdered and his sister Rajyashri's husband was killed. He moved his capital to Kannauj and united much of north India. Our knowledge comes from his court poet Banabhatta's Harshacharita and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who described Harsha's great assemblies at Kannauj and Prayag, where every five years he gave away his treasure to monks, Brahmins and the poor. Harsha wrote three Sanskrit plays, Nagananda, Ratnavali and Priyadarshika, and patronised Nalanda. His southward advance was halted by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II on the Narmada, and his empire fell apart after his death without an heir.

d: Charlemagne ('Charles the Great', about 747–814) became king of the Franks in 768 and spent over 30 years at war, conquering the Lombards in Italy, the Saxons (forcibly converting them, including executing 4,500 at Verden in 782), and Bavaria, and fighting in Spain, where the Battle of Roncevaux inspired the Song of Roland. On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned him emperor in Rome. From his capital at Aachen he sponsored the Carolingian Renaissance, gathering scholars like Alcuin of York, reforming education and promoting a clear new handwriting, Carolingian minuscule, the ancestor of our lower-case letters. He exchanged embassies with the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, who sent him an elephant. His empire split among his grandsons, forming the basis of France and Germany.

d: Rajaraja I (r. 985–1014) transformed the Chola kingdom into an empire, conquering the Cheras and Pandyas, Vengi, Gangavadi, northern Sri Lanka (destroying Anuradhapura) and the Maldives with a powerful navy. He organised a detailed land survey and revenue system, and built the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur (1010), whose vimana rises about 66 m and whose walls record gifts and temple staff. His son Rajendra I extended his conquests to the Ganga and Southeast Asia.

d: Temüjin (about 1162–1227) was born on the Mongolian steppe; after his father was poisoned, his family was abandoned and he survived poverty, captivity and the kidnapping of his wife Börte. Through alliances, loyalty-based promotion and ruthless warfare he united the Mongol and Turkic tribes, and in 1206 an assembly proclaimed him Genghis Khan ('universal ruler'). He organised his army in units of tens, hundreds and thousands, created the Yassa law code, a postal relay system and a script for Mongolian, and allowed religious freedom. His campaigns conquered northern China's Jin and Xi Xia and destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire, with massacres at cities like Nishapur and Merv. He died in 1227, and his sons and grandsons built the largest contiguous land empire in history.

d: Razia (r. 1236–1240), daughter of Iltutmish, was named heir by her father ahead of her brothers. The only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate, she discarded the veil, wore a tunic and turban, held open court and led armies. Her promotion of the Abyssinian noble Jamal-ud-Din Yaqut angered the Turkish nobles (the 'Forty'). Governor Altunia of Bathinda rebelled and captured her; she married him and tried to regain Delhi, but both were killed in 1240.

d: Mansa Musa (r. about 1312–1337) ruled the Mali Empire at its height, controlling gold fields that supplied much of the Old World's gold. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, with thousands of attendants and camels carrying gold, made him famous; his spending in Cairo depressed gold prices for years. He returned with scholars and the architect Es-Saheli, building the Djinguereber mosque and making Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning. The 1375 Catalan Atlas shows him holding a gold nugget.

d: Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529) of the Tuluva dynasty was Vijayanagara's greatest emperor. He defeated the Bijapur Sultanate at Raichur (1520), took territories from the Gajapatis of Odisha and kept Portuguese friendship for horses. He built gopurams at Hampi and Tirupati, and his court hosted the 'Ashtadiggajas', eight great Telugu poets, as well as Tenali Rama of folk tales. He wrote Amuktamalyada, a Telugu poem on statecraft and devotion.

d: Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur (1483–1530) was descended from Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's. He became ruler of Fergana at 11, repeatedly won and lost Samarkand, and seized Kabul in 1504. Invited by disaffected Afghan nobles, he invaded India and defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 using matchlocks, field guns and flanking cavalry, then defeated Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527). He founded the Mughal Empire but ruled only four years. His memoir, the Baburnama, written in Chagatai Turkic, is remarkably candid, describing battles, gardens, fruits and his homesickness for Kabul, where he asked to be buried.

d: Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar (1542–1605) became emperor at 13 after his father Humayun's death, with Bairam Khan as regent; his army won the Second Battle of Panipat (1556). He expanded the empire across north and central India, Gujarat, Bengal and Kashmir, and built a system of mansabdars (ranked officials) and a land revenue system with his finance minister Raja Todar Mal. He married Rajput princesses, appointed Hindus to high office, abolished the jizya tax and pilgrim tax, and held debates among Hindus, Muslims, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuits in his Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri. His idea of sulh-i-kul ('peace with all') and his short-lived Din-i Ilahi reflected religious tolerance. Though illiterate, he patronised the 'nine jewels' of his court, including Tansen and Birbal, and Abul Fazl wrote his history, the Akbarnama.

d: Shah Jahan (r. 1628–1658), the fifth Mughal emperor, presided over the empire's architectural golden age. He built the Taj Mahal (1632–1653) in Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their 14th child; the new capital Shahjahanabad with the Red Fort and Jama Masjid in Delhi; and the jewelled Peacock Throne. Costly wars and building strained finances. His son Aurangzeb defeated his brothers and imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort, where he died in 1666 looking at the Taj.

d: Elizabeth I (1533–1603), daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, who was executed when Elizabeth was two, survived imprisonment under her Catholic half-sister Mary I to become queen in 1558. She restored a moderate Protestant Church of England and never married, cultivating the image of the 'Virgin Queen'. d: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948), born in Porbandar, Gujarat, studied law in London and went to South Africa in 1893, where being thrown off a first-class train at Pietermaritzburg started his fight against racial discrimination. There he developed satyagraha, non-violent mass resistance, and founded Tolstoy Farm. Returning to India in 1915, he led the Champaran (1917), Kheda and Ahmedabad campaigns, the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22), the Salt March (1930) and Quit India (1942), spending about six years in prison. He opposed Partition and fasted to stop communal violence in Calcutta and Delhi; on 30 January 1948 he was shot by Nathuram Godse. His methods inspired Martin Luther King Jr. and Nelson Mandela.

After the Sharpeville massacre (1960), he helped found the ANC's armed wing and was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964, spending 27 years in jail, 18 of them on Robben Island. Released in 1990, he negotiated the end of apartheid with F. W. de Klerk, shared the Nobel Peace Prize (1993) and became South Africa's first Black president in 1994, promoting reconciliation. India awarded him the Bharat Ratna in 1990.

d: Winston Churchill (1874–1965), a British aristocrat, soldier and journalist, served in India, Sudan and the Boer War before entering Parliament. As First Lord of the Admiralty he backed the disastrous Gallipoli campaign (1915). In the 1930s he warned against Hitler, and as Prime Minister from May 1940 he refused to negotiate with Nazi Germany, rallying Britain with speeches like 'We shall fight on the beaches'. He worked closely with Roosevelt and Stalin, won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature, and returned as PM in 1951–55. In India he is remembered for opposing independence, calling Gandhi a 'half-naked fakir', and for his war cabinet's role in the Bengal famine of 1943.

d: Franklin Delano Roosevelt (1882–1945), the only US president elected four times, took office in 1933 at the depth of the Great Depression. His New Deal created jobs programmes, Social Security, banking reforms and huge public works like the Tennessee Valley Authority, greatly expanding government's role. Paralysed from the waist down by polio at 39, he hid his disability from the public. He led the US into World War II after Pearl Harbor (1941), shaped the Atlantic Charter with Churchill, and planned the United Nations, but died in April 1945, weeks before victory in Europe. He also ordered the internment of Japanese Americans.

d: Adolf Hitler (1889–1945), born in Austria, was a failed artist and World War I corporal who led the Nazi Party. Exploiting resentment over the Treaty of Versailles and the Great Depression, he became German Chancellor in 1933 and quickly made himself dictator. His regime persecuted Jews, Roma, disabled people and political opponents, rearmed Germany, and started World War II by invading Poland in 1939. Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust. Facing defeat, Hitler killed himself in his Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945. He is history's most notorious example of how democracy can be destroyed from within.

His five-year plans forced rapid industrialisation, and collectivisation of agriculture caused famines, including the Holodomor in Ukraine. The Great Purge (1936–38) executed about 750,000 people, and millions passed through the Gulag. He signed a pact with Hitler in 1939 but, after Germany invaded in 1941, led the USSR to victory at enormous cost, then imposed communist rule on Eastern Europe, beginning the Cold War.

The Great Leap Forward (1958–62) caused a famine that killed perhaps 15–45 million people, and the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) unleashed Red Guards against intellectuals and officials. He unified China and raised literacy, but at a massive human cost.

d: Kong Qiu (551–479 BCE), known as Kongzi or Confucius, was a minor official in the state of Lu during the Spring and Autumn period. He taught that society is harmonious when people follow ritual (li), practise humaneness (ren), honour their parents (filial piety) and rulers govern by virtue rather than force. He travelled among states seeking a ruler to apply his ideas, without success, and taught many students who compiled his sayings in the Analects. Under the Han dynasty Confucianism became the state ideology, shaping East Asia for 2,000 years.

d: Siddhartha Gautama was born in Lumbini (Nepal), a prince of the Shakya republic, probably in the 5th century BCE. Moved by seeing old age, sickness and death, he left home at 29, tried severe asceticism, then found the 'Middle Way' and attained enlightenment under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya. He preached his first sermon at Sarnath on the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, founded the sangha including nuns, and taught for 45 years under the patronage of kings like Bimbisara. He died at Kushinagar aged 80.

At 30 he renounced his home, practised austerities for 12 years and attained kevala jnana (omniscience). He taught the five vows — non-violence (ahimsa), truth, non-stealing, chastity and non-attachment — and organised monks, nuns and laity. He is the 24th tirthankara of Jainism and attained nirvana at Pawapuri.

Accused of impiety and corrupting youth, he was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock in 399 BCE, refusing to escape.

His dialogues, such as the Republic, Symposium and Phaedo, discuss justice, love, the soul and his theory of Forms — that the physical world is a shadow of eternal ideas (the Allegory of the Cave). The Republic imagined a state ruled by philosopher-kings. Alfred North Whitehead said Western philosophy is 'a series of footnotes to Plato'.

d: Aristotle (384–322 BCE), from Stagira, studied at Plato's Academy for 20 years, tutored the young Alexander the Great, and founded the Lyceum in Athens. He wrote on logic, biology, physics, ethics, politics, poetry and rhetoric, classifying animals and developing syllogistic logic. His works were preserved by Islamic scholars and dominated European thought in the Middle Ages.

d: Chanakya, also called Kautilya or Vishnugupta, was a Brahmin scholar, traditionally from Taxila, who helped Chandragupta Maurya overthrow the Nanda dynasty around 322 BCE and served as his chief minister. He is credited with the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft, economics, law, espionage and war, rediscovered in 1905. His realism has led to comparisons with Machiavelli. Legends also attribute aphorisms (Chanakya Niti) to him.

d: Panini, a grammarian from Shalatula near Gandhara (around the 5th–4th century BCE), wrote the Ashtadhyayi, about 4,000 concise rules (sutras) describing Sanskrit's sounds, word formation and syntax. His grammar standardised Classical Sanskrit.

d: Archimedes (about 287–212 BCE) of Syracuse in Sicily was the greatest mathematician of antiquity. He approximated π, calculated areas and volumes using methods close to integral calculus, discovered the principle of buoyancy (reportedly shouting 'Eureka!' in his bath), and explained levers ('Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth'). He designed war machines to defend Syracuse against Rome and was killed by a Roman soldier during the city's fall.

He is called the 'father of surgery'.

His book on Indian numerals introduced decimal place-value arithmetic to the Islamic world and, when translated into Latin, to Europe; the word 'algorithm' comes from the Latin form of his name. His Canon of Medicine, a five-volume encyclopaedia, described contagion, clinical trials of drugs and hundreds of medicines, and was a standard textbook in Europe until the 17th century. His Book of Healing covered philosophy, logic and science, integrating Aristotle with Islamic thought.

He later ran the Royal Mint and was President of the Royal Society. He also spent years on alchemy and biblical prophecy.

d: Sargon (reigned about 2334–2279 BCE) founded the Akkadian Empire, often called the world's first empire. He made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess at Ur, and his dynasty ruled for about 150 years.

He led Athens into the Peloponnesian War and died in the Plague of Athens.

d: Herodotus (about 484–425 BCE) was born in Halicarnassus (Bodrum, Turkey), then under Persian rule, and travelled to Egypt, Babylon, Phoenicia, Scythia and across Greece. His Histories, written to explain 'why the Greeks and Persians fought one another', describe the rise of Persia under Cyrus, Darius and Xerxes and the Persian Wars, including Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis. Cicero called him the 'Father of History', while critics called him the 'Father of Lies'; modern archaeology has confirmed many of his descriptions.

The Hippocratic Corpus contains about 60 works, and the Hippocratic Oath, with principles like 'do no harm', still inspires medical ethics.

d: Sima Qian (about 145–86 BCE) succeeded his father as Grand Historian at the Han court of Emperor Wu. d: Xuanzang (602–664), a Chinese Buddhist monk, left Chang'an in 629 without permission to seek authentic texts. His Great Tang Records on the Western Regions guided archaeologists to Indian sites, and he inspired the novel Journey to the West.

d: Ramanuja (traditionally 1017–1137) was a Tamil Vaishnava philosopher who taught Vishishtadvaita ('qualified non-dualism'): the soul and world are real, distinct parts of Brahman (Vishnu), and liberation comes through devotion (bhakti) and surrender. He reorganised worship at Srirangam and, according to tradition, shared the sacred mantra publicly from a temple tower so all castes could be saved. He is said to have fled Chola persecution to the Hoysala court, where he converted King Vishnuvardhana.

d: Basava (Basavanna, 1105–1167), a minister of the Kalachuri king Bijjala at Kalyana in Karnataka, founded the Lingayat (Veerashaiva) movement. He rejected caste, temple ritual and gender discrimination, teaching devotion to Shiva symbolised by a personal linga, and that 'work is worship' (kayaka). Her grandson Prataparudra succeeded her.

He is credited with developing qawwali and the tarana, and legends credit him with inventing the sitar and tabla, though historians doubt this. He called himself the 'Parrot of India'.

d: Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406), born in Tunis, was a scholar, judge and diplomat in North Africa, Spain and Egypt. His Muqaddimah (1377) analysed why dynasties rise and fall: tribal groups with strong solidarity (asabiyyah) conquer settled societies, then grow soft and lose power within about four generations. He is seen as a founder of sociology and economics. In 1401 he met Timur outside Damascus.

d: Zheng He (1371–1433), born to a Muslim family in Yunnan, was captured as a boy by Ming armies, castrated and became a eunuch servant of Prince Zhu Di (later the Yongle Emperor). He commanded seven 'treasure fleet' voyages (1405–1433) with up to 300 ships and 27,000 men, visiting Java, Sri Lanka, Calicut, Hormuz, Mecca and East Africa, and bringing back envoys and a giraffe. After his death, the Ming abandoned the voyages.

She was declared innocent in 1456 and made a saint in 1920.

Living in the Aravalli hills with Bhil allies and supported by the merchant Bhamashah's wealth, he waged guerrilla war and regained much of Mewar except Chittor. He remains a symbol of Rajput pride.

She fought the Portuguese for decades, reportedly using fire arrows at night, before being captured. She is celebrated as one of India's first freedom fighters.

d: Lachit Borphukan (1622–1672) was commander of the Ahom army. Legends say he beheaded his own uncle for failing to complete a defensive wall overnight. Lachit Divas is celebrated on 24 November.

d: Ahilyabai Holkar (1725–1795) was widowed at 29 and lost her father-in-law Malhar Rao and son, then took over as ruler of the Holkar state of Malwa from Maheshwar. She ruled for 28 years with justice and prosperity, defended her lands and built or restored hundreds of temples, ghats and rest houses across India, including the Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi (1780) and Somnath. Indore's airport and university are named after her.

A skilled general, he defeated Spanish and British forces, abolished slavery and governed the colony. Napoleon sent an army to restore slavery; Toussaint was captured by trickery and died in a French prison in 1803. Haiti won independence months later.

He liberated Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia (named after him) and led Gran Colombia, but his dream of a united South America collapsed amid regional rivalry before his death.

d: Born Dhanpat Rai Srivastava in Lamhi near Varanasi, Premchand worked as a schoolteacher and inspector before resigning in 1921 in response to Gandhi's Non-Cooperation call. He wrote first in Urdu (his 1907 story collection Soz-e-Watan was banned and burned by the British) and then Hindi, producing about 300 stories and over a dozen novels. He presided over the first Progressive Writers' Association meeting in 1936 and is called 'Upanyas Samrat' (emperor of novels).

d: Born Norma Jeane Mortenson in Los Angeles, Monroe spent much of her childhood in foster homes and an orphanage. She became Hollywood's biggest star of the 1950s in films like Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, The Seven Year Itch and Some Like It Hot (Golden Globe, 1960). She founded her own production company in 1955 — rare for an actress — to fight studio control, and studied at the Actors Studio. Her struggles with fame, depression and addiction, her marriages to Joe DiMaggio and Arthur Miller, and her death from a barbiturate overdose at 36 made her an enduring icon of glamour and of the costs of celebrity.

In The Great Dictator (1940) he mocked Hitler. Accused of communist sympathies during the McCarthy era, he was barred from re-entering the US in 1952 and settled in Switzerland. Legend says he was once a robber named Ratnakara who became a sage after meditating so long that an anthill (valmika) grew over him. The epic, composed over centuries, spread across Asia in countless versions, from Tamil Kamban and Tulsidas's Hindi Ramcharitmanas to Thailand's Ramakien and Indonesia's Kakawin Ramayana.

d: Vyasa (Krishna Dvaipayana) is traditionally the compiler of the Vedas and the author of the Mahabharata, the world's longest epic (about 100,000 couplets), which includes the Bhagavad Gita. Legend says Ganesha wrote it down as Vyasa dictated. The epic tells of the war at Kurukshetra between the Pandavas and Kauravas and explores dharma, duty and fate.

d: Homer is the legendary blind poet credited with the Iliad, about the wrath of Achilles in the Trojan War, and the Odyssey, about Odysseus's ten-year journey home. The epics grew out of oral tradition and were written down after the Greek alphabet was adopted. They shaped Greek education, religion and identity, and remain foundational works of Western literature.

d: Tulsidas (1532–1623) was born in Rajapur in Uttar Pradesh and, according to legend, was abandoned as an inauspicious child and raised by a servant woman. After his wife rebuked his attachment to her, he became a devotee of Rama and spent much of his life in Varanasi and Ayodhya. He wrote the Ramcharitmanas (1574–1577) in Awadhi, retelling Valmiki's Ramayana in a devotional form accessible to ordinary people; it became the most widely read religious text in north India. He also wrote the Hanuman Chalisa and the Vinaya Patrika, and his poetry is the basis of the Ramlila performances held every Dussehra.

d: Surdas (about 1478–1583) was a poet-saint of the Bhakti movement who, according to tradition, was blind, perhaps from birth. A disciple of Vallabhacharya, he sang in the temple of Shrinathji at Govardhan. His Sur Sagar, written in Braj Bhasha, contains thousands of songs, especially about Krishna's childhood in Vrindavan — stealing butter, playing with the gopis — and the longing of Radha and the gopis after he left. His tender lyrical style made Braj Bhasha the main literary language of north India for centuries; legend says Akbar visited him.

d: Mirza Asadullah Baig Khan, 'Ghalib' (1797–1869), was born in Agra to a family of Turkish soldiers and lived most of his life in Delhi. He wrote ghazals in Urdu and Persian full of wit, scepticism, love and philosophical depth, and served as poet-tutor to Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor. He witnessed the 1857 uprising and the British sack of Delhi; his letters and Persian diary Dastanbuy describe the devastation. Often in debt and denied his pension, he remains the most quoted Urdu poet, with verses such as 'Hazaron khwahishen aisi ki har khwahish pe dam nikle'.

d: Muhammad Iqbal (1877–1938), born in Sialkot, studied philosophy at Cambridge and earned a doctorate in Munich. He wrote poetry in Urdu and Persian, including 'Saare Jahan Se Achha' (1904), still sung in India, and the Persian Asrar-i-Khudi on self-development (khudi). Later he became concerned with the revival of the Muslim world; in his 1930 presidential address to the Muslim League at Allahabad he proposed a Muslim state in north-west India, an idea that influenced the Pakistan movement. He is Pakistan's national poet, and his poetry is also loved in India and Iran.

d: Bankim Chandra, one of the first graduates of Calcutta University and a colonial official, wrote the first major Bengali novels. His Anandamath (1882), set during the Sannyasi rebellion, contained the song 'Vande Mataram', which became a rallying cry of the freedom movement and India's national song.

d: Subramania Bharati (1882–1921), born in Ettayapuram, Tamil Nadu, mastered Tamil, Sanskrit, Hindi and English. As a journalist with newspapers like Swadesamitran and India, he wrote fiery patriotic poems such as 'Achamillai' ('No fear') that inspired the freedom movement. Facing arrest, he lived in French-ruled Pondicherry from 1908 to 1918, where he met Aurobindo. He championed women's education, opposed caste and child marriage, and modernised Tamil poetry with simple language. He died at 38 after being injured by a temple elephant; his works were nationalised by the Tamil Nadu government in 1949.

d: Jalal al-Din Rumi, born in Balkh, fled the Mongols and settled in Konya. His friendship with the wandering mystic Shams of Tabriz transformed him into an ecstatic poet. His Masnavi, 25,000 Persian couplets, is called 'the Quran in Persian', and his followers founded the Mevlevi 'whirling dervishes'.

d: Abu'l-Qasim Ferdowsi (940–1020) was a landowner from Tus in Khorasan who spent about 30 years writing the Shahnameh ('Book of Kings'), about 50,000 couplets, completed in 1010. It retells Iran's history from the creation of the world through mythical kings and heroes like Rostam and Sohrab to the fall of the Sasanian Empire to the Arabs. Written in Persian with very few Arabic words, it helped preserve the Persian language and identity after the Islamic conquest. Legend says Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni paid him in silver rather than the promised gold. The Shahnameh influenced Persian, Turkish and Mughal culture, and its illustrated manuscripts are among the masterpieces of Persian painting.

d: Dante Alighieri (1265–1321) was a Florentine poet and politician who was exiled in 1302 after his political faction lost power, and never returned. In exile he wrote the Divine Comedy, an epic in which the poet Virgil guides Dante through Hell (Inferno) and Purgatory, and his beloved Beatrice guides him through Paradise. Written in Tuscan Italian rather than Latin, it helped create the Italian literary language. Dante placed popes and political enemies in Hell, and the work's vision of the afterlife shaped European imagination. He died in Ravenna, where he is buried.

d: Miguel de Cervantes (1547–1616) fought at the naval Battle of Lepanto (1571) against the Ottomans, where he lost the use of his left hand. Pirates captured him in 1575, and he spent five years as a captive in Algiers, attempting four escapes before being ransomed. Back in Spain he worked as a tax collector and was jailed for accounting irregularities. He wrote Don Quixote (1605, 1615), about a man who reads too many chivalric romances and sets out as a knight with his squire Sancho Panza; it is often called the first modern novel. He died within a day of Shakespeare's death in 1616.

d: Count Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) was born on his family estate, Yasnaya Polyana, served in the Crimean War and wrote the Sevastopol Sketches. His novels War and Peace (1869), set during Napoleon's invasion of Russia, and Anna Karenina (1877) are among the greatest ever written. In middle age he had a spiritual crisis and embraced a radical Christian ethic of non-violence, simplicity and rejection of property and the state, and was excommunicated by the Orthodox Church. His 'Letter to a Hindu' (1908) and correspondence with Gandhi influenced satyagraha; Gandhi named his commune in South Africa Tolstoy Farm. He died at a railway station after leaving home aged 82.

d: Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821–1881) joined a radical intellectual circle and was arrested in 1849; he faced a mock execution before being sentenced to four years of hard labour in Siberia, an experience recounted in Notes from the House of the Dead. Struggling with epilepsy, gambling debts and poverty, he wrote Crime and Punishment (1866), The Idiot, Demons and The Brothers Karamazov (1880), exploring guilt, faith, free will and the dangers of radical ideologies. His psychological depth influenced existentialism and modern fiction.

d: Victor Hugo (1802–1885) was a leading figure of French Romanticism, writing poetry, plays and novels. The Hunchback of Notre-Dame (1831) helped save the cathedral by reviving interest in Gothic architecture. A supporter of the 1848 Republic, he denounced Louis-Napoléon's coup in 1851 and spent 19 years in exile on Jersey and Guernsey, where he finished Les Misérables (1862), a story of the ex-convict Jean Valjean, poverty and the June Rebellion of 1832. He campaigned against the death penalty and for universal education. Two million people attended his funeral in Paris.

d: Charles Dickens (1812–1870) was sent at 12 to work in a boot-blacking factory when his father was imprisoned for debt, an experience that shaped his concern for the poor. He became a journalist and then the most popular novelist of Victorian Britain, publishing in monthly instalments: The Pickwick Papers, Oliver Twist (workhouses and child crime), A Christmas Carol (1843), David Copperfield, Bleak House, Hard Times (industrial towns), A Tale of Two Cities (the French Revolution) and Great Expectations. His vivid characters such as Scrooge and Fagin, and his criticism of social injustice, influenced reforms. He gave reading tours in Britain and America.

d: Jane Austen (1775–1817), a clergyman's daughter in Hampshire, wrote six novels — Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park, Emma, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion — published anonymously ('By a Lady'). With irony and wit she portrayed the gentry, marriage, money and women's limited options in Georgian England, set against the backdrop of the Napoleonic Wars. She never married and died at 41. Her novels pioneered free indirect speech and remain hugely popular through films and adaptations.

d: Samuel Clemens (1835–1910) grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi, where he became a riverboat pilot; his pen name means 'two fathoms deep'. As a journalist and humorist he wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), in which the boy Huck helps Jim, an escaped slave, a novel Hemingway said all modern American literature comes from. He criticised racism, imperialism and hypocrisy. In 1896 he toured India and wrote in Following the Equator that India was 'the cradle of the human race'.

d: Lu Xun (pen name of Zhou Shuren, 1881–1936) studied medicine in Japan but turned to literature after seeing a slide of Chinese spectators watching passively as a countryman was executed. His 'A Madman's Diary' (1918), the first major story in vernacular Chinese, attacked Confucian tradition as 'cannibalism'. 'The True Story of Ah Q' (1921) satirised Chinese apathy after the 1911 revolution. He is considered the father of modern Chinese literature and was later championed by Mao.

d: Murasaki Shikibu (about 973–1014) was a lady-in-waiting to Empress Shōshi at the Heian court in Kyoto. Educated in Chinese classics by eavesdropping on her brother's lessons, she wrote The Tale of Genji, about the loves and life of the 'Shining Prince' Genji, in 54 chapters using Japanese kana script. It portrays court life, poetry and the Buddhist sense of impermanence (mono no aware). Often called the world's first novel, it has been illustrated in scrolls since the 12th century. She also kept a diary of court life.

d: Chinua Achebe (1930–2013), an Igbo writer from Nigeria, wrote Things Fall Apart (1958), the story of Okonkwo, a proud leader whose world collapses under British colonialism and Christian missionaries. Written partly in response to European portrayals of Africa, such as Conrad's Heart of Darkness, which he criticised as racist, it has sold over 20 million copies in 50 languages. He wrote Arrow of God and No Longer at Ease, supported Biafra in the Nigerian civil war, and taught in the US after a car accident left him paralysed.

d: Gabriel García Márquez (1927–2014), known as 'Gabo', was a Colombian journalist and novelist raised by his grandparents in Aracataca, whose stories inspired his fiction. One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967), the saga of the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo, made 'magical realism' famous and sold tens of millions of copies. He also wrote Love in the Time of Cholera and Chronicle of a Death Foretold, and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982. His work reflects Latin America's history of colonialism, civil wars and dictatorship.

d: Michelangelo Buonarroti carved the Pietà (1499) and the 5-metre David (1504) from a block other sculptors had abandoned. For Pope Julius II he painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508–12) lying on scaffolding, and later The Last Judgement. As architect he designed the dome of St Peter's Basilica. He was the first artist whose biography was written in his lifetime.

d: Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890), a Dutch pastor's son, worked as an art dealer and lay preacher among coal miners before becoming a painter at 27. Influenced by Impressionism and Japanese prints in Paris, he moved to Arles in southern France in 1888 and painted brilliant, emotional works with thick brushstrokes: Sunflowers, The Bedroom, Café Terrace at Night. After a breakdown in which he cut off part of his ear, he entered an asylum at Saint-Rémy, where he painted The Starry Night (1889). Supported financially by his brother Theo, he sold almost nothing in his lifetime and died of a gunshot wound at 37.

d: Pablo Picasso (1881–1973), born in Málaga, Spain, was a child prodigy who spent most of his life in France. His Blue Period and Rose Period gave way to Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907), inspired partly by African masks, and with Georges Braque he founded Cubism, showing objects from many viewpoints at once. In 1937 he painted Guernica in response to the bombing of the Basque town by Nazi and Italian planes during the Spanish Civil War; it became the century's most famous anti-war image. He produced about 50,000 works in painting, sculpture, ceramics and prints.

d: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756–1791) was born in Salzburg and toured Europe's courts as a child prodigy with his father Leopold and sister Nannerl, composing from age five. Moving to Vienna, he wrote over 600 works, including 41 symphonies, 27 piano concertos and operas such as The Marriage of Figaro (1786), Don Giovanni (1787) and The Magic Flute (1791). Despite success he was often in debt. He died at 35 while composing his Requiem, leaving it unfinished; rumours that rival Salieri poisoned him are unfounded.

d: Ludwig van Beethoven (1770–1827) was born in Bonn and moved to Vienna, where he studied briefly with Haydn. From his late twenties he began to lose his hearing, writing in the 1802 Heiligenstadt Testament of his despair, yet he composed his greatest works when almost completely deaf. His nine symphonies, including the Third ('Eroica'), originally dedicated to Napoleon until he crowned himself emperor, the Fifth, and the Ninth with its 'Ode to Joy' (now the European anthem), bridged Classical and Romantic music. His piano sonatas and late string quartets remain landmarks.

d: Tansen (about 1500–1586), born Ramtanu near Gwalior, trained with Swami Haridas of Vrindavan and in the dhrupad tradition of Raja Man Singh Tomar's Gwalior court. He served the Rewa court before Akbar summoned him in 1562; he became one of the nine jewels (navaratnas) of Akbar's court. He composed ragas such as Miyan ki Malhar, Miyan ki Todi and Darbari Kanada, and legends say his singing of raga Deepak lit lamps and Megh Malhar brought rain. His tomb in Gwalior hosts the Tansen Samaroh music festival every December.

d: Raja Ravi Varma (1848–1906), from the royal family of Kilimanoor in Travancore, learned oil painting from a visiting Dutch-trained artist. He painted portraits of royalty and scenes from the Mahabharata, Ramayana and Kalidasa's works, such as Shakuntala and Hamsa Damayanti, combining European realism with Indian subjects and sarees. In 1894 he set up a lithographic press near Mumbai, producing cheap colour prints of gods and goddesses that reached ordinary homes and shaped how Indians imagine their deities. Some critics accused him of Westernising Indian art.

d: Dhundiraj Govind Phalke (1870–1944) was a printer, photographer and magician in Maharashtra. Inspired by watching The Life of Christ in a Bombay cinema in 1911, he pawned his wife's jewellery to learn filmmaking in London. He made India's first full-length feature film, Raja Harishchandra (1913), a mythological drama in which men played female roles because women were unwilling to act. He made about 95 films and 26 shorts, including Lanka Dahan and Kaliya Mardan, but was ruined by the coming of sound. India's highest cinema honour, the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, is named after him.

Inspired by Italian neorealism (Bicycle Thieves), he made Pather Panchali (1955), about a poor Bengali boy, Apu, with non-professional actors and a tiny budget; it won a prize at Cannes. Ray went on to make Aparajito and Apur Sansar (the Apu Trilogy), Charulata, Jalsaghar and Shatranj Ke Khilari. He wrote the Feluda detective stories and Professor Shonku science fiction, and received an honorary Academy Award and the Bharat Ratna in 1992.

She became the leading playback singer of Indian cinema from the late 1940s, recording thousands of songs in over 36 languages for films from Mahal (1949) to the 2000s. d: Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) spent his entire life in Königsberg, Prussia, famous for his punctual daily walks. In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781) he argued that the mind actively structures experience through categories like space, time and causality, so we can know things only as they appear to us, not as they are in themselves. In ethics he proposed the categorical imperative: act only according to rules you could will to be universal laws, and treat people as ends, never merely as means. His essay 'What is Enlightenment?' (1784) urged 'Sapere aude — dare to know', and he proposed a federation of states for perpetual peace.

d: René Descartes (1596–1650), a French philosopher and mathematician, served as a soldier during the Thirty Years' War and lived mostly in the Netherlands. In Discourse on the Method (1637) and Meditations, he doubted everything he could and found certainty in 'I think, therefore I am'. He argued mind and body are distinct substances (Cartesian dualism). He invented analytic geometry, the Cartesian coordinate system linking algebra and geometry. He died in Stockholm after being invited to tutor Queen Christina.

d: Karl Marx (1818–1883), born in Trier, studied philosophy and became a radical journalist; expelled from Germany, France and Belgium, he settled in London in 1849, supported by his friend Friedrich Engels. With Engels he wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848), declaring 'Workers of the world, unite!'. In Das Kapital (1867) he argued that capitalism exploits workers by extracting surplus value and would be replaced by socialism. He also wrote on British rule in India, criticising its brutality while seeing it as destroying old structures. His ideas inspired the Russian and Chinese revolutions and labour movements worldwide.

His ideas inspired the French Revolution and Romanticism.

He corresponded with Frederick the Great and Catherine the Great, and wrote Essay on the Customs and Spirit of Nations, which praised India and China.

d: John Locke (1632–1704), an English physician and philosopher, lived in exile in the Netherlands for political reasons and returned after the Glorious Revolution of 1688. In Two Treatises of Government he argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, that governments exist by the consent of the governed, and that people may overthrow a government that violates their rights. In An Essay Concerning Human Understanding he argued the mind is a 'blank slate' shaped by experience. His ideas influenced the US Declaration of Independence. He also helped draft the constitution of the Carolina colony and invested in the slave trade, a contradiction critics note.

d: Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527) served as a diplomat and official of the Florentine Republic until the Medici returned in 1512; he was imprisoned and tortured, then exiled to his farm. There he wrote The Prince (1513), advising rulers to be practical, use deception when necessary and, if they cannot be both, to be feared rather than loved. His Discourses on Livy praised republican government. 'Machiavellian' became a byword for cunning, but scholars see him as a founder of realist political science, often compared with India's Chanakya.

d: Mencius (Mengzi, about 372–289 BCE), the most important Confucian after Confucius, was raised by a famously devoted mother who moved house three times to give him good surroundings. He travelled among the Warring States advising rulers. He taught that human nature is good, with innate sprouts of compassion, shame, respect and right and wrong, which must be cultivated. He argued that the people are most important and that a tyrant who oppresses them loses the Mandate of Heaven and may be overthrown. The Mencius became one of the Four Books of the Confucian canon.

d: Nagarjuna (about 150–250 CE) was an Indian Buddhist philosopher, traditionally associated with the Satavahana kings and the region of Nagarjunakonda in Andhra Pradesh. In his Mulamadhyamakakarika he founded the Madhyamaka ('Middle Way') school, arguing that all things are empty (shunya) of independent existence because they arise dependently. He used logic to show that fixed views lead to contradictions. He is revered as a 'second Buddha' in Tibetan and East Asian Buddhism.

d: Louis Pasteur (1822–1895), a French chemist, showed that fermentation and spoilage are caused by microorganisms, disproving spontaneous generation with his swan-neck flask experiment. He developed pasteurisation to keep wine and milk safe, saved the silk industry from silkworm disease, and helped establish the germ theory of disease. He developed vaccines for chicken cholera, anthrax and, in 1885, rabies, first used on a boy bitten by a rabid dog. The Pasteur Institute he founded continues research; the Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor was founded in 1907.

d: Thomas Edison (1847–1931) had little formal schooling and worked as a telegraph operator before becoming a full-time inventor. At his Menlo Park laboratory, the first industrial research lab, he invented the phonograph (1877), developed a long-lasting carbon-filament light bulb (1879), and built the first commercial power station at Pearl Street, New York (1882). He also worked on motion picture cameras. He held 1,093 US patents. His 'war of the currents' with Tesla and Westinghouse, promoting direct current, was lost to alternating current.

d: Nikola Tesla (1856–1943), a Serbian born in Croatia, emigrated to the US in 1884 and briefly worked for Edison. He invented the induction motor and the polyphase alternating-current system, which George Westinghouse used to power the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and Niagara Falls power station, making AC the global standard. He experimented with radio, wireless power and X-rays. His Wardenclyffe tower for wireless transmission failed for lack of funds, and he died poor in a New York hotel. The SI unit of magnetic field is named after him.

He became Humphry Davy's assistant at the Royal Institution and discovered electromagnetic rotation (the principle of the electric motor, 1821) and electromagnetic induction (1831), the basis of electric generators and transformers. He also discovered benzene and laws of electrolysis. His idea of fields of force inspired Maxwell's equations. He started the Royal Institution Christmas Lectures for children.

d: Alan Turing (1912–1954), a British mathematician, described in 1936 a theoretical 'universal machine' that could compute anything computable, the foundation of computer science. During World War II at Bletchley Park he designed the Bombe machine that broke German Enigma codes, shortening the war. After the war he designed early computers and proposed the Turing test for machine intelligence (1950), and studied pattern formation in biology. Convicted of homosexuality in 1952 and forced to undergo chemical castration, he died of cyanide poisoning in 1954. Britain pardoned him in 2013, and he appears on the £50 note.

He held Newton's chair at Cambridge, and his book A Brief History of Time (1988) sold over 25 million copies.

d: Christopher Columbus (1451–1506), a Genoese sailor, believed he could reach Asia by sailing west, underestimating the Earth's size. After rejections by Portugal, Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain sponsored him; on 12 October 1492 his three ships reached the Bahamas, and he went on to Cuba and Hispaniola. On four voyages he explored the Caribbean and Central and South American coasts, still believing he was near Asia. As governor of Hispaniola he enslaved and brutally treated the Taíno, and was arrested in 1500. His voyages began European colonisation of the Americas, with devastating results for Indigenous peoples.

Under Juan Sebastián Elcano, one ship and 18 men returned in 1522, completing the first circumnavigation.

d: Ho Chi Minh (1890–1969) left Vietnam in 1911 as a ship's cook and lived in France, the US, Britain, the Soviet Union and China, becoming a founding member of the French Communist Party. In Mexico he joined Fidel Castro, and they launched the guerrilla war that overthrew Batista in 1959. He served as Cuba's industry minister and central bank head, and ordered executions of former regime officials. He visited India in 1959, meeting Nehru. d: Harriet Tubman (about 1822–1913) was born into slavery in Maryland, suffered a severe head injury from an overseer, and escaped to Philadelphia in 1849. Later she supported women's suffrage and cared for elderly African Americans.

d: Rosa Parks (1913–2005) was a seamstress and secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP in Alabama, where segregation laws forced Black passengers to give up bus seats to white riders. On 1 December 1955 she refused, and was arrested. Her arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott, led by the young pastor Martin Luther King Jr., which lasted 381 days until the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional. She faced job loss and threats, moved to Detroit, and was later called 'the mother of the civil rights movement'.

d: Maximilien Robespierre (1758–1794), a provincial lawyer inspired by Rousseau, became a leader of the radical Jacobins during the French Revolution, known as 'the Incorruptible'. He opposed the death penalty early on but argued for executing Louis XVI. As the leading member of the Committee of Public Safety, he oversaw the Reign of Terror (1793–94), in which about 17,000 were officially executed, claiming that 'terror is nothing but prompt, severe, inflexible justice'. Fearing they would be next, his colleagues arrested him on 9 Thermidor (27 July 1794), and he was guillotined the next day.

d: Suleiman I (1494–1566), the tenth Ottoman sultan, reigned for 46 years, the longest of any sultan. He captured Belgrade (1521), Rhodes (1522), defeated Hungary at Mohács (1526), besieged Vienna (1529), and took Baghdad and much of North Africa; his admiral Barbarossa dominated the Mediterranean. His architect Mimar Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque. He died during a campaign in Hungary.

d: Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub (1137–1193) was a Kurdish officer who became vizier of Fatimid Egypt in 1169, then abolished the Fatimid caliphate and founded the Ayyubid dynasty. He united Egypt, Syria and parts of Iraq, and on 4 July 1187 destroyed the crusader army at the Horns of Hattin, then took Jerusalem, allowing most Christians to ransom themselves. He fought Richard the Lionheart in the Third Crusade to a truce that kept Jerusalem in Muslim hands. Even European writers praised his chivalry and generosity; he died almost penniless.

He extended the Grand Canal, issued paper money, and welcomed foreigners such as Marco Polo. His invasions of Japan (1274, 1281), Vietnam and Java failed. He patronised Tibetan Buddhism through the lama Phagpa, who designed a script for Mongolian.

d: Timur (1336–1405), known in Europe as Tamerlane from 'Timur the Lame' after injuries to his right leg and arm, was a Turco-Mongol from near Samarkand. He conquered Persia, Mesopotamia, the Caucasus and the Golden Horde, sacked Delhi in 1398, and defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara (1402). His campaigns, marked by massacres and pyramids of skulls in cities like Isfahan and Baghdad, killed an estimated 17 million people. He brought craftsmen from conquered lands to make Samarkand magnificent, building the Bibi-Khanym mosque. He died while marching to invade China. His descendant Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

He ruled the Mughal Empire at its largest, conquering Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687). A devout Sunni, he reimposed the jizya on non-Muslims (1679), banned music at court, destroyed some temples including at Mathura and Varanasi, and executed the Sikh Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675). He spent his last 26 years fighting the Marathas in the Deccan, and after his death in 1707 the empire fragmented. Historians debate how much his policies were driven by religion versus politics.

d: Sher Shah Suri (1486–1545), born Farid Khan, was an Afghan who earned the name 'Sher' by killing a tiger. Rising in Bihar, he defeated Humayun and ruled north India from 1540. In five years he reorganised administration, measured land for fair revenue, introduced the silver rupiya (the origin of the rupee), and rebuilt the road from Bengal to Kabul (later the Grand Trunk Road) with sarais and trees. He died in an explosion while besieging Kalinjar fort. His tomb stands in Sasaram.

She hunted tigers, designed fabrics and gardens, and built her father's tomb, Itimad-ud-Daulah, in Agra. After Jahangir's death, her son-in-law lost the succession to Shah Jahan, and she retired to Lahore.

In 1191 he defeated Muhammad of Ghor at the first Battle of Tarain, but in 1192 Ghor returned and defeated him; he was captured and killed. The later epic Prithviraj Raso by Chand Bardai romanticised him as the last Hindu emperor of Delhi.

d: Alauddin Khalji (about 1266–1316) raided the rich Yadava capital of Devagiri in 1296, then murdered his uncle Jalaluddin and seized the throne. He repelled several large Mongol invasions, built the fort of Siri, and imposed price controls on grain and goods, with markets supervised by officials and a land tax of half the produce. He conquered Gujarat, Ranthambore and Chittor (1303) — the siege later romanticised in the legend of Rani Padmini — and sent Malik Kafur on raids deep into south India. After his death his empire quickly fell into chaos.

d: Muhammad bin Tughlaq (about 1290–1351) was a learned, generous but erratic sultan of Delhi. He raised taxes in the Doab during a famine, moved the capital and much of Delhi's population to Daulatabad in the Deccan, then back again, and issued copper token coins that were easily forged, causing chaos. He planned conquests of Khurasan and Qarachil that failed. Ibn Battuta, who served him as a judge, described both his generosity and his cruelty. Revolts during his reign created the Bahmani Sultanate and Vijayanagara.

Xuanzang visited and praised his warriors. He fought the Pallavas, but in 642 Narasimhavarman I captured Badami and Pulakeshin was probably killed.

d: Chandragupta II (reigned about 375–415), son of Samudragupta, is identified with the legendary King Vikramaditya. He married Kuberanaga and allied with the Vakatakas by marrying his daughter Prabhavatigupta to their king. He defeated the Western Kshatrapas (Shakas) of Gujarat and Malwa, gaining Arabian Sea ports and earning the title 'Shakari'. The iron pillar at Delhi, which has not rusted for 1,600 years, may commemorate him. The Chinese monk Faxian visited his peaceful empire, and Kalidasa may have been at his court.

d: Darius I (about 550–486 BCE) seized the Persian throne in 522 BCE after killing a usurper, recording his victory in the trilingual Behistun inscription, key to deciphering cuneiform. Under his advisers Ay and Horemheb, he restored the worship of Amun and the old gods and moved the court back from Amarna. He died at about 19, possibly from an infection after a leg fracture and malaria. His small tomb in the Valley of the Kings, discovered almost intact by Howard Carter in 1922, contained over 5,000 objects, including the golden death mask, making him the most famous pharaoh today.

He called the Council of Nicaea (325) to settle the Arian controversy, became sole emperor in 324, and founded Constantinople in 330 as the new capital. In his tent he wrote the Meditations, private notes in Greek on Stoic philosophy, urging self-discipline, duty and acceptance of fate. He made his son Commodus heir, ending the era of adoptive succession, and Commodus's misrule followed.

d: Catherine II (1729–1796) was a German princess, Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst, who married the future Peter III of Russia. In 1762 she overthrew her husband in a palace coup (he was killed soon after) and ruled for 34 years. She expanded Russia by annexing Crimea, defeating the Ottomans, and partitioning Poland. She corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot, founded the Hermitage collection and the Smolny Institute for girls, but strengthened serfdom and crushed Pugachev's rebellion (1773–75).

d: Louis XIV (1638–1715) became king at four; his childhood was marked by the Fronde revolts, which made him determined to control the nobility. He fought long wars for French expansion, revoked the Edict of Nantes (1685), driving out Protestant Huguenots, and left France deeply in debt. d: Henry VIII (1491–1547) became king of England in 1509. d: In Greek myth, Perseus was the son of Zeus and the princess Danaë, who was locked away by her father Acrisius because of a prophecy that her son would kill him; mother and baby were set adrift in a chest. Raised on the island of Seriphos, he was sent by King Polydectes to bring back Medusa's head. Using Athena's mirrored shield, Hermes' winged sandals, a cap of invisibility and a magic bag, he beheaded Medusa, then rescued the Ethiopian princess Andromeda from the sea monster Cetus and married her. He later accidentally killed Acrisius with a discus, fulfilling the prophecy, and was said to have founded Mycenae. He and Andromeda became constellations. He is a mythological figure, not a historical one.

d: Son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene, Heracles was hated by Hera, who drove him mad so that he killed his own family. To atone he served King Eurystheus and performed twelve labours: killing the Nemean lion and the Hydra, capturing the Cretan bull and the guard-dog Cerberus, cleaning the Augean stables by diverting rivers, and more. He also killed centaurs and freed Prometheus. Poisoned by the blood of the centaur Nessus, he burned himself on a pyre and became a god. Alexander the Great claimed descent from him, and Hercules became a model of strength in art.

d: Theseus, son of King Aegeus of Athens (or of Poseidon), cleared the road to Athens of bandits, then went to Crete as part of the tribute to King Minos. Athenians credited him with uniting Attica into one city-state.
