d: The atomic bomb releases enormous energy by splitting uranium-235 or plutonium-239 nuclei in an uncontrolled chain reaction.
x: Overview # The atomic bomb releases enormous energy by splitting uranium-235 or plutonium-239 nuclei in an uncontrolled chain reaction. The story behind it # In 1939 Leo Szilard drafted a letter, signed by Albert Einstein, warning President Roosevelt that Nazi Germany might build an atomic bomb. The Manhattan Project (1942–46), led by General Leslie Groves with physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer directing the Los Alamos laboratory, employed about 130,000 people at secret sites in Oak Ridge, Hanford and Los Alamos and cost about $2 billion. The first test, ‘Trinity’, exploded in the New Mexico desert on 16 July 1945; Oppenheimer later recalled the Bhagavad Gita: ‘Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.’ Three weeks later bombs destroyed Hiroshima (6 August) and Nagasaki (9 August). Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # Historians still debate whether the bombings were necessary to end the war, or partly intended to impress the Soviet Union. Germany’s own bomb project, led by Werner Heisenberg, was far behind. Soviet spies inside the project, including Klaus Fuchs and Theodore Hall, passed secrets to Moscow, helping the USSR test its own bomb in 1949; Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed in 1953 for espionage. Oppenheimer himself lost his security clearance in 1954 after opposing the hydrogen bomb, a decision the US government formally reversed in 2022. Downwinders near Trinity and Marshall Islanders affected by later tests received little warning. How it changed the world # The bomb created the Cold War’s nuclear arms race, with about 70,000 warheads at its peak in 1986, and the doctrine of mutually assured destruction. India tested its first device at Pokhran in 1974 and weapons in 1998.

d: Television transmits moving images and sound electronically.
x: Overview # Television transmits moving images and sound electronically. The story behind it # Scottish inventor John Logie Baird demonstrated mechanical television using a spinning disc in London in 1926. In 1927 Philo Farnsworth, a 21-year-old farm boy from Utah who had conceived the idea while ploughing fields in rows, transmitted the first fully electronic image. Vladimir Zworykin at RCA developed rival camera tubes. The BBC began regular broadcasts in 1936; India’s Doordarshan began in 1959. Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # RCA, led by David Sarnoff, fought Farnsworth in a long patent battle; Farnsworth won in 1939, but RCA’s marketing made it seem the inventor. Farnsworth died in obscurity. How it changed the world # Television shaped politics (the 1960 Kennedy–Nixon debate), brought war into living rooms (Vietnam), and in India serials like Ramayan (1987) drew 100 million viewers.

d: Motion pictures project a rapid sequence of photographs to create the illusion of movement.
x: Overview # Motion pictures project a rapid sequence of photographs to create the illusion of movement. The story behind it # Eadweard Muybridge’s 1878 photographs of a galloping horse showed motion could be captured. Thomas Edison’s company, especially his employee William Dickson, built the Kinetoscope (1891) for individual viewing. On 28 December 1895 Auguste and Louis Lumière held the first paid public screening in Paris with their Cinématographe. The Lumières’ films were shown in Bombay’s Watson Hotel in July 1896, and Dadasaheb Phalke made India’s first feature film in 1913. Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # French inventor Louis Le Prince filmed moving images in Leeds in 1888 but vanished on a train in 1890 before he could present his work, a mystery never solved; his son, who testified in Edison patent litigation, was later found shot dead. Edison used patents to control the American film industry until filmmakers moved to Hollywood, partly to escape his lawyers. How it changed the world # Cinema became the dominant art form of the 20th century, used for entertainment and propaganda (Leni Riefenstahl’s Nazi films). India’s film industry is the world’s largest by number of films.

d: Alternating current (AC) changes direction many times a second, so transformers can step voltage up for long-distance transmission.
x: Overview # Alternating current (AC) changes direction many times a second, so transformers can step voltage up for long-distance transmission. The story behind it # Nikola Tesla, who had worked briefly for Edison, patented AC induction motors and polyphase systems in 1888; George Westinghouse bought the patents. In the ‘war of the currents’, Edison’s direct current (DC) could only travel short distances. Westinghouse won the contract to light the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair and to build the Niagara Falls power plant (1895), making AC the global standard. Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # Edison and his ally Harold Brown campaigned that AC was deadly, publicly electrocuting animals and promoting the electric chair using Westinghouse AC — the first execution, of William Kemmler in 1890, was horrifically botched. The elephant Topsy was electrocuted at Coney Island in 1903 and filmed by the Edison company, though Edison himself was likely not directly involved. Tesla tore up his royalty contract to help Westinghouse survive financially and died poor. How it changed the world # AC grids electrified the world’s homes and factories.

d: X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation that passes through soft tissue but is absorbed by bone.
x: Overview # X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation that passes through soft tissue but is absorbed by bone. The story behind it # On 8 November 1895 physicist Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a fluorescent screen glowing near a covered cathode-ray tube. He called the mysterious rays ‘X’; his first X-ray photograph showed his wife Anna Bertha’s hand bones and wedding ring — she reportedly said, ‘I have seen my death.’ He refused to patent it so everyone could benefit and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics (1901). Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # Early users did not understand the dangers: shoe shops used X-ray fluoroscopes to fit shoes until the 1950s, and Edison’s assistant Clarence Dally died of radiation-induced cancer, after which Edison stopped X-ray research. The ‘Radium Girls’, women who painted watch dials with radium, suffered horrific jaw decay; their 1920s lawsuits helped establish workers’ rights. How it changed the world # X-rays revolutionised medicine, crystallography (revealing DNA’s structure) and security screening.

d: Radar detects objects by bouncing radio waves off them.
x: Overview # Radar detects objects by bouncing radio waves off them. The story behind it # In 1935, asked whether a ‘death ray’ could destroy aircraft, Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins showed instead that radio waves could detect planes. Britain built the Chain Home network along its coast, and in 1940 the cavity magnetron, invented by John Randall and Harry Boot, made compact radar possible; the Tizard Mission shared it with the US. Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # Britain spread the myth that its pilots ate carrots to see in the dark, to hide radar’s existence from Germany. How it changed the world # Radar helped win the Battle of Britain and later led to the microwave oven, discovered by Percy Spencer when a chocolate bar melted in his pocket.

d: DNA's double helix structure explains how genetic information is stored and copied.
x: Overview # DNA’s double helix structure explains how genetic information is stored and copied. The story behind it # James Watson and Francis Crick built a model of DNA as a double helix with paired bases in 1953, published in Nature. Crucial evidence came from X-ray diffraction images taken by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling, especially ‘Photo 51’, at King’s College London. Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # Maurice Wilkins showed Photo 51 to Watson without Franklin’s knowledge. Franklin died of cancer in 1958, and Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize; Watson’s memoir disparaged her. She is now recognised as a key contributor. How it changed the world # The discovery led to genetic engineering, DNA fingerprinting, the Human Genome Project and ancient DNA studies.

d: Vaccines against poliovirus prevent paralysis.
x: Overview # Vaccines against poliovirus prevent paralysis. The story behind it # Jonas Salk developed an inactivated vaccine tested on 1.8 million children in 1954, the largest medical trial in history, announced as safe on 12 April 1955; asked who owned the patent, he said, ‘Could you patent the sun?’ Albert Sabin developed an oral vaccine, used in India’s Pulse Polio campaign from 1995. Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # In the 1955 Cutter incident, a faulty batch containing live virus paralysed about 200 children, leading to vaccine regulation. How it changed the world # India was declared polio-free in 2014.

d: The oral contraceptive uses hormones to prevent ovulation.
x: Overview # The oral contraceptive uses hormones to prevent ovulation. The story behind it # Activist Margaret Sanger and heiress Katharine McCormick funded biologist Gregory Pincus and doctor John Rock to develop a hormonal pill, using progestins synthesised by Carl Djerassi and others from Mexican yams. The US approved it in 1960. Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # Early large trials were carried out on women in Puerto Rico in 1956, many poor and not fully informed of risks; early high doses caused side effects. Sanger also supported eugenics, which remains controversial. How it changed the world # The pill transformed women’s education, careers and the sexual revolution.

d: An integrated circuit places many transistors on a single chip.
x: Overview # An integrated circuit places many transistors on a single chip. The story behind it # Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated the first integrated circuit on germanium in 1958; Robert Noyce at Fairchild independently made a practical silicon version in 1959. Noyce co-founded Intel, and Gordon Moore predicted that transistor counts would double about every two years (Moore’s law). Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # Kilby won the 2000 Nobel Prize; Noyce had died in 1990. How it changed the world # Microchips power computers, phones and AI.

d: Liquid-fuel rockets carry payloads into space.
x: Overview # Liquid-fuel rockets carry payloads into space. The story behind it # Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fuel rocket in 1926 and was mocked by the New York Times (which apologised in 1969). In Nazi Germany, Wernher von Braun developed the V-2 missile. In the USSR, Sergei Korolev’s R-7 launched Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961). Rivalries, disputes and hidden history # V-2 rockets were built by concentration camp prisoners at Mittelwerk, where about 20,000 died — more than were killed by the V-2 attacks. After the war, under the secret Operation Paperclip, the US brought von Braun and over 1,600 German scientists, some with Nazi pasts, to America; von Braun designed the Saturn V that took Apollo to the Moon. How it changed the world # Rockets enabled satellites, GPS, the Moon landing and ISRO’s missions.

d: The largest of the Giza pyramids, built as Khufu's tomb, was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years. Its base is level to within about 2 cm and aligned to true north to within a fraction of a degree.
x: Overview # The largest of the Giza pyramids, built as Khufu’s tomb, was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years. Its base is level to within about 2 cm and aligned to true north to within a fraction of a degree. How it was built, step by step # Surveying: the site was levelled on bedrock, probably by cutting water channels or using plumb lines and set squares, and aligned to north using stars such as those circling the pole. Quarrying: most blocks were cut from a quarry just south of the pyramid using copper chisels, wooden wedges and dolerite pounders; casing stone came by boat from Tura across the Nile and granite 800 km from Aswan. Transport: blocks were dragged on wooden sledges; a tomb painting shows a worker pouring water in front of a sledge, which experiments show halves the friction on sand. A harbour and canal brought boats close to the plateau during the flood season. Raising: ramps — straight, zigzagging up a face, or spiralling around the pyramid — carried blocks upward; levers adjusted their final position. A ramp with post holes found at the Hatnub quarry (2018) suggests sledges were hauled with rope-and-post systems. Inner chambers: the King’s Chamber was roofed with nine granite beams, and five relieving chambers above spread the enormous weight; the Grand Gallery’s corbelled roof rises 8.6 m. Casing: polished white limestone blocks were set from the top down as the ramps were removed, making the pyramid gleam; most were later taken to build Cairo. Clever engineering and hidden stories # The diary of an official named Merer, found at Wadi al-Jarf in 2013, records his team shipping Tura limestone to Giza — the oldest inscribed papyri ever found. Workers’ villages excavated by Mark Lehner contain bakeries, breweries, cattle bones and a cemetery where workers were buried with honour, some with healed fractures showing medical care. Gang names like ‘Friends of Khufu’ were painted on blocks. Legacy # The only surviving Wonder of the Ancient World; it shows the organising power of the early Egyptian state.

d: The Flavian Amphitheatre was built on the drained lake of Nero's Golden House, paid for partly with treasure looted from the Jerusalem Temple. It hosted gladiator fights, animal hunts and executions for nearly 400 years.
x: Overview # The Flavian Amphitheatre was built on the drained lake of Nero’s Golden House, paid for partly with treasure looted from the Jerusalem Temple. It hosted gladiator fights, animal hunts and executions for nearly 400 years. How it was built, step by step # Draining Nero’s lake and laying a ring-shaped concrete foundation about 12 m deep. Building a skeleton of travertine piers, linked by arches, in 80 radial walls — so the structure could rise in several sections at once by different teams. Vaulting: concrete barrel and groin vaults over the corridors carried the seating, using wooden centring. Facade: three storeys of arches framed by Tuscan, Ionic and Corinthian half-columns, topped by a solid attic with sockets for the velarium masts. Hypogeum (added under Domitian): underground tunnels, cages and about 60 lifts and trapdoors to raise animals and scenery into the arena. Velarium: a retractable awning of canvas, worked by sailors from the Misenum fleet, shaded spectators. Clever engineering and hidden stories # 80 numbered entrances (vomitoria) let the crowd enter and leave in minutes, and tickets (tesserae) showed seat sections — principles still used in stadiums. The arena may even have been flooded for mock sea battles in its early years. The iron clamps were later looted, leaving the pockmarks visible today. Legacy # The model for modern stadiums; a symbol of both Roman engineering and spectacle based on violence.

d: Nearly 1,900 years later, the Pantheon still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Its 8.2 m oculus is the only source of light.
x: Overview # Nearly 1,900 years later, the Pantheon still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Its 8.2 m oculus is the only source of light. How it was built, step by step # Rotunda walls 6 m thick were built with hidden relieving arches and niches to channel weight. A huge wooden centring (temporary formwork) supported the dome while concrete was laid in horizontal rings. Lighter aggregate was used higher up: heavy basalt at the base, then tuff and finally pumice near the top. Coffers (sunken panels) were moulded into the inner surface, reducing weight while adding beauty. The dome thins from 6.4 m at the base to 1.2 m around the oculus, which is ringed by a compression ring of brick. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Roman concrete with volcanic ash forms crystals that make it stronger over time; MIT research in 2023 found ‘lime clasts’ that let cracks heal themselves when water seeps in. Legacy # It inspired Brunelleschi’s Florence dome, St Peter’s, and the US Capitol.

d: Aqueducts carried water by gravity alone from springs in the hills to cities, feeding fountains, baths and toilets. Most of their length ran underground; the famous arches were only needed to cross valleys.
x: Overview # Aqueducts carried water by gravity alone from springs in the hills to cities, feeding fountains, baths and toilets. Most of their length ran underground; the famous arches were only needed to cross valleys. How it was built, step by step # Surveyors used a chorobates (a 6 m levelling table with a water channel) and groma to plan a route with a gentle, constant slope — the Pont du Gard’s aqueduct drops just 12.6 m over 50 km. Tunnels were dug through hills from shafts at intervals, teams meeting in the middle. Valleys were crossed with arcades of stacked arches, or with inverted siphons — lead or stone pipes going down and up under pressure. The channel (specus) was lined with waterproof mortar and covered against dirt and sunlight. Settling tanks removed sediment; at the city, a distribution castle (castellum) split water to public fountains first, then baths, then private houses. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Frontinus, water commissioner in 97 CE, wrote a manual exposing illegal taps by citizens. Some aqueducts, like Segovia’s, worked until the 20th century. Legacy # Modern water supply systems follow the same principles; the Aqua Virgo still feeds the Trevi Fountain.

d: Roman roads let legions march 30 km a day and carried trade and messages across the empire; 'all roads lead to Rome'.
x: Overview # Roman roads let legions march 30 km a day and carried trade and messages across the empire; ‘all roads lead to Rome’. How it was built, step by step # Surveying a straight route with a groma. Digging a trench about 1 m deep. Laying a foundation of large stones (statumen), then rubble in lime (rudus), then fine gravel concrete (nucleus). Setting fitted paving stones (summa crusta) with a camber so rain drained into side ditches. Adding milestones every Roman mile and way-stations (mansiones) for changing horses. Clever engineering and hidden stories # The Via Appia (312 BCE) is still walkable today. The cursus publicus courier system could carry messages 80 km a day. Legacy # Many modern European highways follow Roman routes.

d: Not one wall but many, built over 2,000 years to defend against northern nomads. The brick sections tourists see near Beijing are Ming, mostly 16th century.
x: Overview # Not one wall but many, built over 2,000 years to defend against northern nomads. The brick sections tourists see near Beijing are Ming, mostly 16th century. How it was built, step by step # Early walls were rammed earth: soil packed in layers between wooden frames. Qin Shi Huang’s general Meng Tian linked older walls after 221 BCE with 300,000 men. The Han extended walls into the Gansu desert using layers of reeds, gravel and sand. The Ming rebuilt sections in brick and stone, with watchtowers on ridges. Beacon towers used smoke by day and fire by night to send warnings hundreds of kilometres in hours. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Chemists confirmed (2010) that Ming builders mixed sticky rice soup with lime, creating mortar stronger and more water-resistant than lime alone. It is not visible from the Moon with the naked eye — a famous myth. Legacy # A symbol of China, and a UNESCO site.

d: Stonehenge's giant stones align with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Bluestones were dragged about 225 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales.
x: Overview # Stonehenge’s giant stones align with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Bluestones were dragged about 225 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales. How it was built, step by step # A circular ditch and bank were dug with antler picks around 3000 BCE. Bluestones were brought from Wales, probably on sledges and rollers. Sarsens were shaped by pounding with stone hammers. Stones were tipped into pits and hauled upright with ropes and A-frames. Lintels were lifted on timber platforms and fixed with woodworking joints — mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Analysis in 2024 traced the Altar Stone to northern Scotland, over 700 km away. Legacy # A UNESCO site and icon of prehistory.

d: Built 6,000 years before Stonehenge by people who did not farm, it overturned the idea that monuments only came after agriculture.
x: Overview # Built 6,000 years before Stonehenge by people who did not farm, it overturned the idea that monuments only came after agriculture. How it was built, step by step # Pillars were cut from the limestone plateau with flint tools. T-shaped pillars were carved with foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and human arms and belts. Pillars were set in stone walls in circles, with two central pillars. Large feasts with wild game and possibly beer brought people together to build. Enclosures were later deliberately backfilled. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Its builders were hunter-gatherers; nearby, some of the earliest domesticated wheat appeared, suggesting monument building may have encouraged farming. Legacy # Called the world’s first temple.

d: Built in under six years after the Nika riots, it was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years.
x: Overview # Built in under six years after the Nika riots, it was the world’s largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years. How it was built, step by step # Justinian ordered rebuilding weeks after rioters burned the previous church in the Nika riots of 532. Four huge piers and great arches formed a square base about 31 m across. Pendentives — curved triangular sections — made the transition from the square base to the circular dome, a breakthrough in architecture. The shallow dome of light bricks rose on 40 ribs, with 40 windows at its base that make it seem to float on a ring of light. Two semi-domes on east and west extended the nave into a vast open space. Walls were covered in coloured marble and gold mosaics; legend says Justinian declared, ‘Solomon, I have surpassed you!’ Clever engineering and hidden stories # The original dome collapsed after an earthquake in 558 and was rebuilt higher; Ottoman architect Sinan later added buttresses. Legacy # Church, mosque (1453), museum (1934), mosque again (2020).

d: Petra, the Nabataean capital, was a rich caravan city controlling incense and spice routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean. Its most famous monuments, like Al-Khazneh ('the Treasury') and the Monastery, are carved directly into rose-red sandstone cliffs.
x: Overview # Petra, the Nabataean capital, was a rich caravan city controlling incense and spice routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean. Its most famous monuments, like Al-Khazneh (‘the Treasury’) and the Monastery, are carved directly into rose-red sandstone cliffs. How it was built, step by step # Masons cut steps into the cliff to reach the top. They carved downward from the top, so no scaffolding was needed. Chambers were hollowed out behind facades. Dams, cisterns and channels captured flash floods to supply water. Clever engineering and hidden stories # The Nabataeans were masters of desert water: dams diverted flash floods away from the narrow Siq gorge, and clay pipes and rock-cut channels fed cisterns, pools and even a garden with a swimming pool, supplying about 20,000–30,000 people. Earthquakes in 363 CE damaged the water system, and the city declined; the outside world rediscovered it in 1812 when Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt visited disguised as a pilgrim. Legacy # A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

d: A royal estate perched on a ridge, built without mortar, wheels or iron tools.
x: Overview # A royal estate perched on a ridge, built without mortar, wheels or iron tools. How it was built, step by step # Engineers built foundations — perhaps 60% of the work is underground. Terraces with layered drainage stopped landslides. Granite was split along natural cracks and shaped with harder stones. Ashlar blocks were fitted so precisely no blade fits between them. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Inca walls use ‘ashlar’ masonry, blocks fitted so tightly without mortar that they move during earthquakes and settle back. Engineers built extensive drainage: layers of topsoil, sand, gravel and rock in terraces, and 129 drainage channels, which is why the site has survived heavy rains for 500 years. It was abandoned around the Spanish conquest, and Hiram Bingham publicised it in 1911, although local farmers knew it well. Legacy # A UNESCO site rediscovered by the outside world in 1911.

d: Angkor, capital of the Khmer Empire, was a 'hydraulic city' covering about 1,000 km² — perhaps the largest pre-industrial urban complex. A network of reservoirs (barays), canals and moats captured monsoon rain to support rice farming and the temples.
x: Overview # Angkor, capital of the Khmer Empire, was a ‘hydraulic city’ covering about 1,000 km² — perhaps the largest pre-industrial urban complex. A network of reservoirs (barays), canals and moats captured monsoon rain to support rice farming and the temples. How it was built, step by step # Engineers built huge barays (reservoirs) with earthen dykes. Canals moved water and stone. Moats around temples stabilised the sandy soil under the foundations. Lidar shows a city covering 1,000 km². Clever engineering and hidden stories # Angkor Wat’s 5–10 million sandstone blocks were floated on canals from quarries at Phnom Kulen about 40 km away; marks on stones suggest a precise system. The moat around Angkor Wat keeps the groundwater stable, stopping the sandy foundation from shifting. Later, alternating mega-droughts and floods in the 14th–15th centuries damaged the system, contributing to Angkor’s decline. Legacy # Its decline may have been caused by droughts and floods overwhelming the system.

d: Mohenjo-daro had the world's most advanced urban sanitation of its time: nearly every house had a bathing area, many had toilets, and covered drains ran under the streets.
x: Overview # Mohenjo-daro had the world’s most advanced urban sanitation of its time: nearly every house had a bathing area, many had toilets, and covered drains ran under the streets. How it was built, step by step # The city was built on huge mud-brick platforms to protect against Indus floods. Streets were laid in a rough grid with main roads up to 10 m wide. Houses drained waste water through clay pipes into covered brick street drains with removable lids for cleaning. Soak pits and cesspools caught solids before water flowed out of the city. About 700 wells provided water. The Great Bath was waterproofed with fitted bricks, gypsum mortar and a layer of bitumen. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Brick sizes were standardised across hundreds of sites over 1,000 km apart, showing shared standards without any known central king. Legacy # Urban sanitation on this scale was not seen again in many places until the 19th century.

d: The largest monolithic rock-cut structure in the world, carved from the top down out of one mountain of basalt as a replica of Shiva's Mount Kailash.
x: Overview # The largest monolithic rock-cut structure in the world, carved from the top down out of one mountain of basalt as a replica of Shiva’s Mount Kailash. How it was built, step by step # Three trenches were cut down into the cliff to isolate a huge block of rock. Sculptors carved from the top downward, so they never needed scaffolding. The block was hollowed into a shrine, halls, a bridge and gateway, all one piece of stone. Life-size elephants, pillars and panels such as Ravana shaking Mount Kailash were carved in place. Plaster and paint once covered it white, like the snowy Kailash. Clever engineering and hidden stories # There was no room for mistakes — nothing could be added back. Experts still debate how the work was planned, given there are no plans or debris piles nearby. Legacy # Part of the UNESCO Ellora Caves, with Hindu, Buddhist and Jain monuments side by side.

d: The Big Temple's vimana was the tallest in India; granite is not found near Thanjavur.
x: Overview # The Big Temple’s vimana was the tallest in India; granite is not found near Thanjavur. How it was built, step by step # Foundations were laid on hard ground. Granite blocks were interlocked without mortar. The hollow pyramidal vimana rose in 13 tiers. The capstone (shikhara) was lifted, according to tradition, up an earthen ramp several kilometres long, or with scaffolding. Inscriptions recorded the temple’s staff, donations and dancers. Clever engineering and hidden stories # The tower is hollow inside, reducing weight; it has survived several earthquakes. Legacy # UNESCO site; celebrated its 1,000th year in 2010.

d: The pillar has resisted rust for 1,600 years.
x: Overview # The pillar has resisted rust for 1,600 years. How it was built, step by step # Iron was smelted from ore with charcoal in small furnaces. Lumps of hot iron (blooms) were forge-welded together by hammering. The pillar was hammered to shape and finished. An inscription in Sanskrit was carved praising a king named Chandra. Clever engineering and hidden stories # IIT Kanpur’s R. Balasubramaniam showed high phosphorus in the iron formed a protective film of ‘misawite’, preventing rust. Legacy # A wonder of metallurgy.

d: An inverted temple descending to groundwater, with over 500 sculptures; it appears on India's ₹100 note.
x: Overview # An inverted temple descending to groundwater, with over 500 sculptures; it appears on India’s ₹100 note. How it was built, step by step # Engineers dug a deep trench down to the water table. Terraced levels with pillared pavilions led down. Walls were lined with sculptures of Vishnu’s avatars. A cylindrical well at the end collected water. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Stepwells let people reach water as levels fell in the dry season and stayed cool. Legacy # Silted up and rediscovered in the 1940s; a UNESCO site.

d: Built by King Chanda of the Nikumbha dynasty in the 9th century, Chand Baori in Abhaneri, Rajasthan, is one of the deepest and largest stepwells in India: about 3,500 narrow steps over 13 storeys descend 30 m to the water. Its geometric pattern of steps is mesmerising.
x: Overview # Built by King Chanda of the Nikumbha dynasty in the 9th century, Chand Baori in Abhaneri, Rajasthan, is one of the deepest and largest stepwells in India: about 3,500 narrow steps over 13 storeys descend 30 m to the water. Its geometric pattern of steps is mesmerising. How it was built, step by step # A square shaft about 35 m wide was dug into the ground to reach groundwater. Double flights of steps were built in a zigzag on three sides, letting many people reach the water at once. On the fourth side, pillared pavilions and royal chambers were built for rest. A temple to Harshat Mata was built next to it. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Because air at the bottom is 5–6 °C cooler than at the surface, the stepwell served as a gathering place in hot summers. Stepwells were important to women, who fetched water, and many were built by queens. Legacy # Featured in films like The Dark Knight Rises.

d: Golconda began as a Kakatiya mud fort and became the capital of the Qutb Shahi sultans (1518–1687), famous for its diamond trade — the Koh-i-Noor and Hope diamond came from nearby mines. Its acoustic design lets a hand clap at the Fateh Darwaza entrance be heard at the Bala Hisar pavilion about 1 km away.
x: Overview # Golconda began as a Kakatiya mud fort and became the capital of the Qutb Shahi sultans (1518–1687), famous for its diamond trade — the Koh-i-Noor and Hope diamond came from nearby mines. Its acoustic design lets a hand clap at the Fateh Darwaza entrance be heard at the Bala Hisar pavilion about 1 km away. How it was built, step by step # Massive granite walls (about 10 km in total) with 87 bastions were built around a 120 m granite hill. Gates were studded with iron spikes against war elephants. Persian wheels and terracotta pipes lifted water uphill to the palaces and gardens. Domes and corridors were shaped to carry sound, serving as an alarm system. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Aurangzeb took the fort in 1687 after an eight-month siege, only after a traitor opened a gate. Legacy # Once famous for its diamond markets, linked to the Koh-i-Noor.

d: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. Considered the jewel of Mughal architecture, it combines Persian, Central Asian and Indian elements and changes colour with the light.
x: Overview # Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. Considered the jewel of Mughal architecture, it combines Persian, Central Asian and Indian elements and changes colour with the light. How it was built, step by step # The foundation on the Yamuna’s bank used wells filled with rubble and ebony and mahogany wood, which stay strong when kept moist by the river. A brick core was faced with white Makrana marble brought from Rajasthan by about 1,000 elephants. A double dome makes the outer dome tall while keeping the inner chamber proportional. Pietra dura: semi-precious stones like jade, lapis lazuli and carnelian were inlaid in floral designs. Four minarets were built leaning slightly outward. Clever engineering and hidden stories # The minarets tilt outward so that in an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb. Calligraphy grows larger towards the top so it appears the same size from the ground. Air pollution has yellowed the marble, so it is cleaned with a mud pack (multani mitti). Legacy # A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

d: Built around 1250 by Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, the Konark Sun Temple is shaped like the Sun god Surya's giant chariot, with 24 carved stone wheels pulled by seven horses. Its main tower, which collapsed long ago, may have been about 70 m tall.
x: Overview # Built around 1250 by Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, the Konark Sun Temple is shaped like the Sun god Surya’s giant chariot, with 24 carved stone wheels pulled by seven horses. Its main tower, which collapsed long ago, may have been about 70 m tall. How it was built, step by step # The temple was built of khondalite stone on a platform near the sea. Iron beams were used inside the structure; one, about 10.6 m long, is among the largest forged iron beams of the era. The 24 wheels were carved with spokes acting as sundials. Walls were covered in carvings of daily life, music, war and love. Legend says a powerful magnet at the top once caused ships’ compasses to fail. Clever engineering and hidden stories # The wheels’ shadows can tell the time accurately. The main sanctum was filled with sand by the British in 1903 to stop it collapsing. Legacy # UNESCO site; featured on the ₹10 note.

d: The last surviving Inca suspension bridge is rebuilt every June in three days from grass. The Inca road network once had about 200 such bridges.
x: Overview # The last surviving Inca suspension bridge is rebuilt every June in three days from grass. The Inca road network once had about 200 such bridges. How it was built, step by step # Each family twists q’oya grass into thin cords and brings its share. Cords are braided into six thick main cables, each as thick as a thigh. Cables are pulled across the gorge and tied to stone anchors on each side. Four cables form the floor and two the handrails; weavers dangle over the river to tie side walls. The old bridge is cut loose and allowed to fall into the river. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Grass ropes in tension can carry several people; renewing them yearly keeps the bridge safe and the community bonded. UNESCO listed the ritual as intangible heritage in 2013. Legacy # Shows how pre-industrial peoples built suspension bridges centuries before Europe.

d: The world's oldest standing open-spandrel stone arch bridge, still in use after 1,400 years.
x: Overview # The world’s oldest standing open-spandrel stone arch bridge, still in use after 1,400 years. How it was built, step by step # A shallow segmental arch — not a semicircle — kept the deck low and easy to cross. 28 parallel arch rings were built side by side, so one could be repaired without closing the bridge. Iron dovetails tied the stones together. Four small arches were opened in the spandrels (the sides above the main arch). Clever engineering and hidden stories # The spandrel openings cut weight by about 15% and let flood water pass through, protecting the bridge. Europe did not build open-spandrel bridges until the 14th century. Legacy # It has survived at least eight wars, ten floods and many earthquakes.

d: The tallest Roman aqueduct bridge carried water 50 km to Nîmes.
x: Overview # The tallest Roman aqueduct bridge carried water 50 km to Nîmes. How it was built, step by step # Wooden centring frames supported each arch during building. Blocks were lifted by treadwheel cranes powered by men walking inside wheels. Three tiers of arches were stacked, the lowest carrying a road. Protruding stones held scaffolding and centring. Clever engineering and hidden stories # The whole 50 km aqueduct from Uzès to Nîmes falls just 12.6 m — about 25 cm per kilometre — showing extraordinary surveying precision. It carried about 40,000 m³ of water a day. Builders left protruding stones and holes for scaffolding and inscribed numbers on blocks to guide assembly. Legacy # A UNESCO site.

d: Built over the River Severn at Coalbrookdale, where Abraham Darby I had pioneered smelting iron with coke in 1709, the Iron Bridge (1779) was the first major bridge made of cast iron. It became a symbol of the Industrial Revolution.
x: Overview # Built over the River Severn at Coalbrookdale, where Abraham Darby I had pioneered smelting iron with coke in 1709, the Iron Bridge (1779) was the first major bridge made of cast iron. It became a symbol of the Industrial Revolution. How it was built, step by step # Iron was cast in moulds at Coalbrookdale. Ribs were assembled using carpentry joints — dovetails and mortise-and-tenon — because there were no iron-construction techniques yet. Ribs were lifted into place with a timber scaffold. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Builders used woodworking joints for iron, showing a technology in transition. Legacy # A UNESCO site.

d: The first steel-wire suspension bridge; a family tragedy and triumph.
x: Overview # The first steel-wire suspension bridge; a family tragedy and triumph. How it was built, step by step # Caissons — huge upside-down wooden boxes filled with compressed air — were sunk into the riverbed so men could dig foundations. Granite towers rose 84 m. Cables were spun in place from 5,434 galvanised steel wires each. Diagonal stays added stiffness. The deck was hung from vertical suspenders. Clever engineering and hidden stories # John Roebling died of tetanus after an accident; his son Washington was paralysed by caisson disease (the bends). His wife Emily learned engineering and managed the project for 11 years, and was the first person to cross it. Legacy # A symbol of New York.

d: After the Tay Bridge collapsed in a storm in 1879, killing about 75 people on a train, Scottish engineers built the Forth Bridge to be visibly massive and safe. Opened in 1890, it was the world's longest cantilever bridge and carries trains to this day.
x: Overview # After the Tay Bridge collapsed in a storm in 1879, killing about 75 people on a train, Scottish engineers built the Forth Bridge to be visibly massive and safe. Opened in 1890, it was the world’s longest cantilever bridge and carries trains to this day. How it was built, step by step # Three huge double cantilevers (‘balanced arms’) were built out from three main piers. Tubular steel members, some 3.7 m in diameter, gave strength. Suspended girder spans connected the cantilevers. The bridge was painted constantly, giving rise to the phrase ‘like painting the Forth Bridge’ for an endless task. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Baker demonstrated the cantilever principle with two men sitting on chairs holding poles, and a third man in the middle. Legacy # UNESCO site (2015).

d: Built during the Great Depression across the Golden Gate strait with its strong currents and fog, the Golden Gate Bridge was the world's longest suspension span (1,280 m) when it opened in 1937. Its 'International Orange' colour makes it visible in fog.
x: Overview # Built during the Great Depression across the Golden Gate strait with its strong currents and fog, the Golden Gate Bridge was the world’s longest suspension span (1,280 m) when it opened in 1937. Its ‘International Orange’ colour makes it visible in fog. How it was built, step by step # The south tower foundation was built in open sea, inside a concrete fender. Steel towers rose 227 m. Each main cable was spun from 27,572 wires. The deck was hung from suspender cables. Clever engineering and hidden stories # A safety net under the bridge saved 19 workers, the ‘Halfway to Hell Club’. Legacy # An icon of engineering.

d: Built during World War II to replace a floating pontoon bridge over the Hooghly, the Howrah Bridge (Rabindra Setu) is a cantilever bridge riveted without nuts and bolts, using steel mostly from Tata Steel. It opened in 1943 without a ceremony, fearing Japanese bombing.
x: Overview # Built during World War II to replace a floating pontoon bridge over the Hooghly, the Howrah Bridge (Rabindra Setu) is a cantilever bridge riveted without nuts and bolts, using steel mostly from Tata Steel. It opened in 1943 without a ceremony, fearing Japanese bombing. How it was built, step by step # Two 85 m high towers were built on both banks. Anchor arms and cantilever arms were extended out over the river. A suspended span joined the two cantilevers in the middle. The whole structure was riveted together. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Carries over 100,000 vehicles and 150,000 pedestrians daily; bird droppings and spit (from paan) corrode its steel. Legacy # Symbol of Kolkata.

d: Opened in 1914, the Pamban Bridge links Rameswaram island to mainland India across the Palk Strait. It was India's first sea bridge, with a central Scherzer rolling lift span opening for ships. A new vertical-lift bridge opened alongside it in 2025.
x: Overview # Opened in 1914, the Pamban Bridge links Rameswaram island to mainland India across the Palk Strait. It was India’s first sea bridge, with a central Scherzer rolling lift span opening for ships. A new vertical-lift bridge opened alongside it in 2025. How it was built, step by step # Piers were built in a corrosive marine environment. A double-leaf bascule span opened manually to let ships pass. The 2025 bridge uses a 72 m vertical lift span raised electromechanically. Clever engineering and hidden stories # It survived the 1964 cyclone with damage; E. Sreedharan restored it in 46 days. The new 2025 bridge has a vertical-lift span. Legacy # Linked Rameswaram to the mainland.

d: On the Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla railway, the Chenab Bridge spans a deep gorge with a 467 m steel arch, 359 m above the river — higher than the Eiffel Tower. It opened in 2025, linking Kashmir by rail.
x: Overview # On the Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla railway, the Chenab Bridge spans a deep gorge with a 467 m steel arch, 359 m above the river — higher than the Eiffel Tower. It opened in 2025, linking Kashmir by rail. How it was built, step by step # Two cable cranes, with the world’s largest such pylons, carried materials across the gorge. The arch was built out from both sides in segments, held back by temporary cables. The arch closed in April 2021. The deck was launched over the arch. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Designed to withstand blasts and earthquakes. Legacy # Part of the line linking Kashmir by rail.

d: In the rain-soaked hills of Meghalaya, Khasi and Jaintia communities grow bridges from the roots of the rubber fig tree. Unlike timber, which rots, these living bridges grow stronger over time and can last centuries.
x: Overview # In the rain-soaked hills of Meghalaya, Khasi and Jaintia communities grow bridges from the roots of the rubber fig tree. Unlike timber, which rots, these living bridges grow stronger over time and can last centuries. How it was built, step by step # Roots are guided across the river along bamboo or areca palm scaffolds. Over 15–30 years they grow and fuse. Stones fill gaps to form a walkway. Clever engineering and hidden stories # They can last hundreds of years and survive monsoon floods. Legacy # Nominated for UNESCO status.

d: Opened in July 1940, the slender first Tacoma Narrows Bridge swayed so much in wind that it was nicknamed 'Galloping Gertie'. On 7 November 1940, in a 64 km/h wind, it twisted violently and collapsed into Puget Sound — captured on film.
x: Overview # Opened in July 1940, the slender first Tacoma Narrows Bridge swayed so much in wind that it was nicknamed ‘Galloping Gertie’. On 7 November 1940, in a 64 km/h wind, it twisted violently and collapsed into Puget Sound — captured on film. How it was built, step by step # Designers used a shallow plate-girder deck instead of a deep truss, to save money and look elegant. Wind caused vertical oscillations from the start; motorists enjoyed the ride. On 7 November wind triggered torsional flutter — self-reinforcing twisting. A cable band slipped and the deck tore apart. Clever engineering and hidden stories # The only death was a dog. It changed bridge design forever: wind tunnel testing became standard. Legacy # Taught in every engineering school.

d: A vast underground network let guerrillas live, hide and launch surprise attacks right next to a major US base during the Vietnam War. Today it is a museum park visited by tourists.
x: Overview # A vast underground network let guerrillas live, hide and launch surprise attacks right next to a major US base during the Vietnam War. Today it is a museum park visited by tourists. How it was built, step by step # Villagers began digging shelters in the 1940s during the war against France, expanding them in the 1960s. Clay was dug with short hoes and carried out in baskets, then scattered in bomb craters or rivers so the Americans could not spot fresh soil. Tunnels were built on several levels, connected by trapdoors, with dead ends and narrow sections to slow pursuers. Underground spaces included sleeping chambers, kitchens, meeting rooms, weapons workshops, and field hospitals. ‘Hoang Cam’ kitchens vented smoke through long channels to exit far away, low to the ground, like morning mist. Entrances were tiny, hidden trapdoors covered by leaves; ventilation holes were disguised as termite mounds. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Tunnels were often too small for most American soldiers. The US sent ‘tunnel rats’ — volunteers with pistols and torches — and used flooding, gas, dogs and B-52 bombing; fighters disguised air holes with American soap and cigarettes to confuse dogs. Life inside was miserable: darkness, disease, malaria, scorpions and lack of air. Legacy # A symbol of Vietnamese resistance and of the limits of US firepower in guerrilla war.

d: Cheap, hidden traps such as the punji stick pit were a psychological weapon that slowed and frightened US patrols. Military studies estimate booby traps and mines caused about 11% of US deaths and 17% of wounds.
x: Overview # Cheap, hidden traps such as the punji stick pit were a psychological weapon that slowed and frightened US patrols. Military studies estimate booby traps and mines caused about 11% of US deaths and 17% of wounds. How it was built, step by step # Punji pits: camouflaged holes lined with sharpened bamboo stakes. Swinging and falling traps triggered by tripwires on jungle paths. Grenades and mines made from unexploded American ordnance — the US military estimated much of the explosive in Viet Cong mines came from American duds. Warning signs known to locals marked trapped areas so villagers could avoid them. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Traps were often designed to wound rather than kill, because a wounded soldier tied up others for evacuation and lowered morale. Many villagers, children and farmers were also injured, and unexploded ordnance still kills people in Vietnam today. Legacy # Shaped US jungle training and the image of the Vietnam War as a war without front lines.

d: Instead of defending the beaches, Kuribayashi turned the tiny volcanic island into an underground fortress, inflicting about 26,000 US casualties.
x: Overview # Instead of defending the beaches, Kuribayashi turned the tiny volcanic island into an underground fortress, inflicting about 26,000 US casualties. How it was built, step by step # Soldiers dug tunnels by hand in sulphurous heat up to 50 °C. Bunkers, pillboxes and gun positions were linked underground. Mount Suribachi was honeycombed with tunnels on several levels. Defenders held fire until US Marines landed, then attacked from hidden positions. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Almost all 21,000 defenders died; only 216 were captured. The flag-raising photo on Suribachi became famous. Legacy # One of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific War.

t: Okinawa caves and Japanese underground HQ
d: In the Battle of Okinawa (April–June 1945), the bloodiest of the Pacific War, Japanese forces turned Okinawa's natural limestone caves (gama) and dug tunnels into command posts, hospitals and shelters. Civilians also hid in caves, and their fate was tragic.
x: Overview # In the Battle of Okinawa (April–June 1945), the bloodiest of the Pacific War, Japanese forces turned Okinawa’s natural limestone caves (gama) and dug tunnels into command posts, hospitals and shelters. Civilians also hid in caves, and their fate was tragic. How it was built, step by step # Natural caves were enlarged and linked. The underground Navy Headquarters was dug with pickaxes. Field hospitals operated in caves. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Tragically, some civilians were pressured into mass suicides in caves; the Himeyuri student nurses died in cave hospitals. Around 100,000–150,000 Okinawan civilians died. Legacy # Memorials at the former Navy HQ and Himeyuri cave.

d: One of about 200 underground cities in Cappadocia, used as refuges during raids. It was rediscovered in 1963 when a man knocked down a wall in his house.
x: Overview # One of about 200 underground cities in Cappadocia, used as refuges during raids. It was rediscovered in 1963 when a man knocked down a wall in his house. How it was built, step by step # Tuff, soft to carve but hardening in air, was dug with hand tools. Ventilation shafts brought air to the deepest levels and supplied water. Stables, wine presses, chapels, kitchens and schools were carved. Rolling stone doors, 1 m wide, could be closed from inside only. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Tunnels connected to the underground city of Kaymaklı about 8 km away. Legacy # A major tourist site.

d: A chain of underground forts built to stop a German invasion — which Germany simply went around through Belgium in 1940.
x: Overview # A chain of underground forts built to stop a German invasion — which Germany simply went around through Belgium in 1940. How it was built, step by step # Underground forts (ouvrages) were built up to 30 m deep, with barracks, kitchens, power stations, hospitals and electric railways. Retractable steel gun turrets rose to fire and dropped for protection. Anti-tank obstacles and casemates covered the gaps. It ended at the Belgian border, partly because Belgium was an ally and the Ardennes forest was thought impassable to tanks. Clever engineering and hidden stories # It worked as designed — forts were rarely captured — but strategy failed: Germany attacked through the Ardennes. Legacy # A byword for false security.

d: During the Blitz, Londoners defied the government and sheltered in tube stations.
x: Overview # During the Blitz, Londoners defied the government and sheltered in tube stations. How it was built, step by step # People bought platform tickets and refused to leave. The government then provided bunks and toilets. Deep-level shelters were built under some stations. Clever engineering and hidden stories # In the 1943 Bethnal Green disaster, 173 people died in a crush on the stairs. Legacy # Images became symbols of resilience.

d: Built during the Cold War inside a granite mountain near Colorado Springs, the Cheyenne Mountain Complex housed NORAD, which tracks missiles and aircraft over North America. It was designed to survive a nearby nuclear blast.
x: Overview # Built during the Cold War inside a granite mountain near Colorado Springs, the Cheyenne Mountain Complex housed NORAD, which tracks missiles and aircraft over North America. It was designed to survive a nearby nuclear blast. How it was built, step by step # Tunnels blasted into granite. 15 buildings set on giant springs to absorb shock. 25-tonne blast doors. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Designed to survive a nuclear blast. Legacy # Still in use.

d: Prisoners dug a tunnel under a German prison camp; 76 escaped in March 1944.
x: Overview # Prisoners dug a tunnel under a German prison camp; 76 escaped in March 1944. How it was built, step by step # Prisoners dug three tunnels — Tom, Dick and Harry — so that if one was discovered, the others could continue. Harry’s entrance was hidden under a stove in Hut 104. Walls were shored up with about 4,000 bed boards. Air was pumped through pipes made of powdered-milk tins. Sand was hidden in bags inside trousers and scattered in gardens (‘penguins’). Forgers produced false passports and tailors made civilian clothes. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Only three reached freedom; 50 recaptured men were executed on Hitler’s orders. Legacy # Inspired the 1963 film The Great Escape.

d: Pottery began with hunter-gatherers: fragments from Xianrendong Cave in China are about 20,000 years old. The potter's wheel, appearing in Mesopotamia around 4000 BCE, turned pottery into a fast, specialised craft — and may have inspired the wheel for carts.
x: Overview # Pottery began with hunter-gatherers: fragments from Xianrendong Cave in China are about 20,000 years old. The potter’s wheel, appearing in Mesopotamia around 4000 BCE, turned pottery into a fast, specialised craft — and may have inspired the wheel for carts. How it was built, step by step # Digging and cleaning clay, mixing in temper to stop cracking. Shaping by coiling ropes of clay, or ‘throwing’ on a spinning wheel. Drying slowly in the shade. Firing: open bonfires at about 600–800 °C, later updraft kilns over 1,000 °C. Decorating with slips, paint or glaze. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Pots let people boil food, store grain and brew beer, and they changed diets. Archaeologists use pottery styles to date sites — like the Painted Grey Ware of the Vedic period and the Harappan red-and-black wares. Legacy # Led to glazes, porcelain and modern ceramics.

d: A technique for casting detailed metal figures, used for the Indus 'Dancing Girl' and Chola Nataraja bronzes, still practised at Swamimalai.
x: Overview # A technique for casting detailed metal figures, used for the Indus ‘Dancing Girl’ and Chola Nataraja bronzes, still practised at Swamimalai. How it was built, step by step # A model is made in beeswax. It is coated with fine clay to make a mould. The mould is heated; the wax melts out (‘lost’). Molten bronze is poured in. The mould is broken and the figure polished. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Each cast is unique, since the mould is destroyed. Legacy # Swamimalai bronzes have a geographical indication tag.

d: Wootz was a high-carbon crucible steel produced in South India and Sri Lanka from around 300 BCE. Traded to Persia and Syria, it was forged into famous 'Damascus' swords with wavy patterns, sharp and strong.
x: Overview # Wootz was a high-carbon crucible steel produced in South India and Sri Lanka from around 300 BCE. Traded to Persia and Syria, it was forged into famous ‘Damascus’ swords with wavy patterns, sharp and strong. How it was built, step by step # Iron and carbon-rich material sealed in clay crucibles. Heated in furnaces for hours. Slow cooling formed carbide patterns. Ingots forged carefully at low heat. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Studies found carbon nanotubes in Damascus blades. The technique was lost by the 18th century. Legacy # Inspired modern metallurgy research.

d: Qanats are gently sloping underground tunnels that carry groundwater from mountain aquifers to fields and towns using gravity alone. Developed in Iran about 3,000 years ago, they spread to North Africa, Spain, China and India.
x: Overview # Qanats are gently sloping underground tunnels that carry groundwater from mountain aquifers to fields and towns using gravity alone. Developed in Iran about 3,000 years ago, they spread to North Africa, Spain, China and India. How it was built, step by step # A mother well finds the water table. Vertical shafts are dug at intervals. A tunnel connects them with a slight slope. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Qanats reduce evaporation; Iran had about 30,000. Legacy # UNESCO-listed Persian qanats.

d: In the Persian desert, people made and stored ice through scorching summers using yakhchāls — domed ice houses with thick walls of insulating mortar — and cooled homes with windcatchers (badgirs) that funnel breezes.
x: Overview # In the Persian desert, people made and stored ice through scorching summers using yakhchāls — domed ice houses with thick walls of insulating mortar — and cooled homes with windcatchers (badgirs) that funnel breezes. How it was built, step by step # Water was frozen in shallow pools on winter nights. Ice was stored in a deep pit under a thick dome. Windcatchers pulled cool air down. Clever engineering and hidden stories # Passive cooling without electricity. Legacy # Modern green architects study them.

d: Built in 256 BCE by Li Bing, governor of the Shu region for the state of Qin, Dujiangyan controls floods and irrigates the Chengdu plain without a dam — and still works after 2,270 years.
