d: Upper body of a human joined at the waist to the body and four legs of a horse. First attested: Clay figurine from Lefkandi, Euboea (c. 900 BCE); named in Homer's Iliad (8th century BCE).
x: What it looks like # Upper body of a human joined at the waist to the body and four legs of a horse. Powers and weaknesses # Great speed and strength; Chiron was a healer, astrologer and teacher of heroes. Stories and legends # Most centaurs were violent: at the wedding of the Lapith king Pirithous they got drunk and tried to carry off the bride, sparking the battle carved on the Parthenon’s metopes. Chiron, by contrast, tutored Achilles, Jason, Asclepius and Heracles; wounded by one of Heracles’ poisoned arrows, he gave up his immortality and became the constellation Sagittarius (or Centaurus). The centaur Nessus tried to carry off Heracles’ wife Deianira and, dying, tricked her with his poisoned blood, which later killed Heracles. Popular belief and legacy # Centaurs symbolised the struggle between civilisation and wild animal nature. Medieval bestiaries and Renaissance art kept them alive; today they appear in C. S. Lewis’s Narnia and Harry Potter. Could it really exist? # Biologically impossible: no vertebrate has six limbs, and a human torso on a horse’s body would need two sets of lungs and hearts. A popular theory suggests the myth grew from Greeks first meeting expert horse-riding peoples of the steppe or Thessaly, who seemed to be one with their horses.

d: Body, tail and hind legs of a lion; head, wings and talons of an eagle. First attested: Seals and art from Susa and Mesopotamia (c. 3000 BCE); Greek accounts from Aristeas of Proconnesus (7th century BCE), retold by Herodotus.
x: What it looks like # Body, tail and hind legs of a lion; head, wings and talons of an eagle. Powers and weaknesses # Guardians of treasure and of the divine; incredibly strong flyers. Stories and legends # Herodotus describes one-eyed Arimaspians trying to steal gold from the griffins who guard it in Scythia. Griffins pulled Alexander the Great’s flying chariot in medieval romances and appear in Dante’s Paradiso pulling a chariot. Gold Scythian art is full of griffins. Popular belief and legacy # As king of beasts and king of birds combined, the griffin became a symbol of power and protection on shields, coats of arms and buildings. Could it really exist? # No. But folklorist Adrienne Mayor argued in 2000 that Scythian gold-miners in the Gobi and Altai found fossil skeletons of the beaked dinosaur Protoceratops and imagined a beaked, four-legged guardian; palaeontologists have challenged this idea, noting griffin art is older and found far away.

d: A giant water serpent with many heads (often nine); one head was immortal. First attested: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE).
x: What it looks like # A giant water serpent with many heads (often nine); one head was immortal. Powers and weaknesses # For every head cut off, two grew back; its blood was a deadly poison. Stories and legends # Killing the Hydra was Heracles’ second labour. His nephew Iolaus burned each neck stump with a torch so heads could not regrow, and Heracles buried the immortal head under a rock. He dipped his arrows in its poison — the same poison that later killed the centaurs Chiron and Nessus and, finally, Heracles himself. Popular belief and legacy # ‘Hydra-headed’ describes problems that multiply when attacked. The constellation Hydra is the largest in the sky. Could it really exist? # No animal regrows multiple heads. But the tiny freshwater animal named hydra really can regenerate its whole body from small pieces. Some scholars think the myth reflects springs at Lerna that kept bursting out when blocked.

d: Women with living snakes for hair, sometimes with tusks, wings and bronze hands; Medusa was the only mortal of the three Gorgon sisters. First attested: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE); Gorgon faces (gorgoneia) on temples and shields from the 7th century BCE.
x: What it looks like # Women with living snakes for hair, sometimes with tusks, wings and bronze hands; Medusa was the only mortal of the three Gorgon sisters. Powers and weaknesses # Anyone who looked at Medusa’s face was turned to stone; even her severed head kept that power. Stories and legends # King Polydectes sent the hero Perseus to fetch Medusa’s head. With Athena’s polished shield as a mirror, Hermes’ winged sandals and Hades’ cap of invisibility, Perseus beheaded her while she slept; from her neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor. Perseus used the head to turn the sea monster threatening Andromeda, and later Polydectes, to stone, then gave it to Athena, who placed it on her aegis. In Ovid’s later Roman version (8 CE), Medusa was a beautiful priestess punished by Athena after Poseidon assaulted her in Athena’s temple — a version many modern writers read as a story of a victim blamed. Popular belief and legacy # Gorgon faces were apotropaic — protective symbols to ward off evil — carved on temples, armour and coins. Medusa appears on the flag of Sicily and the Versace logo, and is now often reclaimed as a symbol of female rage. Could it really exist? # No creature turns things to stone. The gorgon face may come from older Near Eastern demon masks, or from the frightening faces of predators.

d: Giants with a single eye in the middle of the forehead. First attested: Hesiod's Theogony and Homer's Odyssey (c. 8th–7th century BCE).
x: What it looks like # Giants with a single eye in the middle of the forehead. Powers and weaknesses # Immense strength; master smiths who forged Zeus’s thunderbolts, Poseidon’s trident and Hades’ helmet. Stories and legends # In the Odyssey, Odysseus and his men are trapped in the cave of Polyphemus, son of Poseidon, who eats several of them. Odysseus tells him his name is ‘Nobody’, gets him drunk and blinds him with a burning stake; when Polyphemus cries that ‘Nobody’ is hurting him, the other Cyclopes ignore him. The men escape clinging under sheep, but Odysseus’s boast earns Poseidon’s anger and ten years of wandering. Popular belief and legacy # Later Greeks believed Cyclopes built the giant stone walls of Mycenae and Tiryns, which is why such masonry is called ‘Cyclopean’. Could it really exist? # Not as giants. In 1914 palaeontologist Othenio Abel suggested that skulls of extinct dwarf elephants on Mediterranean islands like Sicily and Crete, with a large central nasal opening, looked like a one-eyed giant’s skull. Cyclopia, a rare and fatal birth defect, exists in humans and animals but such individuals cannot survive.

d: A fire-breathing lion with a goat's head rising from its back and a serpent for a tail. First attested: Homer's Iliad, Book 6 (8th century BCE).
x: What it looks like # A fire-breathing lion with a goat’s head rising from its back and a serpent for a tail. Powers and weaknesses # Breathes fire. Stories and legends # King Iobates of Lycia sent the hero Bellerophon to kill it, expecting him to die. Riding the winged horse Pegasus, Bellerophon shot it from the air and, in some versions, thrust a lead-tipped spear into its mouth; its fiery breath melted the lead and killed it. Popular belief and legacy # The Etruscan bronze ‘Chimera of Arezzo’ (c. 400 BCE) is a masterpiece. Today ‘chimera’ means any impossible hybrid or wild fantasy. Could it really exist? # No — but at Yanartaş near Olympos in Lycia, natural gas has burned from cracks in the rock for over 2,500 years; ancient writers linked these eternal flames to the Chimera. In biology, real ‘chimeras’ are organisms containing cells with two different sets of DNA.

d: A man with the head and tail of a bull. First attested: Greek vase paintings from the 7th century BCE; myth set in Bronze Age Crete.
x: What it looks like # A man with the head and tail of a bull. Powers and weaknesses # Great strength. Stories and legends # Born to Queen Pasiphaë after Poseidon cursed her to love a bull, the Minotaur was hidden in the Labyrinth. The Athenian prince Theseus volunteered as a tribute; Minos’s daughter Ariadne gave him a ball of thread to find his way out. Theseus killed the Minotaur and escaped, but forgot to change his black sails to white, so his father Aegeus threw himself into the sea — the Aegean. Popular belief and legacy # Many historians think the myth reflects Minoan bull worship and the bull-leaping frescoes of Knossos, whose maze-like palace may have suggested the Labyrinth. Could it really exist? # No.

d: A white winged horse. First attested: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE).
x: What it looks like # A white winged horse. Powers and weaknesses # Flight; where his hoof struck Mount Helicon, the spring Hippocrene burst out, inspiring poets. Stories and legends # Born from the neck of Medusa when Perseus beheaded her, Pegasus was tamed by Bellerophon with a golden bridle from Athena and helped him kill the Chimera. When Bellerophon tried to fly to Olympus, Zeus sent a gadfly to sting Pegasus; Bellerophon fell, and Pegasus became a constellation. Popular belief and legacy # A symbol of poetry and inspiration; the emblem of British airborne forces. Could it really exist? # A horse-sized animal could not fly with feathered wings — it would need enormous flight muscles; the largest flying animals, pterosaurs like Quetzalcoatlus, weighed perhaps 200–250 kg using hollow bones.

d: A giant dog with three heads (Hesiod says fifty), a serpent tail and snakes growing from its back. First attested: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE).
x: What it looks like # A giant dog with three heads (Hesiod says fifty), a serpent tail and snakes growing from its back. Powers and weaknesses # Prevents the dead from leaving the underworld. Stories and legends # Capturing Cerberus was Heracles’ twelfth and final labour; he wrestled it with his bare hands and carried it to King Eurystheus. Orpheus lulled it to sleep with music, and the Sibyl drugged it for Aeneas. Popular belief and legacy # The image of a guardian dog of the dead appears in many cultures; Hindu tradition has Yama’s two four-eyed dogs. Could it really exist? # Multi-headed animals do occur rarely (polycephaly), but they rarely survive long.

d: Egyptian: a lion with a human (pharaoh's) head. Greek: a lion's body, eagle's wings and a woman's head. First attested: Great Sphinx of Giza (c. 2500 BCE); Greek sphinx in Hesiod (c. 700 BCE).
x: What it looks like # Egyptian: a lion with a human (pharaoh’s) head. Greek: a lion’s body, eagle’s wings and a woman’s head. Powers and weaknesses # The Greek Sphinx posed a riddle: ‘What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon and three in the evening?’ Stories and legends # Oedipus answered ‘Man’ — crawling as a baby, walking as an adult, using a cane in old age — and the Sphinx threw herself from her rock. The reward, marriage to Thebes’ widowed queen, led to Oedipus’s tragedy. Popular belief and legacy # In Egypt sphinxes were protective symbols of royal power; the Great Sphinx probably has Khafre’s face. Could it really exist? # No, but the Great Sphinx was carved from a natural limestone outcrop.

d: A small serpent with a crown-like mark; medieval versions became a rooster-serpent (cockatrice). First attested: Pliny the Elder's Natural History (77 CE).
x: What it looks like # A small serpent with a crown-like mark; medieval versions became a rooster-serpent (cockatrice). Powers and weaknesses # Kills with its gaze and breath; scorches grass and splits rocks. Stories and legends # Pliny says only the weasel’s odour can kill it. Medieval legends said a basilisk hatched from a rooster’s egg incubated by a toad, and could be killed by seeing its reflection. Popular belief and legacy # Feared through the Middle Ages; Harry Potter revived it. Could it really exist? # No. Its legend may be based on cobras, which spit venom and raise hoods like crowns. The real basilisk lizard of Central America, which runs on water, is named after it.

d: A giant winged reptile with four legs, scales, claws and fiery breath (in medieval Europe). First attested: Mesopotamian serpent-dragons such as the mušḫuššu (from c. 2100 BCE) and Tiamat in the Enuma Elish; Greek drakon from Homer; medieval fire-breathing dragon in Beowulf (c. 700–1000 CE).
x: What it looks like # A giant winged reptile with four legs, scales, claws and fiery breath (in medieval Europe). Powers and weaknesses # Fire breath, flight, poisonous blood, near-impenetrable scales; dragon’s blood or heart could give invulnerability or understanding of birds. Stories and legends # The Babylonian god Marduk slays the chaos dragon Tiamat to create the world. In Greek myth Apollo kills the Python at Delphi, and a dragon guards the Golden Fleece for Jason. Beowulf dies killing a dragon that guards a treasure hoard. Sigurd kills the dragon Fáfnir and bathes in its blood. In the 13th-century Golden Legend, Saint George kills a dragon that demanded a princess as sacrifice in Libya — the image on England’s flag-saint tradition. Popular belief and legacy # European dragons symbolised chaos, greed and evil (the devil in Revelation is a ‘great red dragon’). The red dragon became the emblem of Wales. Could it really exist? # Not as fire-breathing flying giants: no animal produces fire, and a huge four-legged reptile with wings would have six limbs. But fossils of dinosaurs and huge reptiles likely encouraged belief, and real ‘dragons’ exist: the Komodo dragon (up to 3 m) and the gliding Draco lizards. The bombardier beetle sprays boiling chemicals — the closest thing to ‘fire’ in nature.

d: A colossal sea serpent or dragon with impenetrable scales and fiery breath (Job 41). First attested: Ugaritic Baal Cycle (c. 1400 BCE) as Lotan; Hebrew Bible (Job 41, Psalm 74, Isaiah 27:1).
x: What it looks like # A colossal sea serpent or dragon with impenetrable scales and fiery breath (Job 41). Powers and weaknesses # Unbeatable by humans — ‘Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook?’ (Job 41:1). Stories and legends # In the Ugaritic texts, the storm god Baal defeats Lotan, the seven-headed serpent; the Hebrew Bible says God crushed the heads of Leviathan and will slay it at the end of days. Jewish legend says its flesh will be served at a feast for the righteous. Popular belief and legacy # Thomas Hobbes used it as the title of his 1651 book on the all-powerful state. The word now means anything enormous. Could it really exist? # No sea serpent of that kind exists, though whales and crocodiles probably inspired it. Palaeontologists named a giant fossil predatory whale Livyatan melvillei, which hunted whales 12 million years ago.

d: Invisible beings who can take human or animal form; in folklore, ghostly shapes of smoke or fire. First attested: Pre-Islamic Arabian poetry and belief; the Quran (7th century CE), especially Surah al-Jinn (72).
x: What it looks like # Invisible beings who can take human or animal form; in folklore, ghostly shapes of smoke or fire. Powers and weaknesses # Shape-shifting, invisibility, great strength, travel at enormous speed; some are believers and some evil (shayatin). Stories and legends # The Quran says jinn were created from ‘smokeless fire’, have free will and will be judged. King Solomon (Sulaiman) commanded jinn to build for him. The One Thousand and One Nights is full of jinn granting wishes and trapped in bottles; ‘Aladdin’, with the genie of the lamp, was added by the French translator Antoine Galland in 1710 from a Syrian storyteller, Hanna Diyab. Popular belief and legacy # For many Muslims, jinn are part of religious belief rather than folklore; exorcism (ruqyah) is practised. In the West, the ‘genie’ became a comic wish-granter. Could it really exist? # Science cannot test claims about invisible beings; for believers this is a matter of faith. Folklorists note jinn beliefs often explain illness, bad luck and fears of desolate places.

d: A human figure made of clay or mud. First attested: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b (c. 5th century CE): the sage Rava creates a man; Sefer Yetzirah; Prague legend from the 19th century.
x: What it looks like # A human figure made of clay or mud. Powers and weaknesses # Great strength and obedience; brought to life with a holy name or the word ‘emet’ (truth) on its forehead; erasing the first letter to make ‘met’ (death) deactivates it. Stories and legends # In the best-known legend, Rabbi Judah Loew (the Maharal) of Prague created a golem in the 16th century to protect the Jewish ghetto from antisemitic attacks. When it grew too powerful, he deactivated it. The story was popularised in the 19th century. Popular belief and legacy # It inspired Frankenstein, the word ‘robot’ (via Karel Čapek’s play R.U.R.) and debates about artificial intelligence. Could it really exist? # Clay cannot live, but robots and AI are modern ‘golems’ that raise the same question: what if our creations escape control?

d: Humans of enormous size; Norse giants could be monstrous or beautiful. First attested: Mesopotamian Humbaba in Gilgamesh (c. 2100 BCE); Nephilim in Genesis 6 and Goliath in 1 Samuel; Greek Gigantes and Titans in Hesiod (c. 700 BCE); Norse jötnar in the Eddas.
x: What it looks like # Humans of enormous size; Norse giants could be monstrous or beautiful. Powers and weaknesses # Strength; some, like the Titans, were older gods. Stories and legends # Gilgamesh and Enkidu kill Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest. David kills the Philistine champion Goliath with a sling. In Greek myth, the Olympians defeat the Titans and later the Gigantes. In Norse myth the world was made from the body of the giant Ymir. In the Ramayana, Ravana’s giant brother Kumbhakarna fights Rama. Popular belief and legacy # Ancient people found mammoth and mastodon bones and believed them to be giants’ remains, as historian Adrienne Mayor showed. Could it really exist? # Not as mountain-sized beings: bones could not support the weight. But gigantism is real: Robert Wadlow (1918–1940) reached 2.72 m. The extinct ape Gigantopithecus may have been 3 m tall.

d: Small, ugly, mischievous humanoids, often green or grey. First attested: 'Gobelinus', a spirit in Orderic Vitalis's chronicle (12th century); later European folklore.
x: What it looks like # Small, ugly, mischievous humanoids, often green or grey. Powers and weaknesses # Mischief, theft, trickery. Stories and legends # Germany’s kobolds lived in mines (giving their name to cobalt, which miners blamed for poisoning). Tolkien’s orcs are called goblins in The Hobbit. Popular belief and legacy # Goblins explained bad luck, lost items and accidents in mines. Could it really exist? # No. Folklorists link goblin tales to explaining misfortune, and to the dangers of mines (toxic arsenic in ‘kobold’ ores).

d: In Norse sources, giant-like beings; in later folklore, huge, ugly creatures with big noses, or small and hairy. First attested: Old Norse sagas and the Prose Edda (13th century).
x: What it looks like # In Norse sources, giant-like beings; in later folklore, huge, ugly creatures with big noses, or small and hairy. Powers and weaknesses # Turn to stone in sunlight (in later Scandinavian folklore); smell Christian blood. Stories and legends # In ‘Three Billy Goats Gruff’ a troll lives under a bridge. Norwegian painter Theodor Kittelsen’s drawings shaped how trolls look today. Popular belief and legacy # Unusual rock formations across Norway were explained as petrified trolls. Could it really exist? # No. Rocks that look like faces (pareidolia) and fear of wild mountains shaped the legend.

d: A dragon with two legs and two wings, and a barbed tail. First attested: Medieval European heraldry (the word dates from the 17th century, from Old French 'wivre', a viper).
x: What it looks like # A dragon with two legs and two wings, and a barbed tail. Powers and weaknesses # Poisonous tail; flight. Stories and legends # Wyverns appear in heraldry, such as on the arms of the old Kingdom of Wessex. Popular belief and legacy # A symbol of war and pestilence. Could it really exist? # Body plan resembles pterosaurs, real flying reptiles with wings formed from arms. So, unlike the four-legged dragon, a wyvern-like animal did exist — though not breathing fire.

d: In folklore, a bloated, ruddy corpse; after Bram Stoker, a pale, elegant aristocrat. First attested: Slavic and Balkan folklore; the word appears in Habsburg reports from Serbia in the 1720s (Petar Blagojević 1725, Arnold Paole 1726–1732).
x: What it looks like # In folklore, a bloated, ruddy corpse; after Bram Stoker, a pale, elegant aristocrat. Powers and weaknesses # Returning from the dead, drinking blood, shape-shifting into bats or wolves; weakened by garlic, sunlight, crucifixes and stakes. Stories and legends # Austrian officials investigated vampire panics in Serbian villages in the 1720s, exhuming bodies and staking them; their reports spread the word across Europe. John Polidori’s The Vampyre (1819) and Bram Stoker’s Dracula (1897), inspired partly by Vlad the Impaler, created the modern image. In New England, families exhumed relatives suspected of spreading tuberculosis, such as Mercy Brown in 1892. Popular belief and legacy # Vampire fears explained epidemics and deaths in families. Could it really exist? # No undead exist. Decomposing bodies bloat, look rosy and leak blood from the mouth, and nails appear to grow — convincing villagers corpses were feeding. Diseases like tuberculosis, rabies and porphyria have been suggested as inspirations. Real vampire bats drink blood from animals.

d: A human who transforms into a wolf or wolf-human hybrid. First attested: Ovid's Metamorphoses (8 CE) tells of King Lycaon turned into a wolf; Petronius's Satyricon (1st century CE).
x: What it looks like # A human who transforms into a wolf or wolf-human hybrid. Powers and weaknesses # Transformation, often under a full moon (a modern idea from 20th-century films); vulnerable to silver (also modern). Stories and legends # Zeus turned Lycaon into a wolf for serving him human flesh. In 1589 Peter Stumpp was executed in Germany after confessing under torture to being a werewolf. In France, over 30,000 werewolf cases were reported between 1520 and 1630. Popular belief and legacy # Werewolf trials were linked to witch trials. Could it really exist? # No. ‘Clinical lycanthropy’, a rare psychiatric condition, makes people believe they turn into animals, and hypertrichosis causes excess body hair. Wolves really did attack people in pre-modern Europe.

d: A white horse or goat-like animal with a single spiralled horn. First attested: Greek physician Ctesias's account of India (c. 400 BCE); a one-horned animal appears on Indus Valley seals (c. 2600–1900 BCE).
x: What it looks like # A white horse or goat-like animal with a single spiralled horn. Powers and weaknesses # Its horn neutralised poison; only a virgin could tame it. Stories and legends # Medieval tapestries show unicorn hunts. Narwhal tusks were sold as unicorn horns, worth more than gold; Denmark’s throne is made of them. Popular belief and legacy # A symbol of purity and Christ; Scotland’s national animal. Could it really exist? # A one-horned animal is plausible: the extinct ‘Siberian unicorn’ Elasmotherium, a rhinoceros with a huge horn, lived until about 39,000 years ago. The ‘unicorn’ on Indus seals may be a bull shown in profile.

d: A colossal octopus or squid large enough to be mistaken for an island. First attested: Erik Pontoppidan's Natural History of Norway (1752); Norse sagas mention sea monsters.
x: What it looks like # A colossal octopus or squid large enough to be mistaken for an island. Powers and weaknesses # Enormous size; dragging ships down; creating whirlpools. Stories and legends # Linnaeus included it in early editions of his classification. Tennyson wrote a poem; Pirates of the Caribbean popularised it. Popular belief and legacy # Sailors feared it. Could it really exist? # Yes, partly: giant squids (Architeuthis) reach about 13 m and colossal squids weigh up to 500 kg. The first photographs of a live giant squid were taken in 2004, and video in 2012. They do not sink ships.

d: Grotesque stone creatures on cathedral roofs. First attested: Gothic church water spouts from the 13th century; legend of La Gargouille of Rouen.
x: What it looks like # Grotesque stone creatures on cathedral roofs. Powers and weaknesses # In legend, protection from evil; coming to life at night (modern fantasy). Stories and legends # La Gargouille, a dragon, terrorised Rouen until St Romanus subdued it; its head was mounted on a church as a water spout. Popular belief and legacy # They scared away evil spirits. Could it really exist? # They are real carvings designed to throw rainwater away from walls; the word comes from French for ‘throat’.

d: A woman with long hair, washing bloodstained clothes or wailing. First attested: Irish folklore (bean sídhe, 'woman of the fairy mound'); 14th-century texts.
x: What it looks like # A woman with long hair, washing bloodstained clothes or wailing. Powers and weaknesses # Her wail foretells a death. Stories and legends # She followed specific Irish families. Popular belief and legacy # Linked to the tradition of keening — women wailing at funerals. Could it really exist? # No; foxes’ screams at night may explain the sound.

d: Fierce humanoids with fangs, claws and sometimes many heads; masters of illusion who can take beautiful forms. First attested: Rigveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE), where Agni is invoked to burn the rakshas; central in the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
x: What it looks like # Fierce humanoids with fangs, claws and sometimes many heads; masters of illusion who can take beautiful forms. Powers and weaknesses # Shape-shifting, illusion (maya), flight, great strength; strongest at night. Stories and legends # Ravana, ten-headed king of Lanka, abducts Sita in the Ramayana and is defeated by Rama with Hanuman’s help. His brother Kumbhakarna sleeps for six months at a time, and Vibhishana sides with Rama. In the Mahabharata, Bhima kills the rakshasa Hidimba and marries his sister Hidimbi; their son Ghatotkacha fights for the Pandavas at Kurukshetra. Popular belief and legacy # Rakshasas appear across South and Southeast Asian art, from Angkor’s carvings to Balinese masks. Ravana is honoured in some traditions as a great scholar and devotee of Shiva. Could it really exist? # No; scholars think some stories reflect fears of the forest and encounters with unfamiliar peoples.

d: A terrifying spirit with a Brahmin's sacred thread and a demon's form. First attested: Puranic and folk traditions (first millennium CE); Kerala temple traditions.
x: What it looks like # A terrifying spirit with a Brahmin’s sacred thread and a demon’s form. Powers and weaknesses # Vast learning in the Vedas and scriptures combined with demonic power. Stories and legends # A Brahmarakshasa is the spirit of a learned Brahmin who misused knowledge, was arrogant or refused to teach; he is doomed to haunt until he passes on his knowledge or is freed. In one tale, the poet Vararuchi frees one by answering its question. Many Kerala temples have a shrine for a Brahmarakshas. Popular belief and legacy # It warns that knowledge must be shared and used rightly. Could it really exist? # No; a moral folk belief.

d: A spirit that possesses corpses, hanging upside down from trees in cremation grounds. First attested: Vetala Panchavimshati ('25 tales of the Vetala'), included in Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara (11th century).
x: What it looks like # A spirit that possesses corpses, hanging upside down from trees in cremation grounds. Powers and weaknesses # Inhabits and animates dead bodies; knows past, present and future. Stories and legends # King Vikramaditya is asked by a sorcerer to bring a corpse possessed by a vetala. Each time he carries it, the vetala tells a story ending in a riddle; if the king answers, the vetala flies back to its tree. The 25 tales are known in Hindi as Baital Pachisi and were popular on TV as Vikram aur Betaal (1985). Popular belief and legacy # Vetalas are associated with tantric practices and cremation grounds. Could it really exist? # No.

d: Serpents, often cobras, sometimes many-headed or half-human. First attested: Vedic and early Buddhist texts (first millennium BCE); serpent deities in Indus seals are possible precursors.
x: What it looks like # Serpents, often cobras, sometimes many-headed or half-human. Powers and weaknesses # Guardians of water and treasure; can be protectors or dangerous. Stories and legends # The serpent king Vasuki served as the rope when gods and asuras churned the ocean of milk. Vishnu rests on the serpent Shesha. The naga king Mucalinda sheltered the Buddha from a storm. Krishna subdued the serpent Kaliya. Popular belief and legacy # Nag Panchami is celebrated in India, and nagas guard temples in Cambodia, Thailand and Laos. Could it really exist? # Cobras are real and revered; giant many-headed serpents are not. The extinct snake Titanoboa reached about 13 m.

d: A giant eagle-like bird, sometimes with a human body. First attested: Mahabharata (Adi Parva, compiled c. 400 BCE–400 CE).
x: What it looks like # A giant eagle-like bird, sometimes with a human body. Powers and weaknesses # Immense speed and strength. Stories and legends # Garuda stole the nectar of immortality (amrita) from the gods to free his mother from slavery to the nagas, earning Vishnu’s friendship as his mount. Popular belief and legacy # Indonesia’s national emblem, Thailand’s royal emblem and the name of Indonesia’s airline; the Indian Air Force’s special forces are ‘Garud’. Could it really exist? # No bird is that large. The extinct Haast’s eagle of New Zealand, with a 3 m wingspan, hunted giant moa birds.

d: A sea creature combining a crocodile, fish and elephant trunk. First attested: Sculptures from the 2nd century BCE (Bharhut, Sanchi); Vedic texts.
x: What it looks like # A sea creature combining a crocodile, fish and elephant trunk. Powers and weaknesses # Vehicle (vahana) of the river goddess Ganga and the sea god Varuna. Stories and legends # Makaras guard temple gateways and decorate toranas. Popular belief and legacy # The zodiac sign Capricorn is Makara in Indian astrology (Makar Sankranti). Could it really exist? # Inspired by real gharials, crocodiles and river dolphins.

d: A long scaly serpent with four legs, deer antlers, whiskers and no wings. First attested: Dragon figure of clam shells in a tomb at Xishuipo, Henan (c. 4500 BCE); Hongshan jade 'pig-dragons'.
x: What it looks like # A long scaly serpent with four legs, deer antlers, whiskers and no wings. Powers and weaknesses # Controls rain, floods and weather; brings good fortune. Stories and legends # The emperor was called the ‘son of the dragon’ and wore dragon robes. Dragon Kings appear in Journey to the West. Dragon boat races commemorate the poet Qu Yuan. Popular belief and legacy # Unlike European dragons, Chinese dragons are wise and lucky; the Year of the Dragon is considered fortunate. Could it really exist? # No; but ‘dragon bones’ sold as medicine were often dinosaur and mammal fossils — and in 1899 scholars recognised writing on some ‘dragon bones’: the oracle bones of the Shang.

d: A magnificent red and gold bird like an eagle. First attested: Herodotus's Histories, Book 2 (c. 430 BCE), drawing on the Egyptian bennu bird of Heliopolis.
x: What it looks like # A magnificent red and gold bird like an eagle. Powers and weaknesses # Rebirth: at the end of its life it builds a nest of spices, bursts into flames and rises again from the ashes (a later Roman detail). Stories and legends # The Chinese fenghuang, paired with the dragon, symbolised the empress. Popular belief and legacy # Early Christians used it as a symbol of resurrection. Could it really exist? # No.

d: Huge ogres with red or blue skin, horns, tusks, tiger-skin loincloths and iron clubs. First attested: Heian-period Japanese literature (from the 9th–10th centuries).
x: What it looks like # Huge ogres with red or blue skin, horns, tusks, tiger-skin loincloths and iron clubs. Powers and weaknesses # Immense strength. Stories and legends # Minamoto no Raikō and his four warriors killed the oni king Shuten-dōji on Mount Ōe after drugging him with poisoned sake. Momotarō, the peach boy, defeats the oni of Onigashima. Popular belief and legacy # At Setsubun, people throw roasted soybeans shouting ‘Oni wa soto, fuku wa uchi!’ (‘Demons out, luck in!’). Could it really exist? # No; possibly inspired by bandits and outsiders.

d: Foxes with up to nine tails, who can take human form. First attested: Chinese nine-tailed fox in the Shan Hai Jing (c. 4th century BCE); Japanese kitsune in the Nihon Ryōiki (c. 822).
x: What it looks like # Foxes with up to nine tails, who can take human form. Powers and weaknesses # Shape-shifting, illusion, possession; more tails mean more power and age. Stories and legends # Tamamo-no-Mae, a nine-tailed fox in disguise, bewitched an emperor. Popular belief and legacy # Messengers of the Shinto deity Inari. Could it really exist? # Foxes are real; magic is not.

d: Bird-like or long-nosed red-faced mountain beings. First attested: Nihon Shoki (720 CE).
x: What it looks like # Bird-like or long-nosed red-faced mountain beings. Powers and weaknesses # Martial arts, flight. Stories and legends # Tengu taught swordsmanship to the young Minamoto no Yoshitsune. Popular belief and legacy # Once demons, later protectors of mountains. Could it really exist? # No.

d: A large ape-like creature covered in hair. First attested: Sherpa folklore; 'metoh-kangmi' mistranslated as 'Abominable Snowman' after the 1921 Everest expedition.
x: What it looks like # A large ape-like creature covered in hair. Powers and weaknesses # Elusive. Stories and legends # Eric Shipton photographed a large footprint in 1951. Monasteries kept ‘yeti scalps’. In 2019 the Indian Army posted photos of giant footprints near Makalu. Popular belief and legacy # Central to Sherpa and Tibetan folklore. Could it really exist? # A 2017 DNA study of ‘yeti’ hair, bones and teeth found they came from Himalayan brown bears, Asian black bears and a dog. The extinct giant ape Gigantopithecus lived in southern China until about 300,000 years ago.

d: A 2–3 m tall hairy ape-like creature. First attested: Coast Salish 'Sasq'ets' traditions; the name 'Bigfoot' from 1958 footprints in California.
x: What it looks like # A 2–3 m tall hairy ape-like creature. Powers and weaknesses # Elusive. Stories and legends # The 1967 Patterson–Gimlin film shows a figure walking. After Ray Wallace’s death in 2002, his family revealed he had made the 1958 footprints with carved wooden feet. Popular belief and legacy # A cultural icon. Could it really exist? # No body, bones or DNA have ever been found.

d: A long-necked creature like a plesiosaur. First attested: Adomnán's Life of St Columba (c. 700 CE) describes a 'water beast' in the River Ness in 565.
x: What it looks like # A long-necked creature like a plesiosaur. Powers and weaknesses # — Stories and legends # The famous 1934 ‘Surgeon’s Photograph’ was confessed as a hoax in 1994, made with a toy submarine. Popular belief and legacy # A tourism icon. Could it really exist? # Plesiosaurs died out 66 million years ago, and Loch Ness formed after the last Ice Age. A 2018 environmental DNA survey found no reptile DNA but lots of eel DNA.

d: A gaunt, ice-hearted giant, always hungry. First attested: Algonquian peoples' oral traditions (Ojibwe, Cree, Innu); recorded by Jesuit missionaries in the 17th century.
x: What it looks like # A gaunt, ice-hearted giant, always hungry. Powers and weaknesses # A person who resorts to cannibalism can become a wendigo. Stories and legends # In 1879 the Cree man Swift Runner was executed after killing and eating his family during a famine, claiming possession by a wendigo. Popular belief and legacy # A warning against greed and cannibalism in times of starvation. Could it really exist? # No. ‘Wendigo psychosis’ was described by anthropologists as a culture-bound syndrome, but some argue it was largely a colonial construct.

d: A gigantic bird. First attested: Indigenous oral traditions of the Pacific Northwest and Great Plains.
x: What it looks like # A gigantic bird. Powers and weaknesses # Flapping its wings causes thunder; lightning flashes from its eyes. Stories and legends # Thunderbirds appear on totem poles fighting whales. Popular belief and legacy # A powerful spirit. Could it really exist? # No bird that large exists; the extinct Argentavis had a 7 m wingspan.

d: Upper body of a woman, tail of a fish. First attested: Syrian goddess Atargatis, depicted half-fish (c. 1st millennium BCE); Greek sirens were originally bird-women.
x: What it looks like # Upper body of a woman, tail of a fish. Powers and weaknesses # Enchanting songs; storms. Stories and legends # Christopher Columbus reported seeing three ‘mermaids’ in 1493, but noted they were not as pretty as pictured — almost certainly manatees. P. T. Barnum exhibited the ‘Feejee Mermaid’ in 1842, a monkey sewn to a fish. Hans Christian Andersen wrote The Little Mermaid (1837). Popular belief and legacy # Mami Wata in African traditions, Matsya (Vishnu’s fish avatar). Could it really exist? # No. In 2012 the US NOAA stated there is no evidence of mermaids. Manatees and dugongs likely inspired sightings.

d: Spiky-backed creature; later, hairless dog-like animals. First attested: Puerto Rico, 1995 (Madelyne Tolentino's sighting).
x: What it looks like # Spiky-backed creature; later, hairless dog-like animals. Powers and weaknesses # — Stories and legends # The witness’s description resembled the alien in the film Species. Popular belief and legacy # Modern cryptid. Could it really exist? # Hairless ‘chupacabras’ were coyotes or dogs with severe mange.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. The US secretly recruited Nazi scientists after World War II.
x: The claim # The US secretly recruited Nazi scientists after World War II. What the evidence shows # Over 1,600 German scientists, engineers and technicians were brought to the US, many with Nazi Party or SS membership, their records sanitised to avoid immigration rules. Wernher von Braun, who built the V-2 with slave labour, led NASA’s Saturn V programme; Hubertus Strughold, linked to human experiments at Dachau, became a ‘father of space medicine’. The USSR ran a similar programme (Operation Osoaviakhim).

d: Verdict: Documented fact. Japan ran a secret biological-weapons unit that experimented on humans, and its leaders escaped trial.
x: The claim # Japan ran a secret biological-weapons unit that experimented on humans, and its leaders escaped trial. What the evidence shows # Unit 731 near Harbin, led by Shirō Ishii, performed vivisections, frostbite tests and deliberate infections with plague, anthrax and cholera on thousands of prisoners, mostly Chinese, and spread plague over Chinese cities, killing perhaps hundreds of thousands. After the war the US granted Ishii and his staff immunity in exchange for their data; several later held prominent medical posts in Japan.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. The CIA secretly drugged people with LSD in mind-control experiments.
x: The claim # The CIA secretly drugged people with LSD in mind-control experiments. What the evidence shows # Under MKUltra, the CIA funded experiments at universities, hospitals and prisons, giving LSD and other drugs to people, sometimes without consent, and testing hypnosis and sensory deprivation; in Montreal, psychiatrist Ewen Cameron ‘depatterned’ patients with electroshock. CIA director Richard Helms ordered most files destroyed in 1973.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. US health officials deliberately left Black men with syphilis untreated to study the disease.
x: The claim # US health officials deliberately left Black men with syphilis untreated to study the disease. What the evidence shows # The US Public Health Service followed about 600 poor Black men, 399 with syphilis, telling them they were treated for ‘bad blood’. Even after penicillin became the standard cure in 1947, they were denied treatment. Dozens died and wives and children were infected. A whistle-blower, Peter Buxtun, leaked it to the press in 1972. President Clinton apologised in 1997. A related US study deliberately infected Guatemalans in 1946–48.

d: Verdict: Partly true. The second North Vietnamese attack used to justify US war in Vietnam never happened.
x: The claim # The second North Vietnamese attack used to justify US war in Vietnam never happened. What the evidence shows # On 2 August 1964 North Vietnamese boats did attack the USS Maddox. But the reported second attack on 4 August almost certainly did not occur — sonar and radar misreadings in a storm. President Johnson used it to pass the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, escalating the Vietnam War, in which over 3 million people died.

d: Verdict: Documented fact (proposed, rejected). US military chiefs proposed staging fake terrorist attacks to justify invading Cuba.
x: The claim # US military chiefs proposed staging fake terrorist attacks to justify invading Cuba. What the evidence shows # The Joint Chiefs of Staff proposed staging attacks on US targets, including blowing up a ship at Guantánamo and faking the downing of a civilian plane, blaming Cuba. President Kennedy’s administration rejected it.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. Britain destroyed or hid colonial records before independence to cover up abuses.
x: The claim # Britain destroyed or hid colonial records before independence to cover up abuses. What the evidence shows # As colonies became independent, British officials burned or dumped at sea records that might embarrass the government, including evidence of torture in Kenya’s Mau Mau camps. Thousands of files were secretly kept in a Foreign Office archive at Hanslope Park until revealed during a 2011 court case by Kenyan victims, who won compensation in 2013.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. Companies knew radium paint was poisoning women workers and hid it.
x: The claim # Companies knew radium paint was poisoning women workers and hid it. What the evidence shows # Young women painting watch dials with glow-in-the-dark radium paint were told to lick their brushes to a point. Many developed bone decay (‘radium jaw’), anaemia and cancer. Company executives handled radium with protection, while doctors hired by companies blamed syphilis. The women’s lawsuits (1928) helped establish workplace safety laws.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. The industry promoted leaded petrol despite knowing lead was poisonous.
x: The claim # The industry promoted leaded petrol despite knowing lead was poisonous. What the evidence shows # General Motors chemist Thomas Midgley developed tetraethyl lead in 1921; workers at plants died of lead poisoning, and Midgley himself was poisoned. Industry-funded scientist Robert Kehoe claimed for decades it was safe, until Clair Patterson’s research proved widespread lead pollution. Lead exposure lowered IQ of hundreds of millions of children. The last country stopped selling it in 2021.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. Tobacco companies knew smoking caused cancer and addiction but denied it.
x: The claim # Tobacco companies knew smoking caused cancer and addiction but denied it. What the evidence shows # Internal documents show companies knew by the 1950s–60s of the links to cancer and nicotine addiction, yet funded doubt and marketing. Lawsuits led to the 1998 Master Settlement Agreement.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. The FBI secretly spied on and sabotaged civil rights and political groups.
x: The claim # The FBI secretly spied on and sabotaged civil rights and political groups. What the evidence shows # The FBI’s counterintelligence programme infiltrated and disrupted groups including the Black Panthers and the civil rights movement; it sent Martin Luther King Jr. an anonymous letter urging him to kill himself. Activists who broke into an FBI office in 1971 exposed it.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. President Nixon's team burgled opponents and covered it up.
x: The claim # President Nixon’s team burgled opponents and covered it up. What the evidence shows # Men linked to Nixon’s re-election campaign were caught breaking into the Democratic headquarters. Secret White House tapes revealed Nixon obstructed justice; he resigned in 1974.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. The case for the 2003 invasion of Iraq rested on false claims of weapons of mass destruction.
x: The claim # The case for the 2003 invasion of Iraq rested on false claims of weapons of mass destruction. What the evidence shows # The US and UK claimed Iraq had active WMD programmes. No such weapons were found; key claims came from an unreliable source codenamed ‘Curveball’ and a plagiarised dossier. The war killed hundreds of thousands.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. Governments secretly collected the phone and internet data of millions of ordinary people.
x: The claim # Governments secretly collected the phone and internet data of millions of ordinary people. What the evidence shows # Edward Snowden, an NSA contractor, leaked documents showing programmes like PRISM collected data from tech companies, and allies including Britain’s GCHQ tapped internet cables.

d: Verdict: Partly true. The British deliberately gave smallpox-infected blankets to Native Americans.
x: The claim # The British deliberately gave smallpox-infected blankets to Native Americans. What the evidence shows # During Pontiac’s War, British officers at Fort Pitt gave Delaware envoys blankets from a smallpox hospital, recorded in a trader’s journal, and General Jeffery Amherst wrote approving the idea. Whether it caused an epidemic is unclear, as smallpox was already spreading. Most Native deaths from disease were not deliberate.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. The Soviet Union hid a famine killing millions, aided by Western journalists.
x: The claim # The Soviet Union hid a famine killing millions, aided by Western journalists. What the evidence shows # The New York Times correspondent Walter Duranty denied the famine and won a Pulitzer Prize; Welsh journalist Gareth Jones, who reported it, was discredited and later murdered in Manchuria in 1935.

d: Verdict: Disputed and debated. Churchill's government made the Bengal famine worse.
x: The claim # Churchill’s government made the Bengal famine worse. What the evidence shows # About 3 million died. The war cabinet refused repeated requests to divert grain shipments, while India exported rice; Churchill made racist remarks about Indians. Some historians argue wartime shipping shortages limited options and that local hoarding and policy failures were also to blame. Both sides agree British policy failed catastrophically.

d: Verdict: Unresolved. Bose did not die in the 1945 plane crash.
x: The claim # Bose did not die in the 1945 plane crash. What the evidence shows # Japanese and Indian inquiries (Shah Nawaz Committee 1956, Khosla Commission 1970) concluded he died after a crash at Taihoku. The Mukherjee Commission (2005) said he did not die in the crash, but the government rejected its report. Theories that he lived as ‘Gumnami Baba’ in Faizabad were rejected by the Sahai Commission (2022). Ashes at Renkoji Temple, Tokyo, have never been DNA tested.

d: Verdict: Unresolved. India's Prime Minister was poisoned in Tashkent.
x: The claim # India’s Prime Minister was poisoned in Tashkent. What the evidence shows # Shastri died hours after signing the Tashkent Declaration. Officially it was a heart attack; no post-mortem was done in India, his body reportedly turned bluish, and his family raised questions. Key witnesses (his doctor and servant) died in accidents before testifying to a parliamentary committee in 1977. No evidence of poisoning has been proven.

d: Verdict: Disputed. Lee Harvey Oswald did not act alone.
x: The claim # Lee Harvey Oswald did not act alone. What the evidence shows # The Warren Commission (1964) concluded Oswald acted alone. The House Select Committee (1979) said there was ‘probably’ a conspiracy based on acoustic evidence later discredited. Released files show the CIA hid information about its contacts with Oswald, fuelling suspicion, but no conclusive evidence of another gunman exists.

d: Verdict: Disputed. The Nazis set the fire themselves to seize power.
x: The claim # The Nazis set the fire themselves to seize power. What the evidence shows # Dutch communist Marinus van der Lubbe was arrested and executed. Hitler used the fire to suspend civil liberties. Historians debate whether van der Lubbe acted alone or Nazis were involved; either way it was the pretext for dictatorship.

d: Verdict: Documented fact (myth exaggerated). The government seized Tesla's secret 'death ray' plans when he died.
x: The claim # The government seized Tesla’s secret ‘death ray’ plans when he died. What the evidence shows # When Tesla died in January 1943, the Office of Alien Property took his belongings, and an MIT engineer, John Trump, examined his papers for the FBI, concluding they were speculative with no secret weapon. Most papers later went to the Tesla Museum in Belgrade. The secret super-weapon story is unproven.

d: Verdict: Mostly myth. Edison stole Tesla's work and cheated him.
x: The claim # Edison stole Tesla’s work and cheated him. What the evidence shows # Tesla claimed Edison promised $50,000 for improving dynamos and then joked he did not understand American humour. Edison did fight AC with fear campaigns. But AC patents were Tesla’s own and sold to Westinghouse; Edison did not steal them. Many Edison ‘inventions’ were developed by employees.

d: Verdict: Partly true. Antonio Meucci invented the telephone before Bell.
x: The claim # Antonio Meucci invented the telephone before Bell. What the evidence shows # Meucci demonstrated voice transmission and filed a caveat in 1871 but couldn’t afford to renew it. In 2002 the US House passed a resolution honouring him. Historians agree Bell’s patent was decisive but credit Meucci’s early work.

d: Verdict: Debunked. The Apollo Moon landings were faked in a studio.
x: The claim # The Apollo Moon landings were faked in a studio. What the evidence shows # Six missions landed 12 astronauts. Retroreflectors left on the Moon are still used by observatories; 382 kg of Moon rocks are studied worldwide; the Soviet Union, which tracked the missions, never disputed them; and lunar orbiters (including India’s Chandrayaan-2) have photographed landing sites.

d: Verdict: Debunked. Aliens or a lost civilisation built the pyramids.
x: The claim # Aliens or a lost civilisation built the pyramids. What the evidence shows # Archaeologists found workers’ villages, bakeries and cemeteries at Giza, tools, quarries, and the Wadi al-Jarf papyri — the diary of an official named Merer — describing transporting limestone for the Great Pyramid. Such claims often dismiss the achievements of non-European peoples.

d: Verdict: Partly true. The US government hides crashed alien spacecraft.
x: The claim # The US government hides crashed alien spacecraft. What the evidence shows # In 1947 debris found near Roswell came from Project Mogul, a top-secret balloon programme to detect Soviet nuclear tests. Area 51 is real and was acknowledged by the CIA in 2013 as a test site for the U-2 and other spy planes, explaining UFO sightings. There is no evidence of aliens.

d: Verdict: Proven forgery. Emperor Constantine gave the Pope authority over the western Roman Empire.
x: The claim # Emperor Constantine gave the Pope authority over the western Roman Empire. What the evidence shows # Popes used this document to claim political power for centuries. In 1440 Italian scholar Lorenzo Valla proved it a forgery from the 8th century by its anachronistic Latin.

t: Protocols of the Elders of Zion
d: Verdict: Proven forgery. A secret Jewish plan for world domination.
x: The claim # A secret Jewish plan for world domination. What the evidence shows # The text was fabricated by the Russian secret police, partly plagiarised from an 1864 French satire about Napoleon III. The Times exposed it in 1921, but Henry Ford and the Nazis spread it, fuelling antisemitism and the Holocaust.

d: Verdict: Proven hoax. A 'missing link' fossil found in England.
x: The claim # A ‘missing link’ fossil found in England. What the evidence shows # The skull was a human cranium combined with an orangutan jaw stained to look old. It misled science for 40 years until exposed in 1953.

d: Verdict: Debunked. The Titanic was swapped with its damaged sister ship Olympic for insurance fraud.
x: The claim # The Titanic was swapped with its damaged sister ship Olympic for insurance fraud. What the evidence shows # The wreck carries Titanic’s hull number 401 in its propeller; the ship was underinsured; and the theory has no documentary support.

d: Verdict: Partly true. The Nalanda library burned for three months.
x: The claim # The Nalanda library burned for three months. What the evidence shows # Nalanda was attacked around 1193 by Bakhtiyar Khalji’s forces, as Minhaj-i-Siraj records. The detail of the library burning for months comes from a later Tibetan account, and some historians argue Nalanda continued in reduced form for decades.

d: Verdict: Documented journey (curse is myth). The Kohinoor diamond was taken from India and brings misfortune to male owners.
x: The claim # The Kohinoor diamond was taken from India and brings misfortune to male owners. What the evidence shows # The diamond passed from the Kakatiyas (traditionally) to the Delhi Sultanate, Mughals, Nadir Shah (1739), Afghan rulers, Ranjit Singh, and was taken by the British East India Company in 1849 from 10-year-old Duleep Singh. It is in the British Crown Jewels; India, Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran have claimed it. The ‘curse’ is legend.

d: Verdict: Disputed. The atomic bombs were not needed to end the war.
x: The claim # The atomic bombs were not needed to end the war. What the evidence shows # The US Strategic Bombing Survey (1946) concluded Japan would likely have surrendered by late 1945 without the bombs or invasion; others argue the bombs and Soviet entry shocked Japan’s leaders into surrender. Some historians argue impressing the USSR was a motive.

d: Verdict: Myth. A lost advanced civilisation sank beneath the sea.
x: The claim # A lost advanced civilisation sank beneath the sea. What the evidence shows # Atlantis first appears in Plato’s dialogues Timaeus and Critias as a moral allegory. There is no archaeological evidence; some suggest the Thera eruption and Minoan Crete inspired it.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. Authorities ignored warnings before Gandhi's assassination.
x: The claim # Authorities ignored warnings before Gandhi’s assassination. What the evidence shows # On 20 January 1948 Madanlal Pahwa set off a bomb at Birla House as part of the same conspiracy; police knew of the group but failed to stop Godse ten days later. The Kapur Commission (1969) criticised police failures.

d: Verdict: Documented fact. The US government purged thousands of gay employees.
x: The claim # The US government purged thousands of gay employees. What the evidence shows # During the McCarthy era, thousands of gay and lesbian federal employees were fired as ‘security risks’. The US apologised in 2017 (State Department).

d: Verdict: Documented fact. Union Carbide ignored safety warnings and its chairman escaped trial.
x: The claim # Union Carbide ignored safety warnings and its chairman escaped trial. What the evidence shows # Safety systems were off or broken; earlier leaks had been reported. Chairman Warren Anderson was arrested, released on bail, flew out of India and never returned. A 1989 settlement of $470 million was criticised as too low.

t: New fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco and the pan-African origin of Homo sapiens
d: Re-dating of fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, using thermoluminescence on burnt flints gave an age of about 315,000 years, pushing back the origin of Homo sapiens by about 100,000 years. The skulls have modern faces but elongated braincases, suggesting the modern face evolved first and the round brain later. Because the site is in North Africa, far from East Africa, the authors argued our species emerged across the whole continent rather than in a single 'Garden of Eden'.

t: A draft sequence of the Neandertal genome
d: Svante Pääbo's team sequenced about 4 billion base pairs of Neanderthal DNA from bones in Croatia's Vindija Cave. Comparing it with modern genomes, they found that non-Africans carry 1–4% Neanderthal DNA (later refined to about 2%), proving interbreeding. The work helped earn Pääbo the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine and launched the field of palaeogenomics.

t: Human occupation of northern Australia by 65,000 years ago
d: Excavations at the Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land found ground-edge axes, grinding stones and ochre in layers dated by optically stimulated luminescence to about 65,000 years ago. If correct, people reached Australia earlier than thought, implying an earlier departure from Africa; some researchers argue the dates are too old.

t: Early Pleistocene presence of Acheulian hominins in South India
d: Cosmogenic nuclide dating at Attirampakkam near Chennai, Tamil Nadu, showed Acheulean hand-axes and cleavers about 1.5 million years old, among the oldest outside Africa. This showed that hand-axe-making hominins, probably Homo erectus, reached India very early.

t: Middle Paleolithic assemblages from the Indian subcontinent before and after the Toba super-eruption
d: At Jwalapuram in Andhra Pradesh, stone tools were found both below and above the 74,000-year-old Toba ash layer, with similar styles. The authors argued that humans in India survived the eruption, challenging the idea of a global volcanic winter that nearly wiped out humanity.

t: The formation of human populations in South and Central Asia
d: Analysing 523 ancient genomes, this study showed that South Asians descend mainly from a mixture of Indus Valley-related people (themselves a mix of Iranian-related farmers or hunter-gatherers and South Asian hunter-gatherers) and steppe pastoralists who arrived around 2000–1500 BCE. It supported the arrival of Indo-European languages from the steppe.

t: An ancient Harappan genome lacks ancestry from steppe pastoralists or Iranian farmers
d: The first genome from an Indus Valley person, a woman buried at Rakhigarhi in Haryana about 4,500 years ago, showed ancestry from South Asian hunter-gatherers and an early Iranian-related lineage that split before farming, with no steppe ancestry. This suggests farming in South Asia developed locally rather than being brought by West Asian farmers.

t: Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization
d: Using satellite data and sediment cores, the authors showed that the Harappan heartland relied on monsoon-fed rivers rather than a Himalayan-fed Sarasvati, and that a weakening monsoon after about 2000 BCE caused rivers to dry, leading people to move east toward the Ganga plain.

t: Oxygen isotope in archaeological bioapatites from India: implications to climate change and decline of Bronze Age Harappan civilization
d: Oxygen isotopes in animal bones and teeth from Bhirrana, Haryana, showed a weakening monsoon around 7,000–5,000 years ago and drought linked to the 4.2-kiloyear event. Harappans adapted by shifting crops but ultimately abandoned large cities.

d: This review in Science examined collapses of societies from the Maya to the Bronze Age, arguing that climate shocks combine with social vulnerabilities — inequality, rigid institutions and dependence on networks — to cause collapse, and that resilience depends on adaptability.

t: Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe
d: Genomes from 69 ancient Europeans showed that around 4,500 years ago, Yamnaya-related steppe herders replaced about 75% of the ancestry of Central Europe's Corded Ware people. This supported the steppe origin of Indo-European languages.

t: Development and disintegration of Maya political systems in response to climate change
d: A 2,000-year rainfall record from Yok Balum cave in Belize showed that wet periods coincided with Maya population growth and political expansion, while a long drying trend from 660 to 1000 CE correlated with warfare and the collapse of kingdoms.
x: What it found # A 2,000-year rainfall record from Yok Balum cave in Belize showed that wet periods coincided with Maya population growth and political expansion, while a long drying trend from 660 to 1000 CE correlated with warfare and the collapse of kingdoms.

t: Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age from 536 to around 660 AD
d: Tree rings from the Alps and Altai showed a cold period after eruptions in 536, 540 and 547, linking it to the Plague of Justinian, the fall of the Sasanians, Slavic migrations and the rise of the Arab empire.
x: What it found # Tree rings from the Alps and Altai showed a cold period after eruptions in 536, 540 and 547, linking it to the Plague of Justinian, the fall of the Sasanians, Slavic migrations and the rise of the Arab empire.

t: A draft genome of Yersinia pestis from victims of the Black Death
d: DNA from teeth of victims buried in London's East Smithfield plague pit (1348–1350) reconstructed the genome of the Black Death bacterium, showing it was ancestral to all modern plague strains and not fundamentally more virulent.
x: What it found # DNA from teeth of victims buried in London’s East Smithfield plague pit (1348–1350) reconstructed the genome of the Black Death bacterium, showing it was ancestral to all modern plague strains and not fundamentally more virulent.

d: Genotyping 132 people from 25 Indian groups, this study showed that most Indians descend from a mixture of two ancestral populations: 'Ancestral North Indians' related to West Eurasians and 'Ancestral South Indians' found nowhere else. The mixture varies by region and caste, and the paper showed that caste groups have been largely endogamous for thousands of years. It set the framework for later ancient-DNA studies of South Asia.

t: Genetic history of an archaic hominin group from Denisova Cave in Siberia
d: Sequencing the genome from a finger bone found in Denisova Cave revealed a previously unknown human group, the Denisovans, sister to Neanderthals. Melanesians (such as Papua New Guineans) carry about 4–6% Denisovan DNA, showing interbreeding with modern humans in Asia. It was the first time a human group was identified from DNA alone.

t: The complete mitochondrial DNA genome of an unknown hominin from southern Siberia
d: This paper first reported that mitochondrial DNA from the Denisova finger bone was distinct from both Neanderthals and modern humans, diverging about a million years ago. It triggered the discovery of the Denisovans.

t: A complete genome of a Neanderthal from the Altai Mountains
d: A high-quality genome from a Neanderthal woman's toe bone showed her parents were closely related (likely half-siblings), and revealed gene flow among Neanderthals, Denisovans, modern humans and an unknown 'superarchaic' population.

t: Altitude adaptation in Tibetans caused by introgression of Denisovan-like DNA
d: The EPAS1 gene variant that helps Tibetans live at high altitude without excessive red blood cells was inherited from Denisovans — a striking example of archaic genes helping modern humans adapt.

t: A late Middle Pleistocene Denisovan mandible from the Tibetan Plateau
d: A jawbone found by a monk in Baishiya Karst Cave in Xiahe, China, dated to at least 160,000 years ago, was identified as Denisovan using ancient proteins — the first Denisovan fossil outside Siberia, showing they lived at high altitude long before modern humans.

t: Late Middle Pleistocene Harbin cranium represents a new Homo species
d: Described the 146,000-year-old 'Dragon Man' skull from Harbin, with a large braincase and big molars, naming it Homo longi and arguing it was closer to Homo sapiens than Neanderthals were. Later protein analysis linked it to Denisovans.

t: A new small-bodied hominin from the Late Pleistocene of Flores, Indonesia
d: The description of Homo floresiensis, the 'Hobbit', a one-metre-tall human with a brain the size of a chimpanzee's from Liang Bua cave. It showed that small-brained humans survived until recently and sparked debate over island dwarfism.

d: Over 1,500 fossils from at least 15 individuals found deep in South Africa's Rising Star cave described a new species with a mix of primitive and modern features. Later dating showed it lived about 335,000–236,000 years ago, overlapping with early Homo sapiens.
